paragraphs.text: 1. Prologue of the Revelation, and that it is given to him through an angel.
2. The vision in which he beheld Jesus in the midst of seven lampstands.
3. What was written to the angel of the church of the Ephesians.
4. What was disclosed to the angel in the church of the Smyrnaeans.
5. What was signified to the angel of the church of the Pergamenes.
6. What was written to the angel of the church of Thyatira.
7. What was sent to the angel of the church in Sardis.
8. What was written to the angel of the church of the Philadelphians.
9. What was disclosed to the angel of the church of the Laodiceans.
10. On the door in heaven that he saw, and the throne, and the twenty-four elders, and the things shown after them.
11. On the book sealed with seven seals, in the hand of God, which no one of created nature is able to open.
12. On the Lamb with the seven horns, and how he opened it.
13. The opening of the first seal, signifying the apostolic teaching.
14. The opening of the second seal, showing the war of the unbelievers against the faithful.
15. The opening of the third seal, showing the falling away of those who have not believed in Christ.
16. The opening of the fourth seal, revealing the chastening scourges brought upon those who denied the Lord through lack of endurance.
17. The opening of the fifth seal, signifying the outcry of the souls of the saints to the Lord that the consummation may come.
18. The opening of the sixth seal, signifying the plagues brought on at the consummation.
19. On the hundred and forty-four thousand saved from the plague of the four angels.
20. On the innumerable multitude from the nations who reign together with Christ.
21. The opening of the seventh seal, showing angelic powers [?] to God the prayers of the saints as incense.
22. On the seven angels, at the trumpet of the first of whom both fire and blood are cast upon the earth.
23. On the second angel, at whose trumpet the living creatures in the sea perish.
24. The third angel makes the waters of the rivers bitter.
25. The fourth angel darkens a third of the light of the sun and the moon.
26. On the fifth angel, and the spiritual locusts coming up out of the abyss, and the varied appearance of their form.
27. On the sixth angel, and an explanation of the angels released at the Euphrates.
28. On the angel clothed with a cloud and a rainbow, who foretells the universal end.
29. How the Evangelist took the little scroll from the hand of the angel.
30. On Enoch and Elijah, who are to refute the Antichrist.
31. How, after being slain by the Antichrist, they will rise again and astound those who have been deceived.
32. On the seventh trumpet, and the saints who sing hymns to God concerning the coming judgment.
33. On the persecutions of the Church, both the earlier ones and those under the Antichrist.
34. On the war that took place between the holy angels and the evil powers, and the downfall of the dragon.
35. How the dragon does not cease persecuting the Church.
36. On the beast with ten horns and seven heads, one of which he said was as though slain.
37. On another beast having two horns, which brings people to the first.
38. On the name of the beast.
39. On the hundred and forty-four thousand standing with the Lamb on Mount Zion.
40. On an angel proclaiming beforehand the nearness of the coming judgment.
41. On a second angel, proclaiming the fall of Babylon.
42. On a third angel, securing the people of the Lord so that they do not accept the Antichrist.
43. That the one seated on the cloud brings to completion with the sickle the things that spring up from the earth.
44. On another angel, who gathers the vintage of the vine of bitterness.
45. On the seven angels who bring the plagues upon mankind before the consummation; and on the sea of glass, on which he beheld the saints.
46. How, when the first bowl is poured out, a sore comes upon [?].
47. The second plague, against those punished in the sea.
48. How through the third the rivers are turned into blood.
49. How through the fourth people are scorched with heat.
50. How through the fifth the kingdom of the beast is darkened.
51. How through the sixth the way across the Euphrates is opened for the kings from the rising of the sun.
52. How through the seventh hail and earthquake come upon mankind.
53. On one of the seven angels showing the Evangelist the destruction of the harlot city; and on the seven heads and the ten horns.
54. How the angel interpreted the mystery he had seen.
55. On another angel, announcing the fall of Babylon, and on a heavenly voice commanding flight from the city, and on the loss of the delights she had formerly possessed.
56. On the hymn of the saints, and the threefold alleluia they sang over the destruction of Babylon.
57. On the mystical marriage, and the supper of the Lamb.
58. How the Evangelist beheld with fear Christ on horseback with the angelic hosts.
59. On the Antichrist, and those cast with him into Gehenna.
60. How Satan was bound from the coming of Christ until the consummation, and on the thousand years.
61. On the thrones prepared for those who have kept the confession of Christ intact.
62. What the first resurrection is, and what the second death is.
63. On Gog and Magog.
64. On the one seated on the throne, and the general resurrection and judgment.
65. On the new heaven and earth, and the Jerusalem above.
66. On what was said by the one who was seen seated on the throne.
67. On the angel who shows him the city of the saints and measures its wall together with the gates.
68. On the pure river that was seen flowing from the throne.
69. That Christ is the God of the prophets and the Master of all things.
70. On the trustworthiness of the things beheld by the Apostle.
71. How he was commanded not to seal up, but to proclaim the [?]
72. How the Church and the Spirit within her call for the glorious appearing of Christ; and on the curse to which those are subject who tamper with the book as though it had no authority.
Prologue of the Revelation, and that it was given to him through an angel.

The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his servants the things that must soon take place; and he made it known by sending it through his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ . . . all that he saw and all that he heard, and the things that must take place after these.

Some of the more ancient writers treat this book as spurious, as not from the tongue of John the beloved, and attribute it to someone else. But this is not so. For Gregory, who bears the same title as John, counted it among the genuine books, saying, "as the Revelation of John teaches me." When John begins to write his Gospel, he opens by speaking of Christ as God: "In the beginning," he says, "was the Word." And the opening of his Epistle holds to the same theology, setting forth "that which was from the beginning."
The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him.

It is as if he were saying: "This Revelation of mine was given by the Father to the Son, and given by the Son to us his servants." For he began with the humbler aspects of the dispensation and advanced to those more befitting God. Peter, the divine apostle, did the same in his confession: after saying the name "Christ," he added the most perfect title, "the Son of God," since "Christ" alone could not adequately express the dispensation. In the same way John now joins to the name "Christ" the words "to his servants," and so hints at the divinity in Christ. For whose servants were the saints, if not God's? To him it is also said, "All things are your servants." And by adding that Christ did not carry out this initiation into the mysteries in person, but through his angel, he showed the truthfulness of the one who received the Revelation.

A revelation is the disclosure of hidden mysteries, when the ruling part of the soul is illuminated, whether through divine dreams or, while awake, by a divine shining. This divine apostle says that this Revelation was "given," handling his account in a more human manner. He does not proceed here as he does in his Gospel and his Epistle, where he frames his discourse chiefly from the more divine attributes of Christ and dwells on them. Here he starts from the humbler ones, so as to show clearly that both, I mean the more divine and the human, are seen in the one and same Christ, as befits him. For through the ministering angel, and through the name given to those who learn, "servants," he displays the greatness of Christ's divinity, as it is also said, "All things are your servants." He promises that what is revealed will come to pass "soon." He does not say this at random. He is measuring human things against divine things, for which even what is accomplished over long ages and thousands of years is reckoned "as yesterday's day, and as a watch in the night." Or one may take "soon" more ambitiously, as showing that the things revealed will come to pass without delay, since no length of time can hinder their accomplishment, just as today is not [?] a prolongation of yesterday; unless, when what is stored up arrives in due season, it is fitting to dismiss it, since no slowness remains in the matter as regards its reception [?].

He says that the oracle came through an angel to his servant, the servant who bore witness to the word of God and to his testimony. He used the same figure in the Gospels to establish the truth of his own teaching, when he said, "This is the disciple who bears witness to these things and wrote them, and we know that his testimony is true." As there, so here he says that he is a witness of the testimony shown to him through the Revelation given him by Christ. By "testimony" he means a solemn declaration: he solemnly declares to those whom he addresses, for his own acquittal, that he is himself a witness of the divine word shown to him through the Revelation. And what he was to declare and proclaim for his own acquittal was both the things that are and the things that will be, which, as befits a prophet, concern both the present time and the future.
All that he saw and all that he heard.

In another copy these words are added: "and all that he heard, and the things that are, and the things that must take place after these." He says: Christ revealed these things to me as a master to his servant, so that through what I saw I might solemnly testify and proclaim, for the conversion of those who hear, both the things that are and lie hidden from men, and the things that are to come. For he saw both prophetically. This is clear from the words "the things that are, and the things that must take place." These point to the present time and the future, and the excellence of the prophets also lies in them.
Blessed is the one who reads and those who hear the words of the prophecy and keep what is written in it.

With great foresight he pronounces blessed not only those who read (for then many who read would be blessed), but also those who hear, that is, with a hearing that issues in action. The Lord too bore witness that true hearing belongs to such people, when he said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." And who is this? The one whose hearing is ready to keep and guard what has been said as divine laws. He has been trained to live spiritually, not like the natural man, who chooses to live by the senses like the irrational animals. He has scorned every baser pleasure that belongs to this life we are bound up with, and has turned over to what is divine in us, and so he has come to belong wholly to the goodness and care that the Creator showed from the beginning toward the creature he made in his own image.
For the time is near.

The time of blessedness is near. It is near because of the burning love of those who keep God's commandments. For this reason they gain unflagging zeal in these things, and it would not be reckoned as a long stretch of time or as a delay [?]. The patriarch Jacob is a witness: his seven years of endurance for the sake of taking his wives were counted as a single day. Or the time of the prizes is near because the shortness of the present life is measured against the boundlessness of the age to come.

John to the seven churches that are in Asia: grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits that are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.

By the seven churches, through the mystical meaning of the number seven, he signified the multitude of churches everywhere that belong to the present life. In this life the seven-day cycle, once it had begun, revealed that its power dwells in this corruptible creation and pervades all of it. Philo, that most contemplative Jewish man, also thinks it not superfluous to echo this in his discourse on the philosophy of Moses. And the blessed John now shows that the churches have guardian angels equal to them in number.

The phrase "from him who is and who was and who is to come" is equivalent to "from the God of all, and from our Word." For the Father names himself "the one who is" when he speaks to Moses on the mountain: "I am the one who is." The "was" was put forward by this God-wise evangelist in his Gospel, when he said, "In the beginning was the Word," and in the first of his catholic Epistles, when he wrote of the Word of life, "that which was from the beginning." And he calls the divine Spirit "the one who is to come," because the Spirit was not only sent by the Father on the day of Pentecost but always comes to those worthy to receive him, also through holy baptism.
Peace from him who is.

Another interpretation. Perhaps it is not unacceptable to understand "who is and who was and who is to come" in this way as well, as referring to the Father, since he contains in himself the beginning, the middle and the end of all that exists.
And from the seven spirits.

Some have taken the seven spirits to be the operations of the Holy Spirit. But it is more acceptable to understand them as angels. We should not, however, reckon them equal in honor with the almighty Trinity just because they are mentioned together with it. They are servants and ministers, if indeed we are to believe the prophets, who testify that all things are his servants, and especially David, the ancestor of God, who says, "Bless him, all you angels of God, mighty in strength, who do his word." Someone might say that to mention the divine and the angelic nature together shows that the ministering being is equal in honor with the Almighty, the cause of all creation's existence. Such a person does not know, not even remotely; rather, I think, he is unaware that the one who serves is accustomed to be with the master. Paul uses this very thought in his first Epistle to Timothy, where he says something like this: "I charge you before God and the elect angels." So this passage follows the same usage. Moreover, the addition here of "which are before the throne of God" bears witness to their rank as household servants and ministers, not to equality of honor.
The faithful witness.

We must supply "who is," so that it reads: "and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness." Note also that earlier he wrote of the Word before he took flesh, when he said "who was," and now he speaks of him as incarnate, saying "and from Jesus Christ." He does not divide him into two by adding "and from Jesus Christ." Rather, he testifies both of these things of one and the same person: that he is the Word of the Father, and that he became flesh. This is what the name "Christ" is meant to show. According to the blessed Paul, this Christ bore witness as a witness before Pontius Pilate, when he said to him, "My kingdom is not of this world." By these words he leads us to understand that the one seen as a man is also God, and that he declares this very thing. He is a witness, then, for this reason; and "faithful" stands for "true," God and man. Therefore he died as man but rose as God. For he did not rise like those who were raised by divine power through others and died again. He rose by his own power, as God, and so was the first to begin the endless and eternal return to life that is hoped for from him and through him. Therefore he is also called the firstborn of the dead, since he alone began for us such a grace of good things.

Christ is the ruler of the kings of the earth, since Daniel too said to the Babylonian king that "the Most High reigns and is lord over the kingdom of men." If this is understood and seen to refer to the divine lordship, what argument can stand against it? Some deny that everything said of the supersubstantial Trinity in a manner befitting God applies to each of the three hypostases and fits each one, apart from those things that produce their procession, that is, their distinction as hypostases. Instead, they rashly venture to rave that each of the three hypostases withdraws into a separate divine operation proper to itself. And they say this although Gregory, divine in discourse, took the words "who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty" as referring to the Son, since names befitting God fit the three hypostases both in common and individually. This is clear also from the thrice-holy hymn of the Seraphim. According to the Gospel, we learn that it is spoken of the Son. Paul, preaching in Acts, assigned it to the Spirit. And we, following the tradition of the fathers, assign it to the Father in the awesome and bloodless sacrifice, as the blessed Epiphanius explains in his discourse on the Holy Spirit.
And the ruler of the kings of the earth.
He reigns not only over those on earth but also over those in heaven. Here he speaks of the earthly kings; further on he shows him reigning also over the holy orders in heaven.
To him who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father: to him be the glory and the might forever and ever. Amen.

This is written in two ways, with different meanings. A person is "washed" when he is cleansed of stains and spots; a person is "loosed" when he is freed from the charges against him. With "made" we must supply the relative pronoun "who," so that it reads "who made." If it is not understood in this way, the solecism will make the phrase meaningless. So the sense should not be carried on in the preceding dative case but introduced in the nominative.

Another interpretation. What follows will show how the construction of this passage should be understood in full. It is expressed in the figure about to be named, which is called alloiosis, or variation. This occurs when the sense that follows is not brought in in the same case as what came before, but is shifted to suit the new sense being introduced. The dative case was used first in "to him who washed us," and then he added "made us," leaving out the relative article. The full form would be: "to him who washed us in his blood and made us." If the following sense had been brought in in the same case, as in "to him who also made us," we would have no question to deal with here. But since he expressed an action with the verb "made," we necessarily turn to the nominative case, because we want to learn who did it. And how could we find this out unless the nominative case were taken? So the nominative allowed the missing article to be understood in full, thus: "who also made us a kingdom," that is, raised us to royal glory. What that glory is, the written phrase that follows is sufficient to show.
To him be the glory and the might.

The construction of the passage runs back from the last words to the first, thus: "To him be the glory and the might, to him who loved us and washed us in his own blood." And how could he not have loved us, when he gave himself as our ransom, slain like a lamb, and washed us with the [?] and water from his cross, that is, cleansed us of the filth of our sins? He did not stop his kindness toward us there, but also gave us a kingdom. And what is this kingdom? It is the glory given to us by Christ, by which we became priests of God and prophets, though we had contributed nothing worthy of so great a God-given good, a truly divine gift. Through these gifts we come to possess glory not only in the present life, but also good hope of attaining the glory to come.

Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. Yes, amen. "I am the Alpha and the Omega," says the Lord God, who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.

He says that the one who was slain here like a lamb, and washed us with his blood and loosed us from our sins, will himself come again. He will not come as he did the first time, secretly and veiled, which the prophet David hinted at in the rain falling noiselessly on a fleece. He will come openly and manifestly, in the glory of the Father, so that every eye will see him as the impartial judge of all. Clouds are mentioned here too, as at his ascent from earth to heaven: Luke writes in the Acts that a cloud received the Lord. And Mark, in the Gospel he wrote, has the Lord himself say of himself, "And they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven." The clouds here may signify the lofty angelic powers, because of their lightness, just as David, the ancestor of God, places clouds beneath the divine as the chariot he mounts. Or they may signify people who have chosen to live a godly and spiritual life. The same David says of them, "At the brightness before him the clouds passed by." Amos and Isaiah speak of the same people: "Who are these that fly like clouds, and like young eagles?" Clearly he says this figuratively of those who live in a way that pleases God. This meaning should rather be accepted, since the present text is enough to prove it: it says that the judge comes with the clouds, not that he is carried on them. Paul agrees with this when he affirms that "we will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air," meaning those who have lived as Paul did, so as to be with the Lord always. But if some think it better to take these as actual clouds, like the one the account describes covering the Lord and his disciples on Mount Tabor, there is no need to quarrel about it. He says that when the Lord comes in such glory he will be seen by every eye, both by those who faithfully hoped for his coming and by those who gave up hope of it. The former will rejoice; the latter will mourn, all their people together. By those who pierced him he means those who wounded him with the nails and the spear at his passion on the cross, and with them their descendants who blasphemously attack him. He confirms the certainty of what has been said and sets his seal on it with the words "Yes, and amen." "Yes," taken from Greek usage, affirms that what has been said cannot be changed; "amen," from the Hebrews, is added to show that nothing can prevent the threatened things from coming to pass.
Who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.

Above he called him "who is and who was and who is to come," and now "the Almighty." We showed that this is none other than Christ, since it is pious, not impious, to apply what is said in a manner befitting God of the One who exists supersubstantially in the Trinity to each of the hypostases as well, without distinction. He brings this same one in again after he has made known his final coming and how it will happen [?], and after he has also made these further things known.
I am the Alpha and the Omega.

He is Alpha because he is the beginning, since alpha is the beginning of the letters of the alphabet; he is Omega because he is their end. And who would not understand that beginning and end mean "first" and "last"? By "first" we understand "without beginning," and by "last" we understand "without end." Since nothing among humans is without beginning or end, he loosely used the beginning and end familiar to us in place of "without beginning" and "without end." He also said this through Isaiah: "I, the Lord God, am first, and I am also hereafter." And so that no one would suppose that this beginning was brought into being from nothing, he now adds, "who is and who was and who is to come." What these words mean has already been said: that he is everlasting at both the beginning and the end, at the beginning without any lack, at the end without any successor. The one who is all this is also Almighty, as the ruler of all creation, both visible and intelligible, co-eternal with the Father, and rendering to each according to his works. A little earlier he dwelt on the humbler and human things; now he touches also on the more divine things, those worthy of God. He also does this at the beginning of this treatise, but not as clearly there. Here he speaks boldly, as is fitting when speaking of divine things, taking his cue from the holy prophets.
The vision in which he saw Jesus in the midst of seven lampstands.

I, John, your brother and your partner in the affliction, the kingdom and the endurance that are in Christ Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ. I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet, saying: "Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches: to Ephesus, to Smyrna, to Pergamum, to Thyatira, to Sardis, to Philadelphia and to Laodicea."

He calls himself a brother and a partner in the afflictions that he was suffering at the hands of the persecutors of true religion because of the word of God and his preaching. This is why he too had been condemned to live on the island of Patmos. But he shares in the kingdom just as he shares in the afflictions, for afflictions suffered here for Christ's sake win the kingdom. So if he shows himself a partner in every respect, he can rightly claim to be trusted about what he saw and heard.
"Because of the word of God."

By "the word of God" and "testimony" he means the Gospel that he wrote. Eusebius, son of Pamphilus, records in his Chronicle that Domitian exiled him to the island of Patmos. "I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and I heard a voice."

"In the Spirit" is added to show that nothing that acted on him had to do with human need. Rather, what he experienced belongs to those who are seized by divine possession. And it happened on the Lord's day, which bears the memorial of Christ's resurrection. So it is fitting that nothing tending toward new worldly business had any part in the revelation. He heard the "voice like a trumpet" behind him so that, as was due, its fiery and piercing sound might be given to the whole church. He is commanded to write down what he sees and send it to only seven churches. This is not because there were only that many cities in Asia. He is told to do this for those cities because they had become hearers of the gospel preaching. Or else, as has been explained more fully elsewhere, the number seven corresponds to the present perishable age, which clearly ends in the sabbath rest of the age to come. This is why the great Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, wrote of seven heavens and of seven angels who are preeminent above the rest.

Another interpretation. When the divine prophets speak of seeing and hearing, we must not understand these as acts of the senses. They are more divine impressions. Amos and Isaiah speak of these: "He has appointed for me morning by morning an ear to hear, and the instruction of the Lord opens my ears." This belongs not to the man according to the flesh but to the man according to the spirit, who usually remains in God's care and is ruler of the whole world of the senses. Here the prophet doubled "morning," just as other prophets also speak of morning: "Hear my voice," they say, "and in the morning I will stand before you," and "toward morning, morning." He does this not idly. By naming the time he shows great eagerness, for this is the very time at which divine workings are accustomed to linger.

And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me. And when I turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the middle of the seven lampstands one like a Son of Man. He was clothed in a robe that reached to his feet and girded at the breasts with a golden belt. His head and his hair were white like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire, and his feet were like burnished bronze, as though fired in a furnace. His voice was like the sound of many waters. In his right hand he held seven stars, and a sharp two-edged sword came out of his mouth. And his face was like the sun shining in its strength.

The voice was not something the senses could perceive. It was like the impressions made on the ruling spirit of the prophets. He shows this when he says, "I turned," not to hear but to see. For spiritual hearing is the same as seeing, or vision. This is also why he said that the voice spoke to him, instead of saying that it left impressions on the one who received it. To complete the sense, we must supply an article with these words, so that it reads: "the voice of the one who was speaking with me." For what is seen is not the voice but the speaker. It is as if he said: "I turned to see the one whose voice was speaking with me." Construed in this way, the phrase is clear and lacks nothing.
"Seven lampstands."

The seven lampstands are likewise the seven churches, as he will say later on, and he is told to write to them. He called them lampstands rather than lamps, because a lampstand has no light of its own. It only carries the lamp, and the lamp has the light. This is why the holy Apostle Paul urges the teachers who are conformed to Christ "to be like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life", that is, having received the pure light from Christ, who overflows with it. To Christ it is said, "You give light wonderfully from the everlasting mountains" (perhaps meaning the angelic powers), and "Send out your light and your truth," and "the light of your face, O Lord", for he enlightens the faithful spiritually. Since they have come to share in such light, then, they are urged to give light to others with the light of the knowledge of God.
"Golden."

He says the lampstands appeared golden because those who were found worthy to receive the divine radiance are precious and surpassing. Paul calls them lights, since they hold the word of life. Lampstands carry lamps. They have no light of their own, but in a way they share with those whose lot is to give light of themselves.
"And in the middle of the seven lampstands one like a Son of Man."

He appears in this way because he promised to dwell and walk among us. For our sake he humbled himself, even to the form of a servant, and became the fruit of the womb of a mother who knew no marriage. He was clothed in a robe reaching to his feet and girded at the breasts "as a priest," it says, "according to the order of Melchizedek," not according to the order of Aaron. For the worship he handed down to us is not according to the law of Moses. It is the new worship "according to the order of Melchizedek." The divine Paul also speaks of this, saying that Christ has been given to us as high priest and apostle. He offers himself in sacrifice and presents our confession of faith to the Father and the Spirit.
"And girded at the breasts."

Why is he girded at the breasts and not at the loins? Because he is not open to the appetites below the belly. For other people it is salutary to bind those appetites tightly. So he is not girded at the part that those appetites can reach, because God, beyond all reason, was united with it. He is girded at the chest and the breasts, so that his love for humankind may hold in check the boundlessness of the just and divine wrath. This also shows the truth that girds the two covenants, that is, the Master's breasts, by which the faithful are nourished. Of this it is also said: "He shall be girded with righteousness about his loins and anointed with truth on his sides." His loins are girded with righteousness because he is not carried beyond the limits of rational nature. His sides are anointed with truth, as if with divine oil, because he openly shows the truth of his love for the creature he made.
"A golden belt."

He sees the belt as golden, whereas the priests under the law wore garments of many colors. For the difference had to be shown between servants and the shadowy law on the one hand, and the truth on the other.
"His head and his hair were white."

For the precious mystery of Christ, though it is new in its appearing and came about for our sake, is yet before the ages in God's good pleasure. This is why Paul says of it: "the mystery hidden from the ages, but now revealed to his saints." This is what the white hair, like snow, signifies.
"His eyes were like a flame of fire."

His eyes either show that he is full of light, like a flame. This is why Christ says, "I am the light of the world." Or else they threaten burning and punishment against the churches to which the Revelation is sent, because they do not fully follow his laws.
"And his feet were like burnished bronze."

Following Gregory, that divine man of words, we must understand Jesus the God-man as having feet, because he did not come to live among us in bare divinity but through the flesh. The bronze, truly gold-like, signifies the divine nature. Because bronze rings out, it is also taken to mean the preaching. The divine apostles are also the feet of Christ and the foundations of the church. They too were shown to be pure in the fire of trials, though before this they were only moderately so. Christ the teacher was tested by the unbelief of the Jews. In the same way, the apostles displayed their proven worth, as if through fire, in the savagery of the gentiles. The divine Paul, writing to the Corinthians, is a trustworthy witness that Christ too is the foundation: "No one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Christ." As for "burnished bronze" (chalkolibanon), we should understand it either as the bronze mined on Mount Lebanon, since he says that the one who became man is likened to it, or as the bronze-colored frankincense (libanos) that physicians call "male," which gives off fragrant vapors when it touches fire. The bride in the Song shows that both Christ and his divine apostles are fragrant, when she says: "The scent of your garments is beyond all spices." And Christ the bridegroom himself says to the bride about himself: "I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys." So much for Christ. But his apostles are also fragrant. This is why Paul says: "We are the fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing." He fittingly says that the voice resounds like many waters. For Christ's voice is shared with the Spirit, and through the Spirit's working "rivers also flowed from his belly," as the prophetic word says. "And a fountain shall come out of the house of the Lord and water the torrent of the rushes." Who could doubt that here "the house of God" means those who have made themselves ready for the working of the divine Spirit? They have also said that they are temples of God and members in part. No one would doubt it except someone who has willfully ignored these divine and holy oracles. And who will reject the piercing sound that goes out into all the earth? No one, unless perhaps the swinish man who demands that spiritual and divine illuminations work in ways the senses can perceive.
"And in his right hand he held seven stars."

He himself will explain later on that these seven stars are angels, and he will say that they preside over each church. The divine Gregory says the same in his Farewell Oration, drawing his proof for us from this Revelation of John.

He calls the angels stars because of the abundant light of Christ poured out in them. He says that they are also found worthy to be held in the right hand, as though resting in the most honored position. The two-edged sword comes out of his mouth. Yet the ancestor of God commanded him to gird it on his mighty thigh. This is because at that time vengeance against those who break the laws of the gospel had not yet been taught. So he kept the sword hanging on his thigh for the time being, to show that punishment was postponed. But now the sword that comes out of the mouth hints that punishment is fully ready for those under the new covenant who are disobedient. They rush swiftly into a danger to the soul that cannot be escaped, namely being cut in two. The Lord also pointed to this in the Gospels when he threatened that the negligent servant would be cut in two. And Paul says that the punishing word of God is "living and active, and sharper than a sword," since it comes out of the mouth, "piercing even to bones and marrow." It does not do so in a way the senses perceive. This is why John also records the sword as sharp, which amounts to the same thing as Paul's sharpest sword. He shines like the sun in his power, since he is also "the sun of righteousness," according to the prophet Malachi, "enlightening everyone who comes into the world." He does not give light like a transparent body that the senses perceive, but spiritually. This is why he added "in its power." It is as if he were saying that Christ's light works by power. It does not light up bodily sight. It shines spiritually on the eyes of the soul.

When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. And he laid his right hand on me, saying: "Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last, and the living one. I was dead, and see, I am alive forever and ever. Amen. And I hold the keys of death and of Hades."

When the holy prophets see a vision, they are usually struck with amazement. This shows the lowliness of human beings and how far divine things surpass and rise above human things. Joshua son of Nun experienced this before the commander of the Lord's army, and so did Daniel, the man of desires, at the visions he saw. So now the Evangelist undergoes something similar. He says that he was strengthened when the saving right hand of the Son of God touched him. With encouragement, the Son addressed his divine word to him and revealed himself as the first and the last. He is first in his divine nature and last in his saving coming to us. He is the living one: though he was put to death for our sake, he lives all the same and holds the keys of death and Hades. Since John has such a helper, he bids him not to be afraid. He has entrusted himself to the One who lives through endless ages, so he must not shrink back, but write without holding anything back what he saw, what is, and what is to come, that is, things past and present. These belong among the things that exist, not among those that have passed into nonexistence. Together with these he is to write what is going to happen, so that those who come after may know it.
"Do not be afraid."

The Evangelist was struck by the sight and lay like a dead man at the feet of the one he saw. He says that he heard, "Do not be afraid." Holy John could not have survived the shock if the saving right hand had not touched him, the hand that worked very many wonders by touch alone. "For I am," he says, "the one who in the last times lived among you in the flesh for the salvation of you all, and the firstborn of all creation. How then could you suffer any harm from my appearing? I am living and the fountain of life. For your sake I became dead, but I came back to life again, having trampled down death. How then could you, who are living, become dead because of me and my vision? I also hold the keys of death and Hades, and with them I give life, bring down to Hades and bring up again. And as the prophet says, 'mine are the ways out of death.' I would not send my worshippers to death before their due time, before I have set them to write what is worth knowing."

"Write what you have seen, what is, and what is to happen after this. As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are seven churches."

Of the things the saint saw, some have already happened. They had already reached their end in their own time, yet they had not passed into nonexistence. This is why he said of them, "what is." Others are about to pass, and others are going to happen, as the account will say later on.
"The mystery of the seven stars."

Because he made clear to him who the seven stars, the lamps and the lampstands are, John is also taught what must be said to each church. He calls the angels who oversee the churches stars, since they are supplied with light by the Sun of righteousness himself. One of the wise men outside the faith held the same view about the visible sun, that the stars receive their light from it. The lamps are the holy men appointed to be enriched with Christ's light and to scatter the darkness of ignorance in the present life. The churches are the lampstands, since they hold up these lights. These lights are teachers, as Paul says, holding fast the word of life. All the lampstands are golden because the faith within them is unalloyed and precious. As we said, Gregory the Theologian also confirmed by quoting this passage that an angel presides over each church. Having revealed these things, and what the one receiving these divine oracles must solemnly declare to each of the churches, he goes on to say how John must deal with each. He must censure the church that has gone wholly outside the divine aim and praise those that run together in the course of the gospel. He must correct those that stumble in part by sending them the remedies of mutual admonition. And who decrees these things but "he who wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth"? And to whom did he disclose them? To the inspired Evangelist John, through the Revelation now before us.
"The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches."

He speaks to the church through an angel, just as one might speak to a pupil through his tutor. He knows that a teacher tends to take his pupil's successes and failures as his own. It is also likely that the seven stars in the right hand of the one who utters these oracles show that the ordering of the whole universe lies in Christ's right hand, as is sung in the Psalms: "In his hand are the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his."
What was written to the angel of the church of the Ephesians.

To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: These are the words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands. I know your works, your toil and your endurance, and that you cannot bear evil people; you have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not [?], and found them to be false. You have endurance, and you have borne up for the sake of my name, and have not grown weary.

By the angel of Ephesus he means the church there. For the presiding angel had not sinned, so as to need to hear "Repent". He is in the Lord's right hand because of his holiness, being a star, and this is a sign of the shining brilliance of light that comes from the purity of his nature. What need was there to write to one who was present in the right hand of the speaker? And being a spiritual being, he had no need of bodily hearing either. Then too, as the holy guide of the vision goes on, he tells not the angels but the churches to hear what the Holy Spirit says, which makes the point plain. In the same way, throughout the rest of this book, wherever "Write these things to the angel of this church" is found, it is likewise clear that he commands the words to be written not to the angel but about the church.
Who walks among the seven golden lampstands.

This is like saying: these are the words of him who cares for, holds fast and holds together both the angels in heaven and human beings on earth. For these, as has already been said, are the seven stars and the golden lampstands and lamps, and in their midst is the Lord, who promised to dwell in them and walk among them.
I know your works.

"I know," he says, "and nothing has escaped me, who fashioned your hearts one by one and understand all your works. I know that you cannot bear to listen to the wicked, since you hate wickedness, and that you tested those who call themselves apostles and found them to be false apostles." For the Christians in Ephesus were fulfilling the divine command that says not to believe every spirit but to test it, that is, to test the teaching authority these men claimed, whether it accorded with the ordinance of the gospel. They themselves went on restricting themselves to what was barely needed. They did not revel in food and drink and marriages, preferring a life of pleasure to a life of self-control, as did the followers of Cerinthus, who lived at the same time as the Apostle and Evangelist and proclaimed spurious doctrines.
And you have endurance.

"You have toiled," he says, "and endured, and you gave up in the face of nothing that arose against you for my name's sake." This was very fitting, for it is said, "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." It is likely that the false apostles had abused them, yet the church did not think at all of paying them back, but bore with them as one bears with paralysed limbs.
And you have borne up.

"You have borne up" stands for "you have endured". "You have not grown weary" stands for "you did not give up": as it were, you did not lose heart, did not betray, did not desert your post, for my name's sake. By "name" he means glory and renown, as also in the verse "How wonderful is your name in all the earth." And how is it not full of renown that Christians are not eager to repay evil with evil? As the divine Paul also urges, saying, "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers."

But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember then from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you soon and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent. Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.

He approves of the church in two things, namely its endurance of the burden and its refusal to strive against those who opposed it in its toil, and he blames it for this one thing. Between the two, the toil and the endurance, he set his praise for its estrangement from the wicked, along with its testing of the false apostles and of the shameful deeds of the Nicolaitans. But he also blamed its neglect in providing for its neighbours, and he enjoins it to restore this, saying, "Do the works you did at first, in righteousness." "For it does not escape me," he says, "either what your good deeds were at first, or that you have cut off your love toward those in need. Come back, then, now that I have taught you what you have left undone."
I will come to you soon.

"I will come" does not signify movement from place to place on the part of God, who fills all things, but his turning from long-suffering to punishment. The removal of a church is its being stripped of divine grace. Because of this the Church is tossed in surge and storm by evil spirits and by the vile people who serve them, so that the people who hold it together say, "My eye is troubled with anger," and, "My heart is troubled within me."
"Yet this you have," he says, "you hate the works of the Nicolaitans."

Among the painful things he also puts things that lead to good cheer, so that the Church may not be swallowed up by excessive grief. So he says, "I find you ready to repent, since I see that you share my hatred of the Nicolaitans." These are named after Nicolaus, one of the seven deacons. And what kind of shameful deeds they committed, the book of the Panarion by the divine Epiphanius of Cyprus will show.
Another interpretation: some have also taken the removal of the lampstand to mean the episcopal throne of Ephesus, which yielded its precedence to Constantinople.

"This good thing you have," he says, "you hate the works of the Nicolaitans." Thus far the divine message; then he adds on his own account, "Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches."
Let anyone who has an ear hear.

Every human being has a bodily ear, but only one inspired by God has a spiritual one. This is what was given as an addition to Isaiah, and David, the ancestor of God, was granted to hear readily. For this reason he gratefully sings, "At the hearing of the ear he heeded me," as if to say: he likened my longing to that of those to whom hearing brings what is worthy of praise. He says that the Spirit speaks these things either because he himself was moved by the Spirit as he set forth the contents of the Revelation, or because he calls Christ "Spirit" insofar as he is God and is understood as God, just as he is called Son of Man insofar as he is man and is understood as man. That God is called Spirit is shown by the words of Christ himself to the Samaritan woman, when he declares, "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth," and so on. And what does the Spirit say?
To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life.

"To the one who conquers" in the war against the demons, which is usually stirred up through the passions inborn in us. "Tree of life" is meant figuratively: the tree in the middle of Paradise. By Paradise we must understand the blessed and everlasting life, in which wisdom is poured out in abundance, of which Solomon also says, "She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her." And the present Evangelist says of Christ that he is God and eternal life, in whose [?] the saints will come to enjoy the endless life to come.
Of my God.

Let no one who hears this be scandalized. All lowly things befit the dispensation of the God-man undertaken for our salvation. For in the Gospels too he says, "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God," meaning that he is his Father by nature and ours by adoption.
What was revealed to the angel of the church of the Smyrnaeans.

And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: These are the words of the first and the last, who was dead and came to life. I know your works, your affliction and your poverty, yet you are rich. I know the slander of those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan. Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, so that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have affliction. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be harmed by the second death.
It has already been made clear that these commands are addressed not to an angel but to the assembly of the faithful, which is the Church.

An arrangement of the passage quoted above, in brief paraphrases, with what is missing filled in for the sake of clarity: These things are declared by Jesus Christ, who by nature is before the ages, and in the last days became man out of love for humankind. Out of that love he endured the experience of death for three days, and rose again, giving us hope of a return to life that will never fail.

Christ is first and last, as God and man: first by his divine nature, last because he became man for our sake in the last times. The same one was dead for three days, and then through his resurrection opened for us the way of life. And what does he say? "I know your works, your affliction and your poverty," which you endure for my sake, scourged by the unbelievers and stripped of your possessions. So when you are afflicted and poor, do not say, as they did, "Why have we fasted, and you did not see? Why have we humbled our souls, and you took no notice?" For even if these things are so, yet you are rich, since you have among spiritual things the treasure hidden in the field of your heart, which is Christ. Through him you are rich, because you have him as your protector, who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake.
I know your works.

That is, your good works, and the affliction and poverty that came upon you because of them, brought on you out of envy by the blaspheming Jews, the devil's fellow-workers. They are Jews in name only, but in truth they are a synagogue of the devil. "But even if you are poor because of their abuse, you are rich, since you are devoted to me, the dispenser of all good things. So fear none of what the devil's fellow-workers are about to bring upon you, the distress of being shut up in prison and other trials. Their onslaught is short-lived, lasting at most ten days. Be steadfast, then, and do not lose heart until death, and in return you will receive the crown of life."
And the slander.

"I know your" applies to both clauses, so that it should be heard like this: I know your works, and I also know the slander of those who are Jews in word but in deed a synagogue of Satan. For a Jew is not one who is one outwardly, but one who is one inwardly, by the circumcision of the heart. By removing the visible skin that covers the reproductive member, such a person signifies in a figure that he is estranging himself from this whole material life and equipping his soul for divine things. For if "Judah" means "confession" and "Israel" means "a mind that sees God", then surely the true Jews and Israel are those who confess Christ, that is, who give thanks for the great benefits we have received through his coming to us in the flesh. That is what "confession" is meant to signify. And Israel is the one who has been found worthy to see God with the mind, unobstructed by any of the things that usually distract. So those who persist in unbelief without turning back are neither Jews nor Israel. By their slander they show themselves to be a synagogue of Satan, taken captive by him to do his will, since they serve under his command.

"But do not be afraid," he says, "of the things you are about to suffer. The affliction they bring will last a short time, not even worth measuring against ten days. It is given to you as a test of your faith, and so God also works with you, proving you genuine and putting the devil to shame, by whose working evildoers attack the godly." One must persevere until death in exchange for the crown of life. That is why it is said, "The one who endures to the end will be saved," not the one who throws away his shield and yields to softness in the contest.
Let anyone who has an ear hear.
Let the one who is equipped with spiritual perception and who conquers the spiritual forces of wickedness hear the divine Spirit, who anoints him to win the victory over them.
The one who conquers will not be harmed by the second death.

What is said here is precise, for human beings face two deaths. The first is the natural death, the separation of the soul from the body, according to the just and inexorable sentence of almighty God: "You are earth, and to earth you shall return." This death all people, righteous and sinners alike, undergo without exception. Then there is a second and more destructive death, which comes through sin, and which the bait of a licentious, carnal and pleasure-loving life knows how to procure for people. That is why the Lord calls those who pursue such a life dead, when he says, "Let the dead bury their own dead." The one who conquers this death, I mean the life of passion, will not be harmed by the death of Gehenna, which leads to [?] unending.
What was signified to the angel of the church of the Pergamenes.

And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: These are the words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. I know your works, and where you live, where Satan's throne is. You hold fast to my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas, my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan lives. But I have a few things against you: you have there some who hold to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the Israelites, so that they would eat food sacrificed to idols and commit fornication. So you also have some who likewise hold to the teaching of the Nicolaitans.

By the two-edged sword he means either the word of the gospel, which cuts away all the superfluity of the present life and of the evils that from our birth throw a veil of darkness over our vision of divine things, or else the severe sentence passed on the ungodly. Besides being two-edged, this sword is also sharp, that is, swift to take vengeance on those who disobey the divine commands. He calls Pergamum Satan's throne because it was more full of idols than all the rest of Asia. "Yet even though you live in such a place," he says, "you have kept my faith unadulterated. You were not drawn at all into imitating the wicked by living near them, nor did you envy the lawless when you saw the peace and prosperity of sinners."
Even in the days of Antipas, my witness.

Antipas the martyr bore witness in Pergamum, and his shrine is preserved to this day. He spoke with great boldness to those who plotted against him, and as far as it lay with him he went forward to death. The Evangelist now recalls his courage from the divine revelation, so that his virtue and endurance are held up as an example to the faithful, and the cruelty of those led astray is shown up, since they share Satan's dwelling. But since blame touches even the holiest, inasmuch as we all stumble in many ways, according to what is written, "Who is clean from filth?", he says, "Even though you are such as you are in your service of me, I still have something to charge against you, though only a little." For this city of the Pergamenes, it seems, had two grievous things in it: most of its people were pagans, and among those who were called believers the shameful Nicolaitans had been sown like evil tares among the good wheat. How these people behaved, and whom they resembled, he set forth by means of the ancient story.
The teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak.

He says that Balaam taught Balak, meaning that he became Balak's teacher. The story is in the book of the divine Moses called Numbers. Josephus the Jew writes that on Balaam's advice King Balak set the women in front of the people of Israel to entice them into fornication (this was when Phinehas performed his celebrated deed against Zimri), and that besides this licentiousness the same Israelite people were also drawn into eating defiled food, taking as food the meat dedicated to Baal-Peor. Of this David, the ancestor of God, also says, "They were initiated into the rites of Baal-Peor and ate sacrifices offered to the dead," by "sacrifices offered to the dead" meaning the meat offered to idols; and that is why they perished. He says that the Nicolaitans resemble these people both in fornication and in eating defiled food. If anyone asks what these practices were, as I have already mentioned, let him learn from Epiphanius of Cyprus, high priest of God, who for the benefit of many did not disdain to expose plainly and without reserve the filth of the Nicolaitans, both their harlotrous licentiousness and the utterly abominable unclean eating that went with it.

Repent, then. If not, I will come to you soon and make war against them with the sword of my mouth. Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.

O the depth of the riches and goodness of God, that even in his threat there is love for humankind! "I will make war," he says, "not against you, but against the Nicolaitans, who are sick with incurable and useless things." He spared those in Pergamum as believers, blaming them for one thing only, their association with the Nicolaitans. And the swiftness of his coming against those people, how is it not the mark of one who cares, who will not long tolerate his inheritance being corrupted, but grants swift help?
With the sword of my mouth.
What the sword of the mouth is, and why it is called two-edged, we explained a little earlier.
To the one who conquers I will give some of the manna.

As we have already explained, drawing on the holy Epiphanius, the vile Nicolaitans dared to practise in their unclean intercourse a most blasphemous eating, worthy of their godlessness. For this reason he promised that the one who conquers would be given manna to eat instead of that unclean and abominable food. Figuratively, the manna is the bread of life that came down from heaven for our sake, or else all the good things to come, since they too come flying down from heaven, where the Jerusalem above is. To the one who conquers the devil a white stone is also given, that is, one made bright with glory. He has put the white stone here because it was well known from those competing in theatres and stadiums, where it was given to the victors. The new name is one unknown in the present life. "For the good things God has prepared for those who love him no eye has seen, no ear has heard, nor have they entered the human heart," and neither has the name the saints will inherit. For how can incorruptible things be shown by corruptible knowledge?
To the one who conquers: see above [?].
And no one knows it except the one who receives it.
Rightly so, for knowledge, together with perception, accompanies the one to whom the gift is given.
What was written to the angel of the church of Thyatira.

"And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze. I know your works, and your love and faith and service, and your endurance; and your works, the last more than the first."

The one who speaks to the Evangelist gives a clearer sign of who he is, proclaiming himself the Son of God. His eyes are likened to fire, since they can give light to the righteous and are ready to burn up sinners. His feet are likened to *chalcolibanon*. By *chalcolibanon* is meant either the frankincense that physicians call "male," which gives off fragrant vapors when burned (for those who have come over to Christ meet temptations as they would meet fire, and the testing they undergo never fails to spread fragrance to those around them; this is why Paul boasts, "We are the fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing"). Among those being saved means those who press on from the Mosaic law, a more elementary life of godliness, to the more perfect life of faith in Christ; their own steadfastness anoints these people as if with fragrance. So too among those who are perishing, those whose life was dead (I mean dead with the death of idol-madness): once their truly passion-ridden life has been transformed, the blameless life in Christ knows how to make them fragrant. So these too can glory together with the same Paul and say, "I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me." That is the interpretation based on male frankincense. But one may also take *chalcolibanon*, as has already been discussed, to mean the Lord's incarnation, that is, the incarnation of the pre-eternal Word of God in the last times, which uses the deified man as feet, so to speak. The unconfused union of these two natures, divinity and humanity, is something that a human mind trained in piety knows to leave untouched, as a subject of inquiry beyond the grasp of mortals.
"I know your works."

Take "works" to mean only those dedicated to God. Here "to know" signifies closeness, as if he said, "In everything you live as one close to me." So also when he says to Moses, "I know you above all," and in the saying "The Lord knows those who are his," the meaning is simply closeness, as if to say, "I am close to those who devote their efforts to me."

By love he means confidence toward divine things, and the same goes for faith, since sincere love is strengthened by the achievements of each. By service he means help for those in need, and by endurance he means steadfastness in temptations.
"The last more than the first."
By saying "the last more than the first," he showed that as they go on, they toil with tireless effort to grow better by carrying out the divine commandments.

"But I have a few things against you: you tolerate your wife Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, and let her teach and lead my servants astray into sexual immorality and the eating of food sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, and she does not want to repent of her immorality. Behold, I am throwing her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great affliction, unless they repent of her works. And I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches kidneys and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works."

"Although I accept your reverence and endurance," he says, "because of your faith and your provision for the needy, I still have just cause to rebuke you, because you let the heresy of the Nicolaitans flourish among you." He refers to this heresy figuratively by the name of Jezebel, the wife of Ahab, comparing the followers of Nicolaus to her because of their licentiousness and impiety. So he rebukes them for not driving her out, that is, for not rejecting her and shaming her shameless blasphemy. Instead they put up with her sharing the name of Christians with them. Under cover of that name, he says, she secretly lays a stumbling block before the simpler among my servants, leading them not only into fornication but also into unclean eating. By fornication he means either the bodily kind or turning away from God, as in the sayings "They went whoring in their practices" and "They committed adultery with wood." By the eating of food sacrificed to idols he seems to include the other sects as well, which also grow up against the pious in whatever way they can. For the Nicolaitans did not promote eating food sacrificed to idols. They promoted other things, however, which are the height of uncleanness and foulness even to think about. We have often said that the book of the *Panarion* describes what these things are. And this abomination is not the only thing that goes along with the Nicolaitan heresy. She also pretends to be a prophetess, though she is driven by an evil spirit, and she turns the divine gift to vanity. So she is caught ignoring Moses, who plainly cries out, "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain," and she is found estranged from the blessing pronounced by the forefather of God, for she misses the hope that is in God and dwells instead on vanities and false frenzies.
"And leads my servants astray."

That is, she leads those who have lived in simplicity of character into fornication and the eating of forbidden things by deceiving them. "And I gave her." "I," he says, "who do not desire the death of the sinner but seek his turning back, have given her a time for repentance and have held off punishment for a while." But she abused this forbearance through negligence and used the opportunity for her own ruin, instead of holding fast to the turning back that brings salvation.
"And she does not want to repent."

(I know this because I am God, which is why it is said, "God, who tests hearts and kidneys.") So since she did not use the respite she was given for repentance, "Behold, I am throwing her onto a bed," that is, into sickness. For Scripture regularly uses "bed" to mean sickness, as when it says, "You have turned his whole bed in his sickness." There it calls the illness a bed and says that it has been changed for the better, that is, into health. "So I will afflict her in this way. And those who commit adultery with her, the accomplices who help her forge her abominable and filthy doctrines, I will afflict with calamities. Her children" (he calls the successors of such abomination her children) "I will pursue with death." So much for them. "But to you, who have nothing in common with the adulteress, who are rather simple, and who have chosen through simplicity of character to walk in innocence of heart in the midst of your house, I will lay no burden," he says. "For you do not have the strength to stand up against people so wicked and so inventive in the craftiness of their words, since you have not known, as you say, the depths of the evil one and his schemes." (By "burden" he means the battle fought with words.) "For me," he says, "the proof given by your works is enough, achieved by carefully keeping what was handed down to you from the beginning."
"Bed": the sickbed that leads to a kind of relief.
"Unless they repent."

Even in the threat his goodness can be seen. He does not inflict the deserved punishment at once. Instead he holds it in suspense as a bogey, as if urging them to take hold of repentance. You who are reading this, do not blame us if we stir up again here what was set out in the preliminary [?] section. There we presented it in that way to preserve the whole aim of the passage without omission. Here we are pointing out the proper place to those who come to it, and we have preferred clarity to any reluctance to repeat ourselves.
"And all the churches will know."

Some things are hidden from the many because the heretics commit their abominations in secret. These things are hidden from the many, and they escape the notice of the faithful because those people disappear under the name of Christians. "I will expose them," he says, "and make it known to all the churches that I am the one who searches kidneys and hearts." Isaiah also speaks of him: "Will anyone hide in a hiding place and he not see? Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord?" "Since this is so, I will award each person the wages that match his own love of wickedness."

"But to you I say, and to the rest in Thyatira, all who do not hold this teaching and who have not known the depths of Satan, as they say: I do not lay any other burden on you. Only hold fast to what you have until I come. And the one who conquers and keeps my works to the end, I will give him authority over the nations, and he will shepherd them with a rod of iron, as clay vessels are shattered, just as I too have received from my Father. And I will give him the morning star. Whoever has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches."

He has promised that each person will receive a reward worthy of his own labor. Now he adds what a person must spend his effort on in order to obtain what he deserves. "As for those who do not hold the deceiving teaching of the heretics," he says, "I accept them, and I will be content if they keep unspoiled the divine gift they received at the beginning." He will lay no other burden on them because of the simplicity of their ways, which means that they are ignorant even of the depths of Satan, as they say. The burden is the trouble that word-battles bring on those who fight them. And a servant of the Lord must not fight.
"I say to you."

He goes on in an unconnected way, without using a transitional conjunction. The sense [?] is to be understood thus: "But to you in Thyatira." He does this to show that God, unlike human beings, does not have to divide up his time and address each of those he speaks to separately. It is a mark of human weakness not to be able to speak with many people at the same time. For God this is the easiest thing of all: I mean that the one God can engage many people in different conversations at once.

Having threatened the doers of shameful deeds with what they deserve, he turns his words to those who have chosen to live more simply. He demands nothing else of them than to keep the pious deposit of faith unspoiled until his coming. By "coming" he means either the final one, when he will judge everyone at his second coming, or each person's departure from life. When we leave this busy life and go away to him, we will be in a secure state, holding an unfailing hope based on the lives we have lived. It is not unreasonable to prefer this second view.
"I do not lay any other burden on you."
That is, wrangling with the heretics over idle talk that stirs up fights. As Paul too says, "A servant of the Lord must not fight."
"And the one who conquers and keeps."

"For those who keep out of the battle because of their simplicity, keeping the commandments will be enough to please me. But to the one who carries off the prize from the battle and the wrestling, I will give," he says, "authority over the nations to celebrate his victory." This is just as in the Gospels the Lord says to the one who managed the minas and talents well, "Be over ten cities," and to another, "over five cities." And in Daniel there is the saying that the kingdom is given to the saints of God. These passages point to a kind of rule and authority that will be given to the saints over those who are lower and need guidance. That is why the verse "The rod of your kingdom is a rod of uprightness" will also fit this action. By the rod of uprightness the verse seems to hint that it brings in discipline that corrects, not discipline that punishes. But no one will say that the iron rod is given for any other purpose than to punish by shattering those who are fitted out with disobedience and are likened to clay vessels. In the same way, the rod of power sent out from Zion is sent for no other purpose than to rule over enemies. And since the iron rod is promised to everyone who conquers, and these would be the people from the nations who have brought themselves to Christ through ready obedience, they will also be the judges of unbelievers. For the Lord also says that the Ninevites will rise up at the judgment, that is, to condemn the evil generation. As for his saying that he himself received the rod from the Father, the language of giving and receiving came in because he took on flesh, and also to express humility. But if anyone wants to apply this to the divine nature as well, there is no difficulty: the giving and receiving show what is distinctive to each hypostasis, I mean the Father and the Son.
"To the end."

To the end of one's own life. This makes it clear that his "coming" here is not the final one, but for the present means each of us going to him. [?] …wishing to maintain that the divine is one hypostasis, just as it is one nature [?].

Another interpretation. "The one who conquers and keeps": by the grammar of the sentence these cases require the dative. But God, who cares only for our salvation, does not care much about it, I mean about grammar.
"As clay vessels are shattered."

Here "as" is not used in its usual way, to make a comparison or show likeness [?]. It is used causally, in place of "so that." To make this understood: "For this reason," he says, "an iron rod is given, so that the clay vessels will be shattered." The construction may not be good Greek, since an indicative verb is never construed with a subjunctive word. But this will not concern those who gain salvation through the meaning alone, not through exactness of wording. One can also construe it by hyperbaton: "with the iron," that is, "by the iron rod they will be shattered, like clay vessels."
"Just as I too have received from my Father."
"Received" is not used to suggest that the giver is superior, but to show that Father and Son are each a hypostasis. So this too should put to shame the Libyan, the enemy of the truth.
"The morning one."

The prophet Isaiah uses "morning star" of the Assyrian, that is, Satan. Christ too is reported to have seen him fall from heaven like lightning, and he was given to the saints to trample on. Paul also prays that God will crush him under the feet of his disciples. And David, encouraging the one who comes to God Most High, says, "You will tread on the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon." So the divine voice promises to give either this star, or the light-bearer that Peter speaks of, rising in the hearts of the faithful, that is, the light of Christ. John the Baptist too was a star that rose before the coming of Christ the sun. Elijah the Tishbite is likewise the herald of Christ's second coming. We believe that those who conquer the devil will share their portion with these. It is no wonder that we have taken the same term to mean things that are utterly opposed. Christ is a lion springing up from the shoot of Judah, and according to divine Scripture the Antichrist is a lion setting out from Bashan. Each is applied to its own subject. The dawn of the age to come is also meant here. Before it the darkness of the present life will be covered over, even though that life is thought to be light. Also meant is the angel who announces that dawn, since he goes before it, when the sun of righteousness appears to the saints and scatters the gloom of this life.
The message sent to the angel of the church in Sardis.

"And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: Thus says the one who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. I know your works: you have a name, and you are alive, and you are dead. Be watchful, and strengthen what remains, which was about to die; for I have not found your works complete before my God. Remember how you have received, and repent. If then you do not keep watch, I will come upon you like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come upon you."

By the seven stars we understand the divine angels, as we said before, and by the seven spirits the same angels, according to the saying, "who makes his angels spirits"; or else the operations of the life-giving Spirit. Both of these are in the hand, that is, in the authority, of Christ. The angels he holds as their master; the Spirit he bestows as being of one essence with him, as he also said, "I will send you another Paraclete from the Father." For in the blessed and superessential Trinity nothing is seen to belong to one alone, except the mode of existence that makes each person within it distinct.
I know your works.

Here "I know" is meant to signify mere knowledge, not the knowledge that claims someone as its own. That is why he also rebukes the church, as having only the bare name of the life of faith while being dead as far as good deeds are concerned. Scripture is accustomed to call the virtuous life "life" (I mean the life according to God), in keeping with the saying, "For your word has given me life," that is, has set me on the paths of true life. In the same way it calls the sinful life "death," as the divine Paul shows concerning those who had passed from unbelief to faith in Christ, writing to them thus: "And you, who were dead in your trespasses, ... with Christ." And in the book of the Shepherd it is declared that some went down into the water of the font dead, plainly, and came up alive.
You are alive, and you are dead.
You wear the name of life, he says, but in reality you are dead.
Be watchful, and strengthen what remains.

Shake off the sleep of sloth, and strengthen your members that are about to die completely through unbelief.
