For it is not the beginning of good works that crowns the tried and proven worker, but perseverance to the end. "Strengthen" is not said idly; it means, as it were, "make firm and give power to" things that are slack and all too ready to fall. So, he says, while anything remains to you, add some small efforts, so that death may not carry you off entirely. Guard, then, the things that are still alive, and strengthen those that are already sinking toward death. For none of your endeavors is complete: some have already died, and others are about to. As for "before my God," as has often been said, this is put in a more condescending way, from the standpoint of the human nature taken up by the Son of God.
Remember how you have received.

Keep, he says, the tradition you received from the apostles, and repent of your sloth. Keep alive those of your works that still live, and for those that have died, win back their life through repentance. By repentance he means the change away from what is worse and the turn toward what is better. The time of his coming is uncertain. Therefore one must always keep watch, and not abandon such watchfulness by spending one's leisure on other, empty hopes.

"If then you do not keep watch," he says, and do not rise as from the sleep of sloth, "I will come to you like a thief." To those who are prepared he comes as rest from their labors, but to the unprepared as a thief, bringing death to the soul. That is why it is also said, "His master will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know." What, then, is the Lord's coming, and when is it? His coming is, as it were, his speaking to us face to face. And it happens when the end of this corruptible life comes upon us, when the rewards that each one's labors here deserve are no longer stored up for us as promises but are already present and seen, nothing being lacking except the giving itself, which awaits the time when they will be received without any deception.
And you will not know at what hour.
For the time is unknown. And just as the time of death is unknown to each of us, so much more is the time of the Lord's second coming.

"Yet you have a few names in Sardis who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, because they are worthy. The one who conquers will be clothed in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life, and I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. Whoever has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches."

Out of regard for these few, he says, I hold back and am patient with you. The use of "names" should be noted as un-Greek, a disreputable and debased usage. It would have been enough to say "you have a few," not "a few names." For even though what is particular to each one's hypostasis is marked off by a proper name, the select language of Greek speech does not know how to count individual names in order to convey a number, but rather counts what is most specific. It says many or few, or two or three men, but not two or three names. For the one term signifies what is most proper to the nature, which by nature endures, while the name of the individual signifies the succession of individuals, which passes away almost as soon as their existence vanishes.
Who have not soiled.

You possess this good thing, he says: you have some who have not soiled the garment of the flesh with filthy deeds, and who will be clothed in brightness with me in the regeneration. Out of regard for them I meanwhile hold back and am patient with you. By garments that have not been soiled he means the bodies of the saints. So too Jacob the patriarch prophesies concerning the one who sprang from Judah, who is Jesus Christ, that he will wash his robe in wine, meaning the body of the Lord himself, which was cleansed in his spotless passion as a pattern for us. For he did no sin, as Isaiah says: "Because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death. For he did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." And the same Isaiah, as if setting a scene in a drama, says to this Lord, "Why are your garments red, as from a full, trodden winepress?" Concerning the garments, it is worth observing that their being unsoiled hints at the purity of the body. "The one who conquers," he says. Conquers what? The passions of the flesh. This one, then, will be clothed in the garments of his own virtues, which he has cleansed by labors pleasing to God, and he will shine like the sun in the age to come. And his name, which was written in the book of those who live the life that does not fail, will never be blotted out, since I will confess him before my Father. He himself also mentioned this writing in the book and this confession before the Father in the divine Gospels, speaking thus to his disciples: "Rejoice that your names have been written in heaven." The promise that he will confess the name is itself also recorded in the divine Gospels, where he gives assurance that whoever confesses him before men he will confess before the Father at his second coming. This is laid up for all the saints, but especially for the martyrs.
Before my Father and before his angels.

"Before the Father and his angels" is said because the angels are faithful servants and well-disposed members of his household. Sometimes he calls the angels the Father's, sometimes his own, as when he says, "The Son of Man will send his angels with a great trumpet." So calling the angels the Father's here does not take away the fact that the holy angels are also his. For among the things contemplated in the holy nature, one would find nothing that belongs to any one of its three hypostases alone, except the one thing that belongs to it as a hypostasis.
What was written to the angel of the church of the Philadelphians.

"And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: Thus says the Holy One, the True One, who has the key of David; no one will shut except the one who opens, and no one will open except the one who shuts. I know your works. Look, I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut, because you have little power, and you have kept my word and have not denied my name."

The Holy One is the one who is truly holy, who is also the Son of God. And "the True" is referred to the Seraphim's threefold hymn of sanctification, as was revealed to Isaiah the seer, the threefold "holy" being gathered into a single lordship, so that both the threeness of the hypostases of the superessential Trinity might be shown and their inseparability through the oneness of their lordship. But who could express in words how far this rises above our lowly and mortal nature? By the key of David he means the almighty authority, through which alone the treasures of divine wisdom are opened. The first authority he receives according to his human nature, as we may hear him saying, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me." The second he has according to the beginningless Godhead. For Emmanuel is true God, even if Nestorius will not have it so, though he also became man. And indeed he is truly man, not a man in appearance only, even if the God-hated Eutyches dislikes it. Rather, he is what he is: truly God, not by mere relation, as the Nestorians babble, and true man, not in seeming and appearance, as the thunderstruck Eutychianists and the most abominable tribe of the Manichaeans would have it. Since some of the copies have not "the key of David" but "the key of Hades," there is no difference in this either. For this shows that Christ, being God, undoubtedly has authority over life and death.
Who has the key of David.

He calls authority a key. For whoever has authority to shut and to open is also the one entrusted with the house. This can be learned more clearly from the Gospels, where Christ says to Peter, "And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven": that is, to shut and to open, and to bind and to loose, with you beyond the reach of those who oppose them [?].
And no one will open.

Since the key hints at authority, what else does the one who says he has the key of David mean, except that just as David reigned over the visible Israel, so I too reign, not only over the visible but also over the spiritual Israel? Even so, the authority of a man cannot be compared with that of God. That is why Gabriel told the Virgin that the throne of David would be given by the Father to the Son as if it were temporary, although it was given to him as eternal and unending, and likewise the kingdom and the authority. Since, then, Christ bore a likeness of David's kingdom, he fittingly says, "who has the key of David," to open and to shut, meaning by opening to justify and by shutting to condemn. For using his divine and eternal authority he both justifies and condemns. "If God is the one who justifies, who is the one who condemns?" I know your works.
It has been said that "I know" is meant to signify the knowledge that claims someone as its own.
Look, I have set before you.

The door of good things is given open, as being most ready, from the very first inclination toward better things, to grant entry to their enjoyment. That is why the Lord too, saying that "the kingdom of heaven is within you," as though it is offered according to the purpose of whoever wills it, holds that nothing stands in the way of entering. And the promise here entices those who are being brought in, so that they do not give up the attempt by reckoning the hardship of the labors; but once they have begun, and the entry is measured to the small power of the one who chooses to enter, then, when it displays through the open door the swarm of good things heaped up for those who enter, it no longer lets them be troubled by the worry of fainting under the labors spent for that enjoyment. It urges them to hold to their labors without turning back, as one who reckons the toils for these things sweeter than any ease. That the inheritance of eternal good things is won by toil, the divine saying in the Gospels is enough to show: "The kingdom of heaven is taken by force." And that whoever has his senses sweetened by making a beginning knows how to disregard the labors, the divine spirit of David teaches, saying, "Taste and see that the Lord is good." The door is given open because it is measured to the power of the one who receives it. Or the open door may also be understood as the entry of the teaching proclamation, which, once opened, cannot be shut by temptations, since the eagerness of those who have chosen to enter, charmed by the beauty of what is stored within, overcomes the hardship of the temptations. In these things, he says, even if the door is matched to your power, it is nevertheless from me that the open door is given to you. But you yourself held out even beyond the power you had, and did not deny my name. So I will not measure the reward by your small power, but will repay you generously, as is my custom.

"Look, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan, who say they are Jews and are not, but are lying. Look, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will know that I have loved you. Because you have kept the word of my endurance, I too will keep you from the hour of trial that is about to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth. I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one takes your crown. The one who conquers I will make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will never go out of it again; and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven from my God, and the new name. Whoever has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches."

The reward, he says, for confessing my name will be the conversion and repentance of the Jews, who in return for coming to me will receive the illumination that comes from me. These are the ones who show themselves to be Jews in the hidden part of the heart and not outwardly, as Paul also holds. He calls the synagogue of the Jews the throne of Satan, as being held together by falsehood, since Satan was shown to be "the father of lies" from the foundation of the world, if indeed his deception of the first ancestors of our race through the serpent is enough to confirm the statement. These, then, he says, will run to you, not casually, but with great fervor and contrition. This is what bowing down at the feet hints at: choosing to be ranked among the last in the church, and only to be counted worthy of being part of the church. As David the prophet also gladly says, "I have chosen to be cast aside in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners," preferring the despised place in the shared courts [?] to the unconfined and free way of life of sinners.
The word of my endurance.

Not that the one who speaks the oracle himself endured anything; by "his endurance" he means the endurance undergone for his sake and the steadfastness of faith toward him. So too, when David asks God, "Let my judgment come forth from your presence," he means "your justice on my behalf."
I too will keep you from the hour of trial.

By the hour of trial he means either the persecution under Domitian, the second after Nero's, as Eusebius son of Pamphilus records, when the Evangelist himself was condemned by that same Domitian to Patmos; or the worldwide persecution that will be waged against Christians by Antichrist at the end of the age, when he will put Christians to death. From both of these he promises to free those who are zealous for him, by snatching them away beforehand through their departure from this life, so that they may not be tested beyond their strength. That is why the Lord also says, "I am coming soon." For after that tribulation "I am coming soon," that is, without delay. For this is what "soon" signifies: I will come, as it were, hard on the heels of the trials as they are carried out. That is why he also urges us to hold the treasure of faith inviolate, so that the crown of our endurance may not be lost. "For the endurance of the poor will not perish."
Hold fast what you have.
The command is to hold fast what you have [?] in genuine love; if you contend in it to the end, you will have the crown of glory. For the prizes of victory belong to those who endure.
The one who conquers.

By the usage of the Greek language, this is a solecism of syntax. Either the accusative should have been used instead of the nominative, so that the phrase ran, "The one who conquers, him I will make"; or, if the nominative were kept, a verb of being, such as "will be," should have been added and the accusative changed, so that the sentence ran, "The one who conquers will be set by me as a pillar in the temple of my God." But since, as has already been said, the saviors of our souls cared very little for the precision of Greek prattle, we are right to leave these matters to others and to hold ourselves to more serious things.
In the temple of my God.

It has been said before that "my God" does not so much do away with the divine nature contemplated in Christ as present the union of the natures in one being. For it shows that the union of the two natures, I mean Godhead and manhood, in the hypostasis of the Lord Jesus cannot be divided even in bare thought, though they are without confusion. For in a way beyond human comprehension the divine properties are shared with the human, and the human with the divine, as each other's own. This one is set as a pillar in the temple of God, since by God's generosity toward him he supports those whose disposition toward the perfection of our faith in Christ is weaker, urging them too to advance to a like gift of teaching. "In the temple of God": so as to rejoice continually. For this is what it means to become a pillar in the temple of God. The conqueror of the opposing powers is set as a pillar and foundation of the truth, rejoicing unchangeably himself, and supporting others so that they do not fall from their own place in the good.
And I will write on him the name of my God.

On the spiritual pillar, that is, the one who has been fitted by the divine commands to support the weaker, he says the name of God will be written, and the name of the city of God, the new Jerusalem. By the new Jerusalem and its name, and by the name of God, he means nothing other than their glory, or the knowledge of them, as David too says, "How wonderful is your name in all the earth," that is, the honor, the knowledge concerning you. So when there has been written on the tablets of the heart of the spiritual pillar the name of God (that is, the knowledge and the glory), and likewise that of Jerusalem — of God as holy, as just and rendering to each according to his works, as full of all goodness and rejoicing in such servants; and of Jerusalem as the beloved dwelling of God, which sends its citizens on to the heavenly [?] metropolis, while the lower Jerusalem stands as a kind of colony of the upper, holding those who dwell in it for the time being, who use these, as it were, as letters, and order the life below by the life above — then, by this corresponding writing, that is, by memory that does not forget (for such is writing, being the most lasting record of what has happened), they bear the stamp of the glory of God and of the upper Jerusalem; how could they not be called divine? By the new name we understand the name placed on the saints, which belongs to them in addition to the joy of the divine gift and the enjoyment of the beauty of incorruptible good things in the age to come, and which is known to themselves and to those who will receive it, those who are now brothers, friends and servants of Christ.

Concerning "my God," it has already been said that it is spoken by way of condescension and to set forth the indivisibility of the two natures contemplated in the Lord's dispensation. He says that the name of God and of the new Jerusalem (what these are has been explained) come down from above, since the divine [?] began from the angels and came down as far as us, angels, clearly, and ... being joined to one another through Jesus Christ our head ... [?]
What was revealed to the angel of the church of the Laodiceans.

"And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: Thus says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God's creation. I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. I wish you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I am about to spit you out of my mouth. For you say, 'I am rich, I have grown wealthy, and I need nothing,' and you do not know that you are the wretched and pitiable one, poor, blind and naked."

This is equivalent to "Thus says the True One," which was explained earlier. For "amen" means "yes." He is therefore "yes" in everything that is said about him, that is, truth, with no falsehood in it. "The faithful witness" has also been discussed already, and it would be superfluous to go over the same ground again. "The beginning of God's creation" means the kingship and rule that holds sway over all things as creatures. For the "beginning" of creation is the originating cause of creation. The God-fighting workshop of the Arians might perhaps misuse this saying, as though these words revealed the Lord Jesus to be a creature. But we must not be led astray by their villainies. Instead we should consider whether anything of this kind is said about him in another scripture, so that like may be measured by like. Paul, then, writing to the Colossians about Christ, says, "who is the firstfruits, the firstborn of all creation." Firstborn of creation, not first-created. And David says, "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you," not "I created you." And Solomon: "Before all the hills he begets me." As for "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways," "created" is taken in the sense of "appointed," as also in "that he might create the two into one new man," and "Create in me a clean heart, O God." And Gregory, divine in his speech, in his oration on the Son, understands "created" of the Lord's body animated by a rational soul, and "begets" of his divinity. Since the sense of "creation" is confirmed by so many testimonies, "the beginning of creation" (as we have already said) means nothing other than the ruler of God's creation, inasmuch as all things came into being through him. To him it is also given to rule the creatures he made, that is, he was appointed to rule them. "Having received" and "having been appointed" do not imply any lessening of essence or glory, for this has been discussed already.
"Because you are neither cold nor hot."

"Cold" is the one deprived of the working and visitation of the Holy Spirit. "Hot" is the one who is fervent in spirit, as Paul also says. "Lukewarm" is the one who is unsteady between the two and wavers. He received a share in the Holy Spirit through baptism, but he quenched the gift of what gives life to the soul, having grown slack through his concern for present things. Since these things are so, let those who do not understand them in this way be covered with shame, and let them walk in the light of their fire and in the flame they have kindled, and lament [?]. That is why Paul also says of the divine Spirit, "Do not quench the Spirit." Since, then, you are such a one, and were fervent in spirit through baptism but have grown cold through slackness, you have cut off your future hopes of salvation, having condemned the faith you chose. In works the middle course is not to be rejected. Lawful marriage, for instance, lies midway between virginity and fornication and is not to be cast aside. But in faith the middle and lukewarm course is unapproved and has no standing. Therefore he says, "I wish you were cold," that is, wholly without share in the grace of divine baptism, unbaptized, and not lukewarm. For the one who has not yet received the grace of the Spirit through baptism lives in the hope of one day receiving salvation. But the lukewarm, as we have already explained, has been deprived, [?] along with life, even of the prospect of one day being baptized and becoming fervent.
"I am about to spit you out."

He was right to use the metaphor of lukewarmness. Physicians too use lukewarm liquid to provoke vomiting, because it loosens the stomach. Hence for those who have trouble vomiting they induce it by having them gulp down lukewarm water. This is what he says here too: I am about to vomit you out like loathsome food, that is, by the word of my mouth I will cast you out of my fellowship. And what is the reason for this? It is that you set your hope on uncertain riches and choked the seed of the divine word with thorns, that is, with the temptations of this passing wealth and life, so that you failed to recognize your own spiritual and everlasting poverty, pitiableness, wretchedness, nakedness and blindness.
"For I am rich, and I have grown wealthy."

By wealth he means earthly wealth. You do not know that you are the wretched one among those who are perishing. That is why you deserve pity. You have fallen from the height of the virtues, been seized by dizziness when choosing the better things, and been stripped of the divine glory that clothed you until now.

"I counsel you to buy from me gold refined in the fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments to clothe yourself, so that the shame of your nakedness may not be revealed, and eye-salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see. Those whom I love I reprove and discipline. So be zealous and repent. Look, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with me. The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, just as I too conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. Whoever has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches."

If you want to become rich, he says, gain the true wealth from me, for I know how to enrich with things that last. You will gain it with fiery resolve, namely the words of the Lord, which are pure words, refined seven times. And what are these? They are the divine word of teaching. It does not go out to those being taught idly or in vain. It goes out because the teacher has first become rich in it through fiery zeal, for "the righteous man declares a faith that has been shown in deeds." And the good merchant "brings out of the good treasure of his heart things old and new." From the old he brings the greater examples set by the achievements of the men of old, and from the new he brings the achievements he himself has toiled for with fiery fervor. But since no one becomes rich in such things without help from above, the one who speaks says for this reason, "from me." And this wealth is able, like a garment put on, to cover the shameful nakedness of one who lacks virtues. It does not simply cover it, but does so with festal glory, celebrating the triumph won by victory over the hostile demons.
"And eye-salve."

The command is for the one whose sight is dim toward the Lord's spiritual light to anoint the eyes that correspond to it. As the prophet Jeremiah also says, "Look, your eyes and your heart are not good." For this reason he counsels the cleansing power against such blindness. This power is the progress through repentance that he is counseling. In the same way the manure put around the barren fig tree hints at the humbling that comes through confession and a lowlier way of life. Or the eye-salve stands for freedom from possessions. For if gifts blind the eyes of those who see, refusing bribes will surely open them.
"And those whom I love I reprove and discipline."

Oh, what love for humankind! With what great goodness he treats sinners, even sinners such as the passage has described! And rightly so, for the one who loves disciplines with care. This is also proof of the Lord's surpassing kindness toward the disobedient, and the pledge of the riches of that kindness is the love of one who goes after those who deserve punishment. And what is the discipline? It is to be zealous for the better ways of life. Those who have turned from discipline to ignorance should take up zeal again, that is, imitation, through repentance and a change of mind about their past sins, a kind of turning away from them. And what does his love for humankind give in return? It is his patient waiting at the door without causing trouble [?]. By "door" in what follows he means the heart of those called to repentance. Those who open it to the one who knocks for their salvation will receive the following blessings in abundance when the gentle and good guest comes in.
"Look, I stand at the door and knock."

My coming, he says, does not force anyone. I knock at the door of the heart, and I rejoice with those who open it at their salvation. For I count human salvation as my delight and my supper. By it they themselves are fed, and they escape the famine of hearing the word of the Lord and the darkness of error. The good and gentle one knocks at the door, and if it is not opened, he leaves without a sound. This is found in the Song too: "[?] Open to me, my sister, my bride." If anyone opens to him, he comes in. If not, he passes by. The devil is not like this. When someone does not open to him, he uses axe and hammer to break down that person's door.
"And I will dine with him."

Some have taken the supper to be the partaking of the holy mysteries. But he calls "supper" the salvation of the one who readily listened to him who knocked at the door of the heart. When he enters, a supper too will be prepared, and the one who comes in will take the one who opened the door as his companion. For the salvation of the one being saved is food for him who became man for our salvation. That is why he also said that his food and drink is to fulfil the Father's will, and the Father wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. The joy at the supper is shared by both. Salvation does not delight the one who is saved as much as it delights the one who saves him out of his unspeakable love for humankind. He even declared that our salvation sustains his very being [?], when he firmly made the fulfilment of the Father's will his food. And why has this been said to us? Because just as food sustains our life, so famine destroys it. The prophet announces this famine as a threat when he says that the Lord will bring a famine on the land, not of bread and water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. This is truly a famine, for it wastes away the man within us who is according to God.
"The one who conquers, I will give him."

It has already been said that Greek learning calls such a construction and such a sequence of phrases a solecism. The Church cares little about this, holding fast only to what is saving in the meaning. It cares for the words that carry the meaning of saving things only as much as a wise merchant cares for the pack animal from which he unloads his precious goods, worn out though it may be [?]. But what would the faultless form of the expression be? "To the one who conquers, I will give to him," since gifts are expressed by the dative case. By the throne he means rest in the kingdom of the age to come. So he says that those who have conquered the enemy, as I too did, will reign with me. That is why I said, "I have conquered the world." I also promised this: "You too will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." That is, condemning them, or rather sitting there for their condemnation. Though it was possible for them too to be counted worthy of the same honors as their kinsmen, they did not attain them because of their unbelief. The divine Paul also mentions the glory of the age to come, I mean reigning with Christ, when he says, "if indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him." And "as I too have conquered the world" is said in human terms because he took on our nature, as is the word "receive." For the grant of the kingship of the throne is not a prize for virtue given to one who coexists eternally as God. It is said in human terms. Or rather, it shows how, after God the Word was united to human nature, each of the united natures takes the properties of the other as its own. Let Nestorius be put to shame, and the whole chorus of those like him.
On the door he saw in heaven, the throne, the twenty-four elders, and the things shown to him next.

After these things I looked, and behold, a door opened in heaven, and the first voice which I had heard, like a trumpet speaking with me, saying, "Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after these things." And immediately I was in the Spirit.

He does not relate these things because he saw a perceptible door in heaven, opened at some moment and then closed. Rather, it appeared to the Evangelist in such a way that, as through an open door, the things within were necessarily seen. And he says, "I heard a voice," which, sounding like a trumpet, says, "Come up here." By "going up" it does not mean going up in place, but lifting the mind up from earthly and human things. For it is above all those whose ruling faculty is shaped by purity from the stains of material life who obtain these sights, and sights such as these, that are worthy of God.
And the first voice which I had heard.

This too goes against the syntax of the sentence, and why this is so has already been explained. For it ought to have said: "And the voice of the one speaking with me said, Come up here." Put that way, the sentence would have run properly.

And behold, a throne stood in heaven, and on the throne one seated, like in appearance to jasper stone and carnelian; and a rainbow around the throne, like in appearance to emerald; and around the throne, twenty-four thrones. And on the twenty-four thrones, elders seated, clothed in white garments, and on their heads golden crowns. And from the throne go forth lightnings and voices and thunders; and seven lamps of fire burning before his throne, which are the seven spirits of God.
By saying "in the Spirit," he indicated that nothing perceptible should be understood as taking place here.
"Formed by the Spirit," he says, "I beheld a throne," and the throne shows God's rest in the saints. For he is enthroned in them, since they are able to receive divine manifestations.

Another interpretation. He beheld a "throne," but he does not describe its form, just as neither Isaiah nor Ezekiel did. For mortal nature cannot express the surpassing greatness of God's might, nor present an image of his authority drawn from human power, and that authority is what the throne is meant to display. It should be noted that the stones are brought in here not to convey their preciousness. If that were the point, the intellectual spirits would be likened to the emerald, a precious stone, while the jasper, likened to the One who rides upon them, would be less precious, which is impious even to think. So the stones are brought in not for the sake of their preciousness but for the sake of what their color signifies.
Like in appearance to jasper stone and carnelian.

Since he is presenting here the Father who was seen, he does not give him a bodily form, as he did the Son in his earlier vision. Instead he likens him to precious stones. The jasper, being green, signifies what is ever-flourishing and life-giving, as it is said, "making grass spring up for the cattle, and green plants for the service of mankind." For every seed puts forth green growth, appointed by God as food for living things. And it is called jasper because it is like the venom (ios) of an asp (aspis) and resembles it. He is likened to carnelian because God is to be feared, for carnelian is fiery. This is why Moses says, "For God is a fire, a consuming fire." For since kindness is of no profit to those who love sin and to the scornful, God is to be feared for this reason. For with them kindness leads not to repentance but to license for their offenses. And since it would be unbearable for God to exercise his righteous judgment to the utmost (this is why David says, "If you should mark iniquities, who shall stand?"), the carnelian fittingly gives a sign of his forbearance and goodness, as well as of his fearsomeness through its fiery quality. Or perhaps we should say that it also shows his fatherly providence, which comes from his exceeding love for his sons. So the fiery quality signifies fearsomeness, which is why we first took the meaning from the color. In the same way, the power of the same stone reveals another dispensation of his kindness. For they say that jasper not only frightens wild beasts and phantoms, but also has power to heal painful growths that arise on our bodies. The great Epiphanius says that when it is smeared on, it heals swellings and wounds made by iron. It should be noted that the stones were brought in here not for the sake of their preciousness but for what their color signifies.
Like in appearance to jasper stone.

We have already said why the Father is not shown in a form, as the Son is. Instead he is compared to the appearance of stones. First he is compared to jasper, because its color is green, which hints at the beneficence of the Divine, at his care in nourishing all, and at his love for mankind. After it comes the carnelian, which hints through its fieriness at what is to be feared. For although God is by nature loving toward mankind and good, our perversity and crookedness [?] force him, if it is right to say so, to lay aside his gentleness and proceed to severity. For since, as the saint said, "terrible things do not frighten, and bright things do not encourage," what is left except to use severity? Or perhaps we should say that even this is not the work of one who punishes. It is the work of a fatherly mind that wills all of us to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and to come to that knowledge through discipline. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If he does not discipline him, the son is plainly being sent away among the illegitimate sons.
And a rainbow around the throne.

Divine Scripture calls the perceptible rainbow God's bow, when it says, "I set my bow in the cloud." It is formed by the reflection of sunlight. When the light is caught in the thickness of a watery cloud, it is blocked from passing through the cloud and instead presents a varied appearance of colors of every kind. Such is that rainbow. But the one encircling the throne is of a single kind, the color of emerald. He called it a rainbow after our many-colored rainbow, so that we might understand the diversity in the beneficent ministry of the divine angels, whose diversity ends in a single active service, in imitation of their own Master. For the green color of the jasper stone was likewise meant to point to his care in nourishing all and to his beneficence, and the emerald stone, with its leek-green look, resembles it.
Twenty-four thrones.

By "throne" here we should understand nothing other than eagerness to carry out the divine commands. For only a soul prepared in this way becomes a divine chariot that rivals the cherubim. Like them, it has as its rider the one who, as David says, is borne by them: the Maker, who oversees all this.
Elders seated.

As for the number of the twenty-four elders, by what reasoning was it chosen? I may be unworthy, yet, to speak with blessed Paul, as "one untimely born," I will say what comes to mind. It seems to me that the number is meant to show the following. The all-holy Trinity, which is beyond all sovereignty and beyond all divinity, set the number seven as the number corresponding to this visible structure of its creation [?]. In the beginning, according to the unsearchable depth of its own wisdom, it unfolded the number seven as many times as it is itself, and so revealed the number twenty-four. For three times seven makes twenty-one, and the remaining amount of the number twenty-four, which is three, is dedicated to the all-working divine Trinity. So the number seven, unfolded three times, together with what caused it to be unfolded, made twenty-four. And does not the number seven pervade the whole of this perceptible world, by a certain power of its own that mortal nature cannot yet know? That the number seven can be seen pervading the whole perceptible world is ably shown by Philo, the most contemplative and learned man among the Jews. In his treatise on the philosophy of Moses he dwells at length on this number. He establishes it by scientific methods and shows that it extends through all perceptible creation: through everything observed in the motion of the heavenly revolution, and through everything that fittingly adorns things in motion. Of this, I think, the Revelation now presents the twenty-four elders as an example. They sit on the thrones and bear a symbol of the seniority that is from eternity, and through their worship before God, the Originator of all, they signify their relation to him as servants. Those seated are equal in number to the thrones. They are elders and not young men, since the promise of the inheritance of the kingdom is most ancient, being before the foundation of the world. This is why the Judge of the living and the dead says, "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." So the kingdom was prepared for us beforehand. And certainly, for those whose prize was prepared before the foundation of the world, the eternal kingdom is given not as to young men but as to those who have grown old in keeping the divine commands. This is why their clothing is their own, having been whitened often and unceasingly in the purifying baths of virtue. How these too are twenty-four and equal in number to the thrones was shown by the earlier reflection on the number of the thrones. It showed that the number seven, which corresponds to this visible world, when tripled and added to, makes twenty-four. And so it clothes with the most brilliant virtues all who have lived rightly in this world of sevens, and adorns them with victory symbols, as champions over the passions and the invisible enemies. He says the crowns are golden, for he had nothing more precious than gold to set before people living in the present life to give them a clear understanding.
Clothed in white garments.

It should be understood that the custom of history aims to report things that have happened, not things to come or things present. For what need is there to teach what is going on and present? The Evangelist before us kept to this custom until now, but from this point he changed the order, narrating not things that had happened but things that are present. One can say that he did this because he wished to convey how awe-inspiring, fearsome and unceasing these things are. For narrating past events does not strike as much fear into the hearers as what is active and present.
And from the throne go forth lightnings and voices and thunders.

Here he hints at the fearsome and astonishing nature of the Divine. For divine beauty does not find its gladness in some relaxed state or in the pleasure of enjoyment, but in fearsomeness joined with wonder. This is why the prophet says, "Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling." For the joy of closeness to him produces fear in those who love him genuinely, the fear that they may fall short in serving the one they so love. This is why David says, "Fear the Lord, all you his saints," because those who fear him lack nothing.
And seven lamps of fire burning.

He himself interpreted the seven lamps as seven spirits. We should understand these either, as Isaiah does, as the divine gifts of the Spirit (wisdom, strength, counsel and those that follow), or, as Irenaeus and Clement, the author of the Stromata, do, as the ministering spirits that excel the other orders. There are seven because they oversee this world, which corresponds to the number seven, or for the reason we have already given. They are burning because their holy service to the Divine is unremitting and continual. For fire is like this too, this material fire, which unceasingly gives light and blazes. This is why the prophet says, "Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire."

And before the throne there was, as it were, a sea of glass, like crystal. And in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures full of eyes in front and behind. The first living creature was like a lion, the second living creature like a calf, the third living creature had the face of a man, and the fourth was like a flying eagle.

He likens what lies before the throne to a sea, signifying the boundless and incomparable multitude of divine powers that surround God's throne. Daniel too means to show this through his numbers of thousands and myriads. The sea of glass, like crystal, signifies the translucence of the incorporeal natures and the calm of the life about the throne, that is, of angelic life. For it stands fixed and unmoving like glass and crystal, darkened by no stain that might draw it away into senseless agitation. . . . [?] and the nature of heaven has been thought to be crystal-like. We must consider whether through [?] of the floor is signified, having at once a gleam and translucence, unless [?] we seem to be telling you marvels beyond comprehension.
And in the midst of the throne and around the throne.

The throne signifies God's kingdom and the eternal might of his lordship in authority, and concerning [?] the inescapable reach of his providential sovereignty is perceived, and his goodness as well. These holy living creatures are different from those of Ezekiel's vision. For each of those was seen to have four faces and eight wings, and they drew along certain wheels, which were called "gel" [?]. Those were many-eyed too, like these. But here each has a different face and six wings. And those, as Ezekiel himself judges, were named Cherubim, while these, accordingly, are Seraphim, which were shown to the divine Isaiah. Those did not show a likeness of faces as these do, but covered their own faces with two wings, apart from being decked all over with eyes as these are. But if these things now shown to the Evangelist mean to hint at anything, it is at the error that arose from the words of the psalm: "Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds." From this text some came to think that the earthly creation remains unvisited by God because of Adam's transgression and the changeable nature of things on earth. They did not understand the words "his compassions are over all his works." So if earthly things too are God's works, they would rightly be judged worthy of his oversight. The purpose of the vision shown to the Evangelist, then, is to refute the error we have mentioned. It shows that, through these four living creatures, or through creation made of the four elements of fire, water, air and earth, all creation enjoys God's oversight. Each of the living creatures that were seen is taken as a figure of one of the elements of the world. The lion stands for fire, because of its spirit and heat. The calf stands for earth, because of its work on the land. The man stands for air, for man is heavenly and lofty [?] because of the subtlety of his mind. The eagle stands for water, for birds have their origin from the waters. The many eyes signify God's oversight of all things, which he also carries out through the ministry of the intellectual spirits. As David says, "mighty in strength, doing his word, hearkening to the voice of his words," that is, carrying out their ministry without delay at his very command.
Four living creatures full.

Some have taken these four living creatures to be the four Gospels and the four cardinal virtues. The lion indicates courage, and the Gospel according to John, which, as holy Irenaeus of Lyons says, shows the kingship that is before the ages through the words "In the beginning was the Word." The calf indicates justice, since it is content with its own labors, and the Gospel according to Luke, since Luke traced Christ's genealogy in a legal and priestly manner. The eagle indicates temperance, for this animal is attested to have it, and the Gospel according to Mark, which is concise like the eagle's flight and begins from the prophetic Spirit. The man indicates prudence, and the Gospel according to Matthew, since Matthew proclaimed Christ's birth in terms of nature and not of the Law. Perhaps these also show Christ's dispensation: the lion shows him as king; the calf as priest, or rather as sacrifice as well; the man as having become man for our sake; and the eagle as the giver of the life-giving Spirit, who flew down upon all.

And the four living creatures each had six wings round about, and they were full of eyes within. And day and night they have no rest, saying, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come." And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to the one seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders will fall down before the one seated on the throne and worship the one who lives forever and ever. And they will cast their crowns before the throne, saying, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God, the Holy One, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created."

He has spoken of the four living creatures that surround the throne and described the form of each. We too have explained this as far as we could, according to the gift given to us in due measure: that it belongs to God to exercise providential care over all his earthly creation, which is why there are four living creatures, equal in number to the four qualities through which the elemental bodies of this material world came to exist. Now he also presents the swiftness of their ministry. David presents this too through the words "mighty in strength, doing his word, hearkening to the voice of his words." It is as if the command did not even come before the completion of what was commanded; the will was accomplished by the command itself. He says this speed is achieved through the six wings of each one. For this is what "each" indicates, so that no one, hearing of six wings, should think they were shared among them all. "Round about" refers not to the wings but to the position of the four, showing that they stood not in a row but in a circle. The number of the wings hints at the perfection of the ministry and at its goal, for six is celebrated as a perfect number by those who are clever in such matters. Among beings that have risen above sense-perception, nothing is imperfect, nor does anything need to be completed afterward through regret. The divine Dionysius says that the intellectual living creatures are equipped with six wings: with two they cover their faces, with two their feet, and with the middle pair they fly. In this way their reverence appears toward things higher and deeper than their own comprehension, and for this reason they are directed, by the middle wings, to stretch upward toward the primal rays in divine balance. "Round about" is used for their oversight of all things. "Within" is used because nothing can escape the divine, not even what some people do in secret. "They have no rest" does not mean that they suffer any weariness as they minister in unceasing hymnody. For toil belongs to perceptible creation, while everything above matter is untiring. There, as the one who said it put it, "pain, sorrow and sighing have fled away." So "they have no rest" shows not weariness but their unceasing devotion to the divine hymnody, as of beings who delight in what is done for the glory and praise of the Divine. We may understand the three Persons from the threefold repetition of the glory and the holiness. The manifestation of three Persons in the Godhead does not lack witnesses but is supplied from both the Old and the New Scripture. From the Old, it comes from the One who gave the oracle to Moses and bade him say, "He Who Is has sent me." From the New, it comes from the very one who teaches this Revelation, who spoke of the Son in the words "In the beginning was the Word." As for the Spirit, he who became man, he "who was," promised his disciples at the time of his divine passion that he would "send them another Paraclete." What person in his right mind will not call the one who is sent, and who fulfills his mission, "the one who comes"? The command at baptism, to baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, is clearer still.
The twenty-four elders will fall down.

These words show that the elders, as we have understood them, share in the hymnody of the heavenly powers, confessing that they received from God the power to conquer their spiritual enemies. One should also note the precision about time in the narrative. He moves from describing present things to future things. He does not do this through lack of understanding. He does it to show that even before the final proclamation of those who have lived rightly, there is something for those who strip off the present arena of contest in obedience to the limit set for them: a thanksgiving to the One who has fixed what is profitable for each. For they also receive rewards that are in proportion to, and comparable with, the coming age that will never end. These rewards may be an abundance of miracles for those who come to them in need, or other benefactions. So the homage, praise and laudation offered to the incarnate Jesus Christ, the Son of God, by the ministering spirits, and by the people who rival them and have been shown to excel in deed, is not stored up only for the last day. It is offered already in the present, as this apparent breach of the order of time has made clear to those who can see sharply.
And they will cast their crowns.

Casting the crowns before the throne signifies victory, as can still be seen today among those who win contests. The throne signifies lordship and authority, and the crown is also a symbol of kingship. So when they cast their crowns before the throne, what else are they doing but ascribing the real and true kingship, and victory over all, to God who is over all? They are saying, "To you, Master, glory is owed by all, as Creator and Maker, who brings things from non-being into being, and who preserves and sustains them."
On the book sealed with seven seals, which is in the hand of God and which no one of created nature can open.

And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a book written inside and outside, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the book and to break its seals?” And no one in heaven, or on earth, or under the earth was able to open the book or to look into it. And I wept much, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to look into it. And one of the elders said to me, “Do not weep.”

The book was seen at the right hand of God. It means to indicate the right-handed courses of life of the saints of the Old and the New Testaments. What is at God's right hand hints at the goods of the soul. Solomon, the author of Proverbs, likewise shows that these are laid up in the right hand of wisdom, and he indicated them by “life” when he said, “In her right hand is life.” What is at the left hand means the things of the body and of this mortal life, which he hinted at by glory and wealth when he said, “In her left hand are wealth and glory.” As for the throne, it has already been said that it signifies the authority and supremacy of the one seated on it. And what is the book? The all-wise and unerring memory of God. The prophet David and Moses both pointed to it: the one when he said, “All shall be written in your book,” the other when he said, “Blot me too out of the book that you have written.” The book is written inside and outside and secured with seven seals. Written inside would be those from Jerusalem, as people who fear God under the guidance of the law. Written outside, and with the lesser portion, would be those from the nations who turned away from the gentile life and from idolatry. The seven seals take their significance from the number seven and signify the changes and successions of days in this mortal world. What else, then, would they give us to understand, except that no one but God alone can know precisely the course of each of our lives? Either this, then, or else the closing of the book is meant to show that no one has been deemed worthy of divine regard except a very few. For all have turned aside, together they have become worthless, with the worthlessness that came from Adam's sin, and they have lost their freedom of speech before God. But when you hear “all,” do not suppose that no one has been deemed worthy of God's watchful care, but call to mind Abraham and Moses and the inspired company of those like them. For “all” does not always take in the whole of what the statement refers to. Sometimes it falls short of being all-inclusive, because some are left out of its total, as in “All the land was taking its meal.” For this means “for the most part,” not “altogether.”
And no one was able.

No human being was able. But the Lamb certainly was, as has already been said. This was also said through David in the words, “In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you, and you will look upon me.” By “morning” he means the Lord's coming in the flesh. Through that coming we human beings were deemed worthy of divine regard when we stood before him, that is, when we were deemed worthy to stand before the one who raises up what has been cast down and binds up what has been broken. For these reasons his compassionate coming to us was arranged, and through it the prayers of the divine prophets were heard, among them this one: “Bow the heavens and come down.”
No one in heaven above, or on earth, or under the earth was able to open the book or to look into it.

No human being, most divine Angel, one might say to him. Only God who became man could, he who took away sin, tore up the bond that stood against us, by his own obedience [?] our disobedience [?], and wrestled again and reversed our defeat.
And I wept, because no one was found worthy.

For neither an angel nor a human being accomplished these things for us, as Isaiah says: “Not an envoy, not an angel, but he himself saved them, because he loved them.” So none of the bodiless beings, none of those who are in the flesh, and none of those who have departed from the flesh has received exact knowledge of divine things. This is what the book's being folded shut shows: that the judgments of God are beyond the conception of every created nature. That is why they are likened to an abyss: “For the judgments of God,” says David, “are a great deep.” So to created nature the book is folded shut. Not only is no one able to open it; no one can even look into it, that is, no one has had the strength even to gaze steadily at the divine judgments. For how could those who have had the misfortune of being distracted by toil over material things, their mind's eye disabled as if by a mist, be granted the good fortune of beholding divine things? Yet for those so full of unworthiness, once the coming of the Lamb was present to them, what had been impassable became easy to pass, and what had been hard became light and easy. This can be learned from the many people today who count attachment to the affairs of this life as nothing and turn their zeal to what is pleasing to God.

Another interpretation. “The unworthiness of all,” he says, “became the cause of my lamentation, but one of the elders consoled me.” As we have already set out, some take these elders to be among the heavenly powers. They are elders not by age, for they received their being all at once and together, as David said of them, since they were made by God: “For he spoke, and they came into being.” So the word “elders” must be reckoned not by age but by honor. In the same way, in Daniel, in the case of Susanna, those who turned to Daniel himself said, “Come, sit among us and tell us, since God has given you the rank of an elder.” So “elders” should be understood not by age but by honor, that is, by rank and by nearness to what is higher. Yet even nearness is not meant here in a literal sense, for what place can there be for beings made up of immateriality? Rather, they are near in that they resemble it in immateriality and purity. For divine beings are not all of one kind, any more than the things that come into being.
And one of the elders.

One of the elders, that is, of the more divine powers. They too are filled with joy because of their bond with us, as the Lord says: “There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.” If this is so over one sinner, how great must the joy be over many? It is because of this joy that the Lamb came, and he opened the book so that we might know the one who came for our salvation. And the Lord himself teaches us that this is so when he says, “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered.

He conquered the devil, the one who had conquered us. And who is the one who conquered? He who as God is a lion, of whom the patriarch Jacob prophesied, “Lying down… like a lion,” the lion of the tribe of Judah. He is called “the root of David” because he is creator by virtue of his divinity, and yet he also comes from the root of David. For it has been said that from the root of David a rod and a flower would spring up, and the God-wise Paul says, “For it is evident that our Lord Jesus Christ has sprung from Judah.” For Christ is the root, as we have said, and he also comes from the root of David. He is the root as God, the root not only of David but of every intelligible and sensible nature. And he comes from the root of David according to his humanity.
He who opens the book and its seven seals.

There are seven seals because the number seven corresponds to this present perishable life. Some of the Fathers also applied to it Solomon's saying about giving a portion to seven and also to eight. Those who have leisure for such matters would know by whom these things are said and what they concern [?]. Philo the Hebrew discusses them at length in the treatise he entitled Allegory of the Sacred Laws.
On the Lamb with the seven horns, and how he opened the book.

And I saw, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as if it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he came and took the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.
A Lamb standing as if it had been slain.

The Lamb is Christ, who was also prefigured by the lamb sacrificed at the Passover of the Law. And through Isaiah he speaks in the person of Christ: "But I was like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, and I did not know"; and again: "like a lamb silent before its shearer," and whatever follows this passage, depicting for us most vividly the passion of the God-man. That he is said to be not "slain" but "as if slain" shows that he did not remain in death. For Christ came back to life, according to the prophecy of David, "You will not abandon my soul to Hades," which recounts the resurrection, together with all that is discerned in the words that follow this passage. I mean the Lord's being held in Hades for three days. For this is the meaning of "nor let your holy one see" — not "corruption," but "decay." Corruption signifies the separation of the soul from the body, and none of the truly pious Christians denies that Christ underwent this. But decay he did not undergo. For he was not subjected to the complete dissolution of the human parts; rather, at the very moment when decay should have set in, the resurrection was accomplished and blunted the decay. This is also why the Lord's stay in death lasted three days, if indeed we may accept the writer of natural history who says that the bodies of the dead, when they are not consumed by fire, hold out for three days, still animated by natural life, and from then on are handed over to corruption, or rather to decay.
Having seven horns.

"Horns" signify power and glory, as divine Scripture is well able to show: concerning power, when it says, "I will shatter all the horns of sinners"; and concerning glory, "and the horn of the righteous will be exalted." So too when Hannah, the mother of Samuel, offering a boast of thanksgiving to the Lord, sings: "My horn is exalted in my God; my mouth is opened wide over my enemies."
Which are the seven spirits of God.

Why they are seven has also been explained earlier. These seven spirits are the operations of the Spirit: of wisdom, of understanding, of knowledge, of counsel, and of strength, of godliness, and of the fear of God. These are the operations that have been at work in the saints throughout all the earth.
And he took the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.

For whatever one does, even by means connected with virtue, is not accomplished unless it is strengthened by help from above. That is why it is said, "It depends not on the one who wills, nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy," since the earth too is full of the mercy of the Lord. The Lamb's taking the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on the throne must be understood with respect to his humanity, as must his being slain. For with respect to the divinity, nothing of what befits God is divided [?] among the three hypostases except the mode of origin: of the unbegotten, the begotten, and the proceeding. What the right hand is, we have already explained.

Concerning the time-references in the account of the present vision — that the divine Apostle who recounts these things moves among them without distinction, sometimes treating them as past, sometimes as present, and at times as future — we have already spoken, and, I think, to good effect.
And seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.
As it is said: "The eyes of the Lord are over all the earth, watching the good and the evil."

And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sing a new song, saying: "You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you bought us for God from every tribe and tongue and people and nation, and made us kings and priests to our God, and we shall reign on the earth."

Some have interpreted the living creatures as preeminent divine powers which display God's almighty rule over the world fashioned from four elements, since that is what they are; this is why they are stationed around the throne, as heralds, so to speak, of God's oversight of this fourfold world. Others take them as powers, but as overseers of the elements from which this universe came into being, preserving their continuance — just as Moses also teaches that an angel has been appointed by God to preside over each nation. Who the elders are, and why there are so many, we have already said.
They fell down before the Lamb.

When the Lord took the scroll, all worshipped, foreseeing the salvation he was about to accomplish for human beings and the punishment for the unclean demons. That the elders hold harps shows the harmony and sweet sound of the glorification offered to God, as David also says: "Praise him with psaltery and harp." The psaltery signifies receiving the hymn to God through cooperation from above [?], since it alone of the [?] instruments has the source of its sounds above. The harp, on the other hand, has its hollow below, and resounds [?] with pleasure to the plectrum that strikes the strings. [?] seems to [?] the glorification that comes from things below and around us, sending it up at the same time [?] to God, so that no distraction, however great, can keep us from sending up our thanksgiving to God, and so that we reckon everything that distracts us an occasion for salvation, which the good [?] Giver allots to us. For what that is not good would the Good One award? But he does so in order that, by setting endurance against even what seems to be whole, they may find a greater recompense — if indeed it is truly so that "each will receive his wage according to his own labor." The golden bowls are the minds of those who do what is pleasing to God; that is why they are signified by gold, the material most precious among us, since by their persistent ascent toward the divine they have attained a preciousness that grows by progress. From these minds rise the incense offerings that breathe out the remedy for God's just wrath against us, a match for our evil practices. That is why it says "incense" and not "spices." For a remedy, according to the one who said it, "will put an end to great sins." And that the prayers of the saints intercede with God as a remedy for wrath is clear. From the Old Testament, in the words of Samuel: "If anyone sins against God, they will pray for him." [?] soothing God's wrath against the Hebrews for their transgression, when the Godhead declared that it would destroy them, he blunted the divine anger with a most soothing intercession, by saying, "Egypt will hear, and all who have heard your name." Indeed, as for what the Lord said to Peter — Satan's demand for Peter himself, "that he might sift him like wheat," and Christ's prayer for Peter — who would think so little of it as to deny that the prayers of those who love God are a remedy for sins? And from the New Testament, in that the Lord's divine disciples received authority to loose and to bind sins. They sing a new song because the propitiation for wrath is also new, namely Christ slain as a Lamb for the cleansing and salvation of the whole world. For this reason it was granted to him to open the scroll and loose its seals, as the one who bought us with his blood from every nation and every tongue. For this is the new song, through which we who have been illumined from all the earth, freed from the oldness of the written Law and walking in newness of life, have been taught by the divine Spirit to sing songs of thanksgiving.
And to open its seals.

That the scroll is sealed shows that those written in it have no freedom to speak, and that it is not from their own achievements but from God's love for humankind that they receive the call back to salvation. This is why the divine Paul, having drawn from divine Scripture a heavy indictment of human nature for its waywardness, adds: "These things are said to show that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world held accountable to God"; and that it is not from our own achievements but by the grace of God that we have had the good fortune to be saved. "For by grace," he says, "we have been saved."
From every tribe and tongue.

He spoke very carefully in saying "from every tribe and tongue and nation," and not "every tribe and tongue and nation," because not all were acquired for God. For many died in their sins. In harmony with this is what David sings: "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you will take as your inheritance" — not all the earth, but "among all the nations."

The account is given not in the past tense, of a stretch of time already elapsed, but in the present; for this song of thanksgiving is offered up to God without interruption throughout the present age until its consummation, never ceasing to be actively sung.

Saying "from every tribe and tongue" rather than "every tribe and tongue" introduces a distinction: not all, but some, have been counted worthy, through their own labors, to be bought by the blood of the slain Lamb.
And you made us kings and priests to our God.

This they already receive in fulfillment from now on, according to the letter, inasmuch as they continue to be kings and priests, servants of God in the faith. But it can also be understood more contemplatively: kings are those who have bound on the royal crown of victory over the passions, and priests are those who have prepared themselves as a living sacrifice well-pleasing to God. In keeping with this interpretation, anyone who holds that this refers to the land promised by the Lord as an inheritance to the meek would not be counted among those who miss the mark.
And we shall reign on the earth.

The promise of reigning refers to future time, as the divine Paul also holds when he says: "And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised"; and he gives the reason: "so that they should not be made perfect apart from us." Some, it is true, did obtain promises, as Abraham obtained the promised birth of Isaac and the title of father of many nations. But since in this corruptible life nothing is perfect or worthy of the surpassing perfection of the one who made the promise, the promise could not reach its fulfillment in the giving and receiving of such things. What, then, does this mean: "and they shall reign on the earth"? In the obvious sense, the one visible to most people, it hints at the way of life under the Law, which was more introductory and elementary than the most perfect commonwealth in Christ, inasmuch as the Law made nothing perfect. But in its true sense it hints at the blessed life to come, which is eternal and indestructible. That is why it also embraces what is perfect. [?] And it is right to await the reception and enjoyment of it together with all who have contended for it. For it would not befit a just judge of the games, while the labor of the arena is still unfinished — some athletes already released from their toil, others still competing, and for others the contest still to come — to throw open the blessed banquet hall to [?] all before the appointed feast, as though overcome by an incontinent gluttony. And it is uncertain, moreover, whether the banquet of the divine wedding would be granted to all who have been invited but have not put on the wedding garment. So much on these matters.

And I looked, and I heard what sounded like the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders; and their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: "Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power and wealth and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing." And every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and on the sea, and all that is in them, I heard saying: "To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might for ever and ever. Amen." And the four living creatures said, "Amen," and the elders fell down and worshipped.

Why it says "around the throne" and mentions the four living creatures: "around" is meant to signify the intellectual life occupied with divine things, while the four living creatures signify the providence that holds this universe together, which does not lack divine oversight and supervision.
And their number was.

We hear this from the visions of Daniel, where he gives the number of those who minister to God. It is not that they are only so many — for what number could encompass the human beings transferred to the service of God from the beginning of time until the consummation of this life, especially if they are joined to the intellectual ministers as well? But since it was not possible to encompass more in a number, "thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand" [?] signifies the multitude of ministers by the largest number known to us.

The voice is real, but not perceptible to the senses or resounding in the air. That is why the vote proclaiming the Lamb is recounted as belonging to time still to come, and not as something already completed; inasmuch as everyone who commits himself to God, right up to the consummation, is driven by a sober madness, through the memory of the sufferings the Lamb underwent for us in his love for humankind, to hasten to make the Master some return, even if only a servant's. For to speak of a return made as between equals would be superfluous; what great thing is it for a slave to suffer what his master suffered? As for the decree assigning to him, as honors, wealth and power and wisdom and the like, as though for the exaltation of the one receiving them, as if he did not already have them — this is borrowed from human ways of thinking. For the divine has no need of these things, being above all honor, and the whole of what received its being from him falls short of honoring worthily the one who brought it forth. But although creation has so little to give in return, he himself, to whom these things are zealously offered, measures the gifts by the intention and counts them as worthy.
And every creature, and what follows.

By all these — although he has no need of it — the intelligible, I mean, and the sensible, both living things and things that simply exist by their natural principles, God is glorified as the origin of all things; and so are his only-begotten and consubstantial Son and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit. For, as has often been said, no one of the hypostases of the divine Trinity is set apart from what befits God except only in mode of existence; the Son grants renewal to man and to the creation that came to be for man's sake, even if he is said to have received [?] the authority over things in heaven and on earth because of the humanity he assumed.
And the four living creatures.

And through this is shown a single flock of angels and human beings, brought to completion through Christ and standing under one shepherd, Christ; and a single Church through Christ, who broke down the dividing wall of partition that the disobedience of Adam, our first father, had built around us. Together with the twenty-four elders — who they are and to whom they are likened has already been said — they are counted worthy to hymn and worship God, fulfilling the words "all things, your works, are your servants." "Amen" is taken from the Hebrew language and is uttered to express firm assent; it is equivalent to "yes," "truly," and "unalterably so."
And the elders.

The prostration of the elders together with the four living creatures (what these creatures are images of has been stated), as those who represent the full number of the saved, showed by their worship that to the Lamb, for having been slain, is given authority over things in heaven, on earth and under the earth. This we can hear from him himself, saying after his resurrection from the dead: "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me." And even if the gift dates from the very beginning, from his conception — which is why the account also speaks of these things as having already happened, for the gift was there from the moment he was a Lamb — nevertheless it became clearer and better known to all when the dispensation of things on earth reached its end.

The loosing of the first seal, signifying the apostolic teaching. And I saw when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as with a voice of thunder, "Come and see." And behold, a white horse, and its rider had a bow; and a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering and to conquer.

If the sealing of the scroll shows that those written in it have no freedom to speak, and that the mouth of all is stopped before God against every plea of self-justification, as was said above, then the gradual removal of the seals would signify the step-by-step recovery of the freedom to speak to God and of intimacy with him, which he who became our kinsman by becoming man procured for us, setting right our offenses by his own achievements. Here, too, the good order of the heavenly beings is signified, descending from the first ranks to the second. That is why John heard the first voice come from one face among the four living creatures, namely the lion, commanding "Come." And "Come" should be understood as addressed, by way of hint, to the angel who gives the vision its shape, not to the Apostle who beholds the vision. The first living creature, the lion, seems to me to display the kingly spirit of the apostles against the demons. Hence it is said, "The kings of the earth gathered together," and, "You will make them rulers over all the earth." There are some who have taken the loosing of each seal to refer to the Lord's saving incarnation for our sake. The first they take to be the birth, which loosed us from the bonds of fleshly generation, as Paul also holds when he writes: "Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy" — "unclean" as having their existence from fleshly corruption, "holy" as conformed to the incorruptible birth of the one who came to dwell among us from a virgin, and to divine baptism, the second regeneration, which washed away from us the shame of fleshly generation. So much for the first and second seals: the birth from the virgin, and the birth through holy baptism, which, since it is a birth of light, is joined to the birth from the virgin as its equal.
