The loosing of the third seal they take as the working of the Lord's divine signs that followed; of the fourth, as his being brought before Pilate; of the fifth, as his being nailed to the cross; of the sixth, as his being laid in the tomb; of the seventh, as his despoiling of Hades. Some, in turn, have judged these interpretations inconsistent with the contents of the Apocalypse, since these events came before it, whereas the Apocalypse is a revelation disclosing things present and to come. To this we will say: even if these things happened earlier, nevertheless, since the loving-kindness of the Godhead shown in what has already happened is also beheld by each of the saved until the consummation, there is nothing unfitting in counting these things among what was seen in the vision.
And behold, a white horse.

The white horse is a symbol of the apostolic preaching of the Gospel, since through it and through the generation of the apostles the greatest benefit was to come to humankind. The rider on the horse is the one to whom the same most divine Habakkuk solemnly sings, "You mounted your horses upon the sea"; and the bow is the one of which the same Habakkuk prophesies, saying, "Bending, you will bend your bow against scepters, says the Lord." By "bow" he hints at the apostles and the apostolic preaching, aimed against the scepters of demonic authority, which the divine Paul also pointed to when he wrote, "the ruler of this air, which is now at work in the sons of disobedience." And since the release of arrows follows the bending of the bow, the same prophet fittingly indicated the release of the arrows and the reason for it, saying: "Your darts will go forth into the brightness of lightning." What does he mean by this? The gaining of light for the nations darkened by the madness of idolatry, when the coming of the Lord, like brightness, spread over the whole region under heaven and made effective the weapons sharpened by its [?], that is, by the knowledge of God.
Having a bow.

Of the bow it has been said that it hinted at the apostles and the generation of their time, who shot forth the preaching like arrows and brought to God those wounded by the saving arrows. The crown was received by these same most blessed apostles because by the truth they had conquered the author of error, in hope of a second victory: confessing the Master's name even unto death.
And he went out conquering and to conquer.

For by saying "conquering" he indicated one not newly brought into the contest but already trained in other victories, one who had passed the test. Christ was the one "conquering, that he might conquer." Having won the first victory, the turning of the nations from idols — from which he is named "conquering" — he made ready for a second victory, the one over [?] the mortal body: through punishments he trains, as athletes are anointed, those who hold fast to the confession of his name, and crowns them with the crown, the symbol of their victory.
The loosing of the second seal, showing the war of the unbelievers against the believers.

And when he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come and see.” And another horse came out, a red one, and its rider was allowed to take peace from the earth, so that people would slaughter one another. And he was given a great sword.

The second living creature is the calf. It stands for the sacred and spiritual sacrifices of the holy martyrs, while the first creature depicts the authority of the apostles, as has already been said. Some, as we noted earlier, took the opening of the first seal to mean Christ's birth from the Virgin. To match this, they have thought it right to take the opening of the second seal as Christ's baptism in the Jordan and the temptation that followed it, in which the Lord won the victory by putting the devil who tempted him to shame. So the wicked one was to learn that he could be beaten as well as beat others. He was no longer to bite the horseman's heel and trip up our steps toward God. Instead he would fall back like a slave and hear “Get behind me, Satan” from a man he thought he had wrestled to the ground, because he did not know that this man was God. Now for the first time he recognized his own shame and weakness. He had boasted that he would set his throne above the clouds, in the words the divine Isaiah gives him, but he did not get his wish. Instead he got a bed spread beneath him, and the rot of his pride was his reward.
Peace from the earth.

We may take this second seal as the succession of the apostles, which we know was carried on by martyrs and teachers. In that age, as the preaching spread more widely, the peace of the world was broken up and human nature was divided against itself. This fulfilled the Lord's words: “I did not come to bring peace on earth, but a sword,” and to set father and son, daughter and mother, daughter-in-law and mother-in-law against one another to the point of bloodshed. From that time on, the martyrs' sacrifices were offered up to the altar above. The red horse is a symbol of one of two things. It may stand for the martyrs' shed blood. Or it may stand for their fiery love of Christ, which made death seem sweeter to them than life. The text says that the horse's rider was allowed to take peace away. This shows that God, in his perfect wisdom, permits this in order to test his faithful servants through trials.
And he was given a great sword.

The rider of the red horse was given a sword so that people would slaughter one another. That is, it was given to divide and cut apart the harmony that people on earth had in doing evil. They were united in idolatry. “So that they would slaughter one another” means that they would destroy one another's pacts for evil. This is what the uprising of father against son and of daughter-in-law against mother-in-law hints at. The new, turned toward the Lord's way of worshipping God, rise against the old ways, which were more shadowy and had strayed far from what is true and more fitting [?].
The opening of the third seal, which shows the falling away of those who did not hold firmly to their faith in Christ.

And when he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come and see.” And there was a black horse, and its rider held a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying, “A measure of wheat for a denarius, and three measures of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the oil and the wine.”

The third living creature is called the man here, and it points to the falling away of human beings. For this reason the punishment that comes on it is heavier than the falling away. Others, as was said before, say that the opening of the third seal points to Christ's mercy toward us. He did not repay those condemned for turning away from him with a punishment equal to our sins. Instead he did us good through his saving teachings and divine signs, and so he advanced the overthrow of the devil. Through these we learned who is God by nature and truly God. So we were no longer to be tossed about like children by every wind of teaching, nor to worship things our hands have made, exchanging the glory of God for destructive demons. For the teaching of our God and Savior drew all who were taught, as leaven works through flour, as the Lord said. They also enjoyed his miracles, which healed souls more than * * *
And there was a black horse.

The black horse is a symbol of gloom and mourning. The divine instruction had made the devil's overthrow more complete, and so he mourns his own undoing, now that he has been swamped by the martyrs' blood. For so long he had ruled over human nature. The scales stand for fairness and justice: “For you have sat on the throne,” says David, “you who judge rightly.”

[?] the black horse as a sign of mourning and gloom. But this is not the mourning of the tyrant, as we said earlier. It is the mourning of those who were deceived and fell away from faith in Christ, either because they could not bear the punishments or because they wanted the passing pleasures of this pitiful life. The scales test two groups. Some fell away through a fickle mind or vanity. Others, weak in body, were stripped of their faith in Christ by tortures they could not bear. Some have in fact thought it right to explain the passage this way. Since the black horse is a symbol of mourning, they sort out the different people who have cause to mourn. I have set out both views and am content to leave them to my readers' fair and steady judgment.

Another interpretation. The scales, then, are a symbol of God's just judgment. That is why people came to speak out boldly, saying, “You have upheld my right and my cause. You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly one perished.” The ungodly one is the devil, who held them in his power like a tyrant.

This was so that we Gentiles might know that we are human beings, honored with reason, and not like cattle dragged by muzzle and bridle and herded by the demons who tyrannize us. Some of the copies read “I heard a voice” and leave out the comparative word “as.” But leaving it out is not quite right, because the setting of the vision usefully calls for the comparison. What is revealed here is not things that actually exist and act. It is appearances, types and symbols. So “as” is naturally called for by the setting, since it shows that the thing seen matches or corresponds to what it stands for. Besides, it is no clearer to say “voice” without the comparison, as in “I heard a voice saying.” A voice is something spoken, so what else could it do on its own? If someone insists that the text reads “a voice saying,” he misses the point. A voice is spoken; it does not speak. That is why it is called something spoken, since it is the product of the speaker. A product of this kind, produced to convey something, is not complete in itself and cannot produce something like itself. It does not even exist in its own right. It vanishes the moment it is uttered, once its use is over. So if “voice” is to be kept, then instead of “saying” we should read [?] “declaring.”
A measure of wheat for a denarius.

Wheat being sold at a high price is a sign of famine, and such a famine did take place, as will be said later. The passage can also be read figuratively. The wheat is those who competed by the rules for Christ's sake. They were judged worthy of a denarius because they had faithfully guarded the divine image given to them. The three measures of barley are those who [?] like cattle before the judges out of cowardice, but who later repented to a matching degree and washed the soiled image clean with tears. These three measures were valued at one denarius because of the one Christ and his three days in the tomb. He lay there for the sake of the whole world, which had soiled with sin the divine image given to it. He spent the first day in Hades for those who sinned before the law of Moses, and the second for those who lived under the law. Some of them had indeed shown repentance for the wrongs they had done and set it against those wrongs. But they did not yet have a clear hope of forgiveness, because the one who could grant it had not yet been seen, and so they had not yet received it. That is the reason for the second day in Hades. The third day was the day on which he also rose, because Life itself could not be held by decay. So at the very moment decay was to begin, incorruption was brought in instead. This has been discussed more fully and clearly earlier.

Some did not take the wheat as ordinary wheat, which feeds the body and whose shortage causes a real famine. They took the wheat as the word of teaching, which Scripture also figuratively calls seed. So Matthew writes, “The sower went out to sow his seed,” turning the word of the gospel into seed. In the same way the most loyal servants said to their master, “Sir, did you not sow good seed in your field? Then where do the weeds come from?” Seed includes both wheat and barley. The wheat, then, would be the saving word of the gospel. It suits mature people whose faculties have been trained to tell good from evil. The barley is the law of Moses. Just as barley ripens before wheat, so the law came before the preaching of the gospel. It feeds the more animal-like people, the Israelites, given how they were disposed toward divine things. So the one who speaks in the midst of the four living creatures says that a measure of wheat sells for a denarius, but three measures of barley do. The gospel preaching is harder to keep [?] because of the strictness of the book. That is why it lies before the violent as a prize to be seized, sold for a single denarius. The measure of wheat gives those who seek it the image engraved on them from the beginning. Three measures sell for a denarius because it is acceptable for those who come to Christ's preaching in a more ordinary way to bear the divine image formed in them by holy baptism, even if they go on living by the introductory observances of Moses. To show that most people live this way, the number that begins plurality, namely three, was used to indicate it. As for the shortage of life-giving food, you could also call it a shortage of the gospel life described above by the Lord. This is clear from the lawyer. He confirmed that the Lord himself had lived by the observances of the law, and then he heard that he should keep these as enough for salvation. These divine foods were scarce at that time, when, as we find, a famine was sent: a famine not of bread or of water, but of the word. These things came on them because they deserved them. Still, the voice says not to destroy the oil that comes through turning back to God. This is what the sparing of the wine and the oil hints at, as was also said before.
The opening of the fourth seal, which shows the corrective scourges brought on those who denied the Lord because they could not endure.

And when he opened the fourth seal, I heard the fourth living creature say, “Come and see.” And there was a pale horse, and its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a quarter of the earth, to kill with the sword, with famine, with death, and by the wild beasts of the earth.
The fourth living creature is the eagle, which is sharp-sighted and quick to seize its prey. It shows that the blows come from above, out of divinely sent wrath, bringing vengeance for the godly.
And there was a pale horse.

The pale horse is a symbol of wrath. Physicians, too, call bile “pale green.” Death and Hades, understood spiritually, took their stand to make war on the accursed demons and to make them pay for the ruin of human beings. But the account does not yet bring in the complete overthrow of the demons, only that of a quarter of them. This is because, by the logic of the vision before us, it had not yet been accomplished in keeping with [?] the third passion of Christ. The account calls this overthrow “slaughter” figuratively. By “famine” it means the falling away of those who once worshipped the demons and the end of their tyranny. It also speaks of destruction by the wild beasts. The “beasts of the earth” are the demons' attacks and assaults on us, which lead us into destructive passions. They are also the hold the demons gain over us through vanity, for example, through shameful acts and through passions of that kind. These suit us, since we are made of earth. The demons have no bodies, yet they still delight in the passions that wallow on the earth. For it smolders beneath them and devours them as they are thrown out of their rule over humankind, from which [?] Adam … the self-destruction of God's creature, which they contrived out of envy, came about.

[This shows] that healing through turning back to God is not set aside. Christ pointed to this healing through the man who fell among robbers. The oil hints at the gladness of the one who anoints. The wine stands for one who shows kindness without being slack, pouring it on with a certain sharpness and care. This is Christ, who [makes sure] that sinners are not snatched away by death too soon, since through his patience they would go on to win back what they had lost.

In chapter 15 there is the passage “I heard a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying.” In some copies it appears, quite properly, with the comparative “as” added. These copies also change the case and gender of the word that goes with the voice. So the text reads, “I heard as it were a voice in the midst of the four living creatures,” where “saying” agrees not with “voice” but with the one who speaks. The passage set beside the text will show why the reading with this addition and the change of gender and case is the better one.

Another interpretation, from Andrew. Eusebius, son of Pamphilus, writes as follows in the eighth chapter of the ninth book of his Ecclesiastical History. At the height of the persecutions, when Maximinus was emperor of the Romans, famine and plague struck the people along with other calamities. Countless multitudes died, so many that they could not be buried, even though the Christians of that time devoted themselves eagerly to burials and through their kindness led those who had gone astray to the knowledge of the truth. Many were also killed by the sword when the Armenians rose against the Romans. He says that the bodies of the dead were eaten by dogs, so that in the end the survivors took to killing the dogs. They were afraid that when they died, the dogs would become living tombs for them as well. It is quite likely that wild beasts, too, shared the same feast with the dogs, because there was food in plenty. In our own generation, too, we have seen each of these things happen, as present events show.
The opening of the fifth seal, which shows the holy souls crying out to the Lord that the end may come.

And when he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slaughtered for the word of God and for the testimony of the Lamb that they held. And they cried out in a loud voice, saying, “How long, holy and true Master, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” And they were given a white robe, and they were told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers who were to be killed as they had been was complete.

Some, as we have already noted, assign the four earlier seals to Christ's sufferings and to what he accomplished for us in the plan of his saving incarnation. They will naturally connect the opening of the fifth seal, and this outcry, with the prophets and the wise men of God who died before. These men longed for Christ's coming and were troubled by its delay. So they cried out against God's patience, which lasted all the way to the cross. They cried for vengeance on wicked and ungodly men, or else on the demons who had driven those men into a frenzy. They complained that God had allowed such wrongs to be done to them by their own people and kin, while they endured suffering for the sake of godliness. Until the saving passion on the cross, God's vengeance on the ungodly was not so plain to see. But from then on the ungodly met with countless disasters. So says Josephus, if he can be believed. He loved the truth and recorded that not only Jews but also Greeks were wiped out by plagues, famines and civil strife against one another, as we noted a little earlier. It would be pointless to speak of the destruction of the demons and their complete disappearance, since we hear the divine David sing, “The swords of the enemy have failed for ever.” For where is the worship of demons still to be found, though before this they had filled the whole earth with their error? This is how it reads if we apply the outcry to those dear to God before the law and under the law. But if we apply it to the martyrs after Christ, which is the better choice since the oracle also concerns things to come, we would not be straying from what is reasonable.
I saw under the altar.

The altar is naturally the one above, which needs no blood to make it holy. Because the victims were earthly and of mortal nature, it set them apart in the place beneath it. The altar takes up the fragrance rising from the victims, which is pleasing to God. This fragrance cannot be perceived by the senses, since it is not subject to them, even though the vapor that rises from victims can be perceived. In the same way, it is seen by the mind alone. This holds for the martyrs and for all who are counted acceptable because they have finished their good struggles. So the opening of the seal is more fittingly assigned to those who won approval in Christ or after Christ than to those who, before Christ's coming, [suffered] for the godliness of the old [?] … not with a sound the senses can hear. For what arrangement of vocal organs lies beneath it? Rather, the delay itself, stretched out so long, does the work of a voice for those who see it. The outcry does not mean that the Most High is neglecting them, as if he did not care for his own works, not even as much as a father cares for his children. To know how he arranges everything fittingly and in order is beyond our knowledge. We know only as much as encourages those still living not to lose heart when the good things owed to them are delayed. For he is not ready to give them without a purpose.
And for the testimony of the Lamb that they held.
From the mention of the Lamb, and of the slaughter for his sake, the opening of the fifth seal can now, beyond dispute, be assigned to those who came after Christ and lived in Christ.
How long, Master.

The vengeance is not asked for against human beings, for it is not worthy of love to rise up against one's own kind. The saints demand it against the demons, who lead human beings to their own destruction. Then they receive first a white robe, and with this robe they also learn the reason for the delay. The delay is not drawn out without testing them, but for very good reasons, as the passages that follow will show.

Another interpretation, from Andrew. In these words the saints seem to be asking for the end of the world. That is why they are told to wait patiently until their brothers are made perfect, so that they are not made perfect without them, as the divine Apostle says. The white robes show the brightness of the virtues blossoming on them. Clothed in this brightness, they have not yet received what was promised. Yet they rightly rejoice in the hope of it, which they see in the mind as if in a mirror, freed from all bodily heaviness, while they rest in Abraham's bosom. Many of the saints have said that each one who labored at virtue has received a place worthy of him, and from this they also infer the glory to come.
And they were given a white robe.

The white robe is a figure of their having been [?] by their own blood and having put off all filth. At the same time, the whiteness of the robe suggests something else. These martyrs openly and brilliantly confessed Christ, and for that confession they patiently endured leaving this perishable and troubled world. Now that they have reached the harbor of a life free from decay and toil, they should not grow weary of it, as if they had had their fill, and pull back from it [?]. For this reason one of the God-inspired writers has recorded that the angels long to look into the eternal good things. In looking, what else would he be seeking? Or do they persist in unceasing longing just to gain a little knowledge of them? So it is as if the robe reminds them: if you struggled toward the painful and wearisome [lacuna], it is no less praiseworthy now, in a life free from toil, to rise above weariness. This is what the giving of the white robe hints at. And with words of encouragement it tells them [lacuna] to restrain their craving for the truly desirable things stored up for them. For it is not right for them to get ahead of those hurrying with equal zeal to be counted among them by receiving these things first. It is true that they have not yet received the good news, but they live in the hope of it. They see it in the mind as if in a mirror, freed from all bodily heaviness, and, as is fitting, they rejoice in Abraham's bosom. Even so, it is not right that the great festival of all the saved should be seen as incomplete. Nor is it right that God should take his stand in the assembly of the gods and yet no longer judge among them. For how can there be a judgment while some are still missing who are to receive their judgment justly, according to their labor?
The opening of the sixth seal, which shows the plagues to be brought on at the end.

And I saw when he opened the sixth seal: there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth made of hair, and the whole moon became like blood, and the stars of heaven fell to the earth, as a fig tree drops its unripe figs when it is shaken by a great wind.

The loosing of the sixth seal brought about our salvation in its most complete form. For in it Christ destroyed death, restored life, and stripped the conqueror of humankind of his crown, triumphing over him, as it is written: "You ascended on high, you led captivity captive." What, then, is the loosing of the sixth seal? It is the cross of the Lord and his death. These were followed by the resurrection, which all long for, both believed and perceived [?]. It opens up [?] for us a new and living way back from death to life. It benefited not only the living but also those who had fallen asleep before. For when the Lord was in Hades he gave them hope of the promise of life: to those "who were once disobedient," in the words of the apostle Peter. But he gave this hope to those who believe, as Cyril also thinks; [?] for indeed to those who died in unbelief.
And there was a great earthquake.

The vision clearly paints for us once more the signs that took place at the cross: the earthquake and the shaking of the earth, the darkening of the sun, and the change of the whole moon into blood. The word "whole" is used very precisely of the moon. For the moon was full, being on its fourteenth day, and stood diametrically opposite the sun. How, then, could it darken the sun by passing beneath it? Those who have made a study of the subject say that a solar eclipse happens in that way. And again, how could the moon appear like this in the daytime? This is why Dionysius the Areopagite attributes what happened to the sun at the cross to a divine sign, and not to anything that ordinarily happens to the heavenly bodies. The prophet Joel also foretold this, saying, "The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood." This is a recollection of what happened before, as [?], just as has already been explained many times. For what was then accomplished for our sake out of love for humankind did not stop at that time. It has been appointed to remain at work until the end. For [?] whatever saving work may be carried out for us, if you look closely you will find that it bears the image of what took place in Christ our God during his sojourn among us. Thus our regeneration through divine baptism [?] the immaculate birth [?]. The laying in the manger [?] the birth from holy baptism, which through [?] his lying there sets us free from irrationality. And his presentation to the Father on the fortieth day [?] sets us free from the swaddling bands of infancy, that is, from the bonds of [?] that distract us in this life, so that he may preserve those who have come out through him [?] by his oversight, so that one may no longer return to the principles of birth, but may hasten to be restored to the original creation [?] given to human beings. In this way we have [?], in a modest measure at least, the things of the Lord. The rest must be taken up by those who are wiser, using these as starting points. "For give [?] an opportunity," says Solomon, "and the wise will become wiser." Some, however, have taken these things to refer to the siege that took place under Vespasian, and have interpreted everything said here figuratively.
And the sun became black.

Most interpreters, however, have said that "earthquake" here means the passage from the time of the persecutions for Christ's sake to the time of the Antichrist. Scripture is accustomed to call a change of affairs an "earthquake," as in "Yet once more I will shake." For, as the divine Paul says, this signifies the [?] of the things that are shaken. In the Old Testament, too, the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt is called an earthquake, as David says: "The earth shook, and indeed the heavens dropped rain." For they say there will be afflictions such as we have never known to happen before. They wisely foretold this so that people might prepare themselves in advance and not give up before the punishments that the Antichrist will inflict. The blackness of the sun and the lightless, bloody appearance of the moon show that those whom divine wrath has abandoned are left without light. The blessed Cyril often explained [?] it in this way. The falling of the stars means that even those who seem to be lights in the world fall, giving way before what is happening. As the Lord also says, "so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect," who are overcome by the severity of the affliction. That is why these are compared to the unripe figs, that is, the immature fruit, that the fig tree drops when it is shaken by the wind. They stand for those who have not yet ripened in faith over time and have not been sweetened by grace. Under the violent counterblasts of the devil, that is, troubled by the fierce assaults of temptations, they were shaken down. For Scripture knows how to use figs in two senses, both good and the opposite: as with the two baskets of figs shown to Jeremiah, good and bad together, and the withered fig tree mentioned in the Songs. Whether these things should also be taken literally must be left to whoever investigates the question, and before him to God, who knows what is plain [?].

And the heaven departed like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island was moved out of its place. And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the commanders, and the rich, and the mighty, and every slave and free man hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains. And they say to the mountains and the rocks, "Fall on us, and hide us from the face of the one who sits on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb; for the great day of his wrath has come, and who can be saved?"

We have already stated that these things happened at the cross of Christ. They are also recorded in the present Revelation as a reminder of what happened then. This shows that what was then lovingly accomplished for our sake keeps coming about without interruption, both now and in the future, and will never cease as long as this corruptible world remains. In each person who approaches salvation, the things accomplished at Christ's coming [?] in Christ, so that one may see such a person also portraying these things: being born [?], circumcised, and presented to the Father on the fortieth day. We have already explained, modestly and as far as we could, how the things of Christ take place in oneself.

Those who refer these things to Christ's sojourn in the flesh took [?] them to refer to the darkness at the cross. That darkness grew so thick that every heavenly light seemed to have vanished, and they say the passage hints at this. Or else it means that the heavenly powers of the angels were troubled at the outrage done to their own Master and were seized by a kind of dizziness [?], so that, like a scroll being shaken, they darted and shifted this way and that.
Like a scroll being rolled up.

The heaven being rolled up like a scroll hints at one of two things. It may point to the unknown [time] of Christ's second coming, for a scroll is opened silently and in an instant. Or it may mean that the heavenly powers grieve with those who fall away from the faith and will feel a kind of rolling up and sorrow. The rolling of the scroll also suggests another meaning: that the body of heaven does not undergo complete annihilation. Irenaeus of Lyons says this in the fifth book of his Refutation of Knowledge Falsely So Called, in these words: "For neither the substance nor the essence of creation will be annihilated, for true and steadfast is the one who established it. But the outward form of this world passes away, that is, the things in which the transgression took place. That is why David too says, 'You will renew the face of the earth,' and not 'You will change it.'" We think the apostle was following an ancient custom. For the Hebrews used rolls instead of the books we use, and unrolling them brought about not their destruction but the disclosure of what was written. In the same way, the unfolding of the body of heaven signifies the revelation of the good things stored up for the saints.
And every mountain and island.

By mountains and islands he means the bands of the proud demons, as it is written about them: "and mountains are carried into the heart of the seas." That is, they are carried into the salty distractions of the present life, among those who have no refreshing drinking water for salvation [?], plunging them into a bottomless depth of misfortunes, since these demons drive the faint-hearted about in pursuit of their own soul-destroying aim. The same beings are also called islands, because they trouble us amid the floods of life's misfortunes already mentioned. For they are contrivers who set obstacles in the way of our good voyage toward God. From this they gain their boastful height of vanity. That, then, is why they are called mountains and islands.
Were moved out of their places.

The places of the demons one might take to be [?] of the incorporeal demons; or their habitual purposes [?], which arise from envy of the human race. For we know of the opposite of this: the divine blessing that is brought forth "from his place." The prophetic word assigns this [?] to the incorporeal powers, [?] to God, who is contained by no place. It is sent up from the place of his loving judgments by those able to understand his ineffable mercy and his compassion over all his works.

[?] a most shameless impulse, since they were not content to remain in their rightful allotment. This impulse cut them off from the glory of the angels. The Lord too was a witness of this, seeing him, together with all the power under him, fall like lightning. As he says, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven." So, not content to remain in his allotment out of love, but ruled by shamelessness, he becomes a nuisance to human beings.
And the kings of the earth, and the great men.

By the kings of the earth, the great men, and all such grand titles, you should understand the same demons and their ruler Satan, who have ruled over earthly things through deceit and guile. By slaves and free, understand those among the demons who hold high rank and those who are subordinate. So their urging the mountains, with entreaties, to fall on them and hide them is meant figuratively. It hints that they become fugitives from the punishment that Christ will bring on them, a punishment in proportion to [?]. Hence, gripped by this fear, the demons in the Evangelist Matthew, as you hear, address Christ in terror: "What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?" But someone might also take these words to refer to those who crucified Christ. When the Maccabean [?] pressed hard on them, deserving of war as they were, through Titus and Vespasian, they became fugitives in the mountains and caves and holes of the earth, gripped by helplessness. Such a reader would not stray from what is written [?].

Another interpretation. When the apostles asked our Lord and God about the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem, and indeed about the end of the world, at which his second coming will also take place, he did not hesitate to instruct them as far as they could take it in. He did not do so distinctly, point by point, because their question was not of that kind either. Rather, they were asking about the fall of the temple and about the arrival of his coming, together with the signs that would follow. And since nearly the same things were bound to happen both at the fall of the temple, which was brought about by the Romans and Titus, and at the coming of the Lord, he set out in his discourse what they wanted to know. The present Revelation differs from what the Lord declared only in its timeframe. For what the Lord said is cast as events still to come, while the things in the present Revelation are cast as past. What did they mean to show by this? Only that it is true and cannot fail, as they present it as a work already accomplished. As for the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem, Josephus, a fellow tribesman of the Jews and a great lover of truth, shows clearly how much of what the Lord foretold to the apostles befell the Christ-killers. The outcome matched the prediction down to the smallest details, as one can learn from the mother who ate her own child, which Christ foretold when he said, "Woe to those who are nursing in those days." This is especially so when [God's wrath] is kindled by contempt for his commands and by disregard for the unsurpassed compassion of his Son. He was free from suffering, yet he endured sufferings while living among them, for their salvation. But they persisted in their contempt, incorrigible as they were [?], and were not even ashamed to inflict on him the further penalty of death on a cross.
For the great day of his wrath has come.

At the end, an extreme affliction will come with the arrival of the Antichrist, beyond all measure. It will not strike one part of the world, as at Jerusalem, but will fall on the whole world without delay. That terrible affliction, I say, will be brought on all who are eminent, whether in worldly power, whom he indicated by the kings, or in the good order of the Church, whom he figuratively called mountains and islands. By mountains and islands we have not understood simply the leaders of the churches. We follow what is found written in Isaiah about the islands being renewed: they will flee, moving from place to place because of the false Christ. And who are the kings of the earth, the great men and the commanders, and every slave and free man, if not those who wield power over earthly things and have given no thought to the commonwealth in heaven? The slaves are those enslaved to the vanity of the present world. The free, likewise, are those who have thrown off the service of Christ and chosen to live without restraint. They prefer the pleasure of the present age to the narrow and afflicted way, and care for nothing but the broad and spacious one. Therefore, out of fear either of the evils already hanging over them or of the unimaginable and endless punishments [?], they were reduced to despair and found the present life unlivable. For what provision for life could mountains and caves and rocks offer them, even if their prayer [?] for shelter?
Fall on us.

Whose prayer is this, addressed to the mountains? It belongs to those who did not build on the faith the precious material of good works and true doctrines, but built wood and hay, which cannot bear even the smell of an ordinary fire, let alone the threat of fire. For God, as they say, is fire.

And after this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, so that no wind might blow on the earth, or on the sea, or on any tree. And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, holding the seal of the living God. He cried out with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm the earth and the sea, saying, "Do not harm the earth, or the sea, or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads."

From here on, the Evangelist is shown clearly what befell the Jews in the war with the Romans, as a requital for the Lord's sufferings. For the four angels guarded the four corners of the land of the Jews. They filled them with fear of flight, or with certain hardships, or with the pain of exile from their homeland and their dearest wives. This is what is figuratively signified by their being held fast in Judea. And the winds were prevented from blowing either on the land or on the sea. On the land, this means that they found no relief in the war against the Romans, not even the farmers who devoted themselves to tending their plants, since trees too are refreshed when the winds shake them. Nor did those fighting on land find relief, nor those fighting at sea, for they did fight at sea, according to Josephus, who recounts everything precisely in his history of the capture of Jerusalem. Every evil overtook them: the burning of their cities, and the ravaging of their land, with its plants destroyed and cut down. All of it was payment exacted for their insolence against the Savior. But even if this is so, it will be fulfilled more justly and more completely at the coming of the Antichrist. It will happen not in a part of the land of the Jews but in the whole inhabited world, which the ministering spirits have received as their lot at its four corners, east, north, west and south, as those who carry out their services. The holding back of the winds plainly shows the breakdown of creation's good order, and makes clear that the evils cannot be escaped. For it is by the winds that the sea is sailed in the service of human beings, and plants are nourished as the winds refresh them.
Another angel ascending from the rising of the sun.

The divine angel comes from the rising of the sun, not from the setting and the evening. This seems to hint at and signify beneficence. The forefather of the Lord saw it in the Spirit and said, "The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord." The angel rightly commands that no one be harmed for the time being until those Jews who are worthy to be saved have been sealed. This is so that the righteous may not suffer the same fate as those who, in lawlessness, unjustly stretched out their hands against Christ. This agrees with what was revealed long ago to Ezekiel about the man clothed in "badin," a word meant to indicate an astonishing color. He sealed the foreheads of those who groaned, so that the righteous would not perish with the ungodly. This was needed because the virtue of the righteous is hidden, so hidden that even the holy angels do not know it. The same thing is shown here too, where a higher holy power gives the punishing powers a command to do nothing to the offenders indiscriminately before those who are recognized by being sealed have been distinguished as worshippers of the One who truly is. This happened in part long ago in the case of those who had believed in Christ. They did not share in the total destruction of the Jews by the Romans, because a divine oracle moved them out of Jerusalem so that they would not share the fate of the ungodly. The great James, pointing out their multitude to the blessed Paul, said they amounted to many tens of thousands. Even so, as has been said, at the time of the Antichrist's coming, the seal of the life-giving cross will make those who bear the mark of holy baptism even more clearly visible. For these are Christ's portion. That is why the angel says, "Do not harm the earth, or the sea, or the trees."
Do not harm.

Creation was made for our sake. So it shares with us in the scourges when we are being disciplined, just as it shines brightly together with the saints when they are glorified. From this we also learn that even those who live virtuously need the help of angels to support them against the onslaughts of temptations. For what does David the psalmist say? "You have held my right hand." By "right hand" he means the honorable work of our good deeds. The higher power emulates it to the extent that we make it worthy of emulation. So may we too have the good fortune to be sealed, as a sure token of the One who acquired us, and not be among the helpless [?], who have no one but their own sloth to blame.
On the 144,000 saved from the plague of the four angels.

And I heard the number of those who were sealed: a hundred and forty-four thousand sealed out of every tribe of the sons of Israel. From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Gad, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Asher, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Naphtali, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Manasseh, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Simeon, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of [?], twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Issachar, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of [?], twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Zebulun, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Benjamin, twelve thousand sealed.

For those of the Jews who believed in Christ were many, beyond counting. Witnesses to this are those who said to the divine Paul when he came to Jerusalem: "You see, brother, how many tens of thousands of believers there are among the Jews." The one who gives the revelation to the Evangelist says that these would have no share in the total destruction brought by the Romans. For the destruction by the Romans had not yet overtaken the Jews when this Evangelist received these things in prophecy, not in [?] but in Ionia, near Ephesus. For after the Lord's passion he remained in Jerusalem only fourteen years, as long as the God-receiving body of the Lord's mother was preserved in this transitory life after the passion and resurrection of her incorruptible Son. He stayed with her, since she had been entrusted to him by the Lord as a mother. After her death, the story goes, he no longer cared to remain in Judea but moved to Ephesus. There, as has been said, the contents of the present Revelation were also brought about, being a disclosure of things to come, since the affliction came upon the Hebrews after the fortieth year from the Lord's ascension. That those who were saved were too many to count is clear. For not only the believers escaped the destruction by the Romans, but also those who had taken part in the Lord's crucifixion in ignorance, of whom Christ also said, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." Cyril of Alexandria, it is true, in the thirteenth book of his refutation against Julian, saw fit to throw this saying out as spurious; but if he thought so, that is not our view. For not all the Jews who were present shared in the audacity of the high priests, and it is likely that all of these were afterwards sealed by faith, which is why the angel also calls them servants of God.
Out of every tribe of the sons of Israel.

He hints that those sealed and believing from each tribe were not on a par in quantity, but had in their zeal an equal honor of faith, even if not in number. For what equal number from every tribe [?] . . .
From the tribe of Judah.

Whether this number is made up of the faithful from among the Hebrews who were sealed at that time and escaped captivity by the Romans, or, which is the more credible, of those from among the Jews who are saved at the consummation, when, as Paul also says, "after the fullness of the [Gentiles?] has come in, all Israel will be saved"—neither view is unacceptable.

The exactness of the equal number from each tribe seems to indicate the multiplication of the apostolic seed, multiplied twelve times twelve up to the perfect number of thousands, and so producing the thousands mentioned. For they were disciples of the grain that fell into the earth out of love for humankind and sprouted the abundant fruit of the whole world's salvation. It should be noted that the tribe of Dan, because the Antichrist is to be born from it, is not ranked with the others; in its place is the tribe of Levi, which of old, being priestly, was held for a portion of its own. And here he has put Joseph in place of his son Ephraim. From the interpretation of the names of the others one can learn some meaning and apply it to each of the tribes, as we shall presently set out, with God's help. To begin with, we say that the tribe of Judah, which is interpreted "confession," hints at those who are saved through repentance and love toward Christ, who sprang from him. The number mentioned, that of the twelve [?] heads of the tribes, is fitting for these; hence the disciples too, equal in number to them, are the Lord's rulers and the [heads of the] brotherhoods of the saved, about whom it was also foretold: "In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you will make them rulers over all the earth." And since the promise concerning the founders of the tribes of Israel still rings [?] . . . to explain also about their names, given prophetically by those who bore them, as Moses has recorded in the book of Genesis, where Leah and Rachel, under divine inspiration, named the children born to them; and indeed their father Jacob, at the end of his life, together with the blessing of his offspring, prophesies to them [?] some of the things laid up for the future. It is not out of place to recall these for [?] comparison with the work before us. The tribe of Reuben, the name meaning "a son who sees" or "son of vision," [signifies] the pure in heart who see in the spirit. That of Gad, which means "temptation" or "place of trial," those who through afflictions and temptations have been refined like gold by the testing of their faith. That of Asher, by which blessedness is signified, those who by keeping the beatitudes taught by God will attain unending blessedness. And who justified a harlot and a thief through confession. That of Naphtali, interpreted "intelligent" or "stem," those who are attached to the eternal goods, those who with understanding lean upon the Master's stem, that is, the cross of Christ, and are crowned with understanding, and by it gore the demons, as it is said: "In you we will gore our enemies." That of Manasseh, which is interpreted "from forgetfulness," those who forget their ancestral ways for Christ's sake, according to the words, "Forget your people and your father's house," so that the King may desire your beauty—the beauty of the soul—and count you worthy of the [?] in the mystical marriage. That of Simeon, which means "hearing," those who obey the divine commandments through good and pure deeds. Therefore they also win God's ready hearing for themselves, so as to be deemed worthy to be heard by him; about them it is also said, "He who dwells in the help of the Most High will not be tried by the thing that walks in darkness." That of Levi, which means "taken beforehand," those taken beforehand by God for election, according to the saying of the psalm, and who are to dwell in the divine courts, as those who will serve as priests of the eighth [age], which follows the present age. This eighth, according to the great Gregory, is both the first of those after it and the eighth of those before it, higher than the high, since it bears the type of the age to come; and so the tribe of Levi has here been allotted the eighth place in the order by the one who gives this revelation. That of Issachar, which is "reward," those who set the virtues as their wage toward receiving the future prizes, and who pursue them for the sake of the good itself, laboriously, yet without making merchandise of them. That of Zebulun, which is interpreted "a flowing taken up," those who distribute their wealth to the poor and are taken up by Christ; who also heal the flowing away of the soul's fruits, that is, the corruption that vainglory breeds, by remembering the fire of Gehenna. That of Joseph, which is "addition of Iao," as it were an addition of the divine name—for they say that Iaoth means this—those who have been taken up into the kingdom of heaven by way of addition, and who receive the necessities of life from the Master who does not lie. That of Benjamin, which is interpreted "son of pain" or "son of the day," those who, according to the multitude of the pains in their heart, as David sings, receive divine consolations in equal measure, so as to be called sons of light and of the day. These things have been set out from the unfolding of the Hebrew names. But it should be considered that the inspired writer did not mention the name of Dan, although he too was the head of a tribe. From this one may conjecture that this is not only because the Antichrist is supposed to be born from him—as the patriarch Jacob foretold him as a serpent sitting by the road and biting the heel—but also because it is a grave thing to judge another's servant. For what does the Lord say? "Do not judge, so that you may not be judged." Since, then, "Dan," rendered into the Greek tongue, signifies "judgment," that is, "according to judgment," the one giving the revelation did not see fit to take any from this tribe into the portion even at that time, when it is plainly evident that it has become abhorrent, and when it would procure for itself a glory, though an accursed and false one.

So much concerning those of the blood of Israel who were sealed for salvation, either at the time of the total destruction brought upon them by the Romans, which was vengeance for the murder of the Lord, or at the final coming of the Antichrist, in which the tribe of Dan is also cast out from salvation, since it serves as midwife to the Antichrist, is marshalled by him, is devoted to him, and holds him up as its boast—an inglorious and ruinous glory.
On the countless multitude from the nations who reign together with Christ.

After this I looked, and behold, a great crowd that no one could count, from every nation and tribe and people and language, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands. And they were crying out with a loud voice, saying, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!" And all the angels stood around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures. And they fell on their faces before his throne and worshipped God, saying, "Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God for ever and ever. Amen."

So that nothing of what is seen in the vision may be left out, the one who gives the revelation also shows the Evangelist a great crowd beyond all number. David could fittingly have said of them, "I will count them, and they will be more than the sand." These myriads come from all the nations and from every tribe, and they have run to Christ. They may be those who long ago contended as martyrs and made their robes white by shedding [?] blood. In return they were granted a place standing around the throne of God's rest, with palm branches in their hands. In the [?] mystery of the vision the Lord is shown as all but arriving at his second coming, and the saints are all [?] caught up beforehand in the clouds to meet the Lord. So the vision shows them already caught up and already in possession of the blessedness laid up for them. For what is more blessed than to remain forever around the [?] throne and to gaze on the divine good things? Some have asked how those who were [?] to Christ through a martyr's blood came to be clothed in white robes rather than crimson ones. Our answer is that shedding their blood for Christ freed them from every stain. Baptized in their own blood, they came up white from that washing to Christ their king, like the ewes in the Song that are "white from the washing." Those ewes prefigured the souls of the saints, which rise white out of this muddy world into the spotless and eternal world. And what else do the palms mean to show? In athletic contests the palm is the customary symbol of throwing one's opponents in wrestling, according to the [?] about it. Perhaps even those who first made it a symbol of victory had thought this through. First, the plant likes to be grown in dry places, and nothing could be more welcome to those who live according to God and who earnestly turn away from a soft, well-watered way of life. Second, it has a lofty crown and always rises upward, almost to heaven. Who will deny that this belongs, throughout their lives, to those whom God loves, together with those who practise the ascents, that is, who practise rising above earthly things with the words, "To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven"? The heart of the plant is also white by nature, and so it wins a share in the Lord's beatitudes [?] for the one who imitates the plant and keeps his heart ever fresh. Then, by intently attending to the things on high, he gloriously attains to seeing God. The palm also bears its fruit from its trunk, and the fruit is sweet and astringent at once. That is why David sings that the righteous will flourish like the palm. How could anyone deny that these things work all the more richly in those zealous for the kingdom of heaven? The astringent, that is, the pressure of the hardships of the present life borne with endurance, earns them the sweetness of the age to come. Let this, then, be our reflection on the robes and the palms.
"Before the throne."
Having said "before the throne," he added "and before the Lamb." He wanted to show that this countless multitude, drawn from every race, [?] to him through the slaughter of the Lamb.
"And crying out with a loud voice."

This stands for "they cried out." For, as we have already explained, a writer who in his meaning arranges what will save his hearers pays less attention to the sequence of time. And what is the cry? "Salvation to him who sits on the throne." This is said elliptically, as is common elsewhere in divine Scripture, which aims at brevity of speech. The full form, without ambiguity and plain, is: [?] our salvation has been accomplished by him who sits on the throne and by the Lamb. How? By our being empowered by them to conquer the ruler of the darkness of this air, and the idolatrous men moved by him. Another example is "The salvation, O God, may it help me." Written out in full, so that it lacks nothing and is clear, it would be: "May your salvation, O God, help me."

They cried out, he says, because we were empowered by the Lamb to conquer the ruler of this darkness and the idolatrous men moved by him. And those who of old appeared to men in a terrifying way, as they did to Daniel when he [?] the visions, will then, at the Lord's second coming, I mean, become fellow ministers with men. I mean with men who have been transformed into incorruption by the change for the better. For they are not changed in their matter as well, as the divine Paul teaches through the example of the seed that is brought to life, when he asks, "With what kind of body are the dead raised?" This is also what is meant now by their being counted worthy to stand with the angels, the elders and the four living creatures. We have set out what these are when we [?] them. Their standing with these, then, shows the surpassing honor of the Incarnation, and the common thanksgiving will be sent up to God for the benefits, worthy of God, that he has bestowed on his creation for our sake.
"And all the angels stood around the throne and the elders and the four living creatures."
See, one church of angels and men.
"And they fell before the throne."
Not every falling signifies the servile and obedient [?] goodwill that prostration expresses. It is also used of punishment, as in "fire fell upon them."
"And they worshipped God, saying, Amen."

The spirits who minister among men, together with the elders, answered "Amen." Their reverent honor to God extended to the number seven. This is not only because, as we have already explained, this number corresponds to the present age. It is also because, just as this number is not produced from any other number within ten, so too God, to whom these acclamations are made, does not receive these divine excellences from anyone else.

Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, "Who are these, clothed in white robes, and where have they come from?" I said to him, "My lord, you know." And he said to me, "These are the ones who are coming out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. For this reason they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his temple; and the one who sits on the throne will shelter them. They will hunger no more and thirst no more; the sun will not strike them, nor any scorching heat. For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and guide them to springs of the water of life, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes."
"And one of the elders answered."

The elder's question to the Evangelist did not come from someone who did not know the answer. He was prompting the Evangelist to learn about and search out the things he was seeing. And the Evangelist, by confessing his ignorance, is taught by him what he did not know.
"These are the ones who are coming out of the great tribulation."

How could that tribulation not be great? Its punisher, public executioner and hangman is the one who exalts himself above every god and object of worship, together with every other deed and name of such activity. "And they washed their garments," meaning the glory that surrounds them, "in the blood of the Lamb." By blood we must understand zealous imitation. The Lamb himself was prefigured by Moses in the Passover sacrifice, and Isaiah prophesied of him as "a lamb silent before its shearer." In mercy toward his own creature he did not cling to his Father's glory but endured to take on the form of the creature, with its human sufferings. And he taught his followers that whoever wishes to follow him must disregard all the concerns of this life and take up only the instrument of death, that is, the cross. So those who obeyed these teachings fittingly washed their garments by imitating him. What the washing is we have already explained, and it would be superfluous to repeat ourselves.
He means the martyrs of Christ, who took up the cross and imitated his death. That is what "they washed" means: they washed nowhere else than in the blood of the Lamb.
"And they serve him day and night."

This means either that their service is unceasing, or that the thanksgiving of those whom God governs is unwavering, whether his dealings are plain to see or carried out in the unsearchable depth of his wisdom. For there is no night there, only one day, since all things are illuminated by the Sun of righteousness. Perhaps night stands for the hidden and deep mysteries of knowledge, and day for those that are clear and easily grasped. The temple of God is the whole creation renewed by him through the Spirit, but above all those who have kept the pledge of the Spirit unquenched. The promise that cannot lie is that he will dwell and walk among them. It is as though he will dwell more generously and more truly in their [?] most steadfast endurance, as he looks upon the temptations brought against them.
"He will dwell among them."
What else does "to dwell" signify than to remain without ceasing, with good pleasure and delight?
"They will hunger no more."

The saints have always passed from one temptation to another, and those from the nations will do so most of all at the coming of the Antichrist. But after that time they will be filled without ceasing with indescribable good things. Their bread will be the heavenly bread that came down to earth for their salvation, and their water the abundant outpouring of the Spirit. Of this the Lord said, "Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly." Drinking deeply of these, the saints will then live in exultation and endless gladness. Partial knowledge will be done away with, and the most perfect knowledge will be brought in for their enjoyment, in proportion to how eagerly each has sought to draw close to God. The divine Paul also speaks of this knowledge when he says "that we may know God, even as we have been known by God." That is, just as we eagerly sought to draw close to him, so God has generously unfolded to us his hidden good things. That Scripture habitually calls the lack of divine good things "hunger" is sufficiently confirmed by the prophet who threatens that a famine of hearing the word of the Lord will come. As for the sun striking them: divine Scripture interprets the sun figuratively in various ways. In one place the prophet says, "The sun will not burn you by day, nor the moon by night." That is, when you are brought safely back to your ancestral home, with the God of your fathers as your helper, you will have no open enemy oppressing you with thirst and want of what you desire, nor those that are harder to perceive [?]. Or by the light of the moon, which gently warms and chills, he hinted at certain enticing temptations that approach at first in a gentle and pleasant way but bring one to a deadly [?] of evils. The writer of Proverbs says this happens with adultery, which "for a season makes your throat smooth." Not only does the prophetic word compare the sun to temptations; Christ himself spoke of the seeds sown on rock that sprang up for a short time and were scorched by the sun, and he likened the sun to temptations. Let the seeds that sprang up briefly on the rock convince you: they sprouted all at once but were immediately scorched by the sun.
"For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and guide them to springs of the water of life. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes."

When [?] has been completed and all have passed over into incorruptible life, the Lamb himself, unveiled, [?] the sight of himself, the cloud of his flesh having been changed into something more godlike. This holds if we are to trust the divine Gregory, who boldly declares the flesh to be co-divine with him. "In the midst of the throne" is said instead of "from the midst of the throne," as though from the Father's glory, that is, his lordship. The economy of the flesh has given way to the onset of divine illuminations, or rather to the unchangeable Godhead. What follows is plainly fitting for God and belongs to the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. To him it will belong to shepherd and guide the flocks created by him through the economy. No tear will trouble them any longer, since the causes of tears will have perished, as in an unchanging life. Instead they will be shepherded to rest by pastures of waters, the divine and immaterial thoughts. Then the wolves too will be handed over to the eternal fire. They will have earned this wage, along with the devil their ruler, in this corruptible life, as envious demons who out of malice led men far astray.
The opening of the seventh seal, showing angelic powers bringing the prayers of the saints to God like incense.
And when he opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour. And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.

He narrates things to come as though they had already happened. This may be because, as we have often said before, divine Scripture does not fuss over intervals of time. That is why it speaks of past things as future, as in “they shall pass through the river on foot,” and of present things in place of future ones, as in “Jerusalem, built as a city.” Jerusalem had been destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar and was still to be rebuilt, once the captives had come back to it safely. The words that follow this saying, “for there the tribes went up,” likewise bring in a past sense for things still to come. Either, then, Scripture says these things without concern for intervals of time, or it shows that something will certainly happen by treating future events as already accomplished. So much for this. The number seven is taken up quite often here, as it is now, because it corresponds to the sabbath-rest of this age. I have already explained this. The loosing of the seventh seal signifies the dissolution of earthly turmoil, with seven angels ministering the punishments due to the ungodly. The silence shows the good order and reverence of the angels, and their ignorance about the Lord's second coming, as about his first. The half hour indicates the shortness of the time in which, while the plagues are brought on and the things on earth are brought to an end, the kingdom of the Lord will appear.
There was silence in heaven.
It is as though all creation, both the supramundane and the angelic power, were struck with awe at the [?] of the glory of the one who is coming, and so fell silent.
And I saw the seven angels who stand before God.

We have already discussed how the present Revelation is arranged in sevens. When it speaks of standing “before God,” do not think of a presence in a place. It means that they carry out their ministries according to his will. David too says of them: “mighty in strength, doing his word, to hear the voice of his words.” These are the ones who perform what is commanded without delay, at the very moment they hear it. This, then, is the meaning of “before.” To confine in a place the one who fills all things belongs to gross, fleshly people who can conceive of nothing beyond [?] sense perception.
And seven trumpets were given to them.

“Seven trumpets,” as when a king is arriving. According to Paul, wise in the things of God, writing to the Thessalonians, these same trumpets are also going to wake the dead. According to the same Apostle, the dead will rise to incorruption, in the likeness of the Lord, who was raised from the dead himself and was no longer subject to death. That is why, as the one who first began this kind of rebirth [?], he is called the firstborn from the dead. It should be understood that although the things seen are given shape in materials and colors, whether an altar, a censer or anything else, they are nevertheless invisible and spiritual. Standing at such an altar, then, the angel held the censer, that is, the vessel that receives the frankincense, and offered the prayers of the saints to God as incense. He calls it golden because gold is the material people prize and desire most. By this he hints that the prayers of the saints are also judged worthy of such acceptance with God. The angels who watch over us bring these prayers to God like first-fruits and a precious offering. The prayers are fragrant by nature, but they become more fragrant through the help of the angel who handles them, since he brings them in a special way to God, who appointed angels to watch over human beings. That the prayers of the saints are acceptable is indicated by the gift of incense from God. This is why David asks God that his prayer be set forth as incense. Through the universal consummation, they asked that the punishing scourges justly prepared for the ungodly and lawless might be brought to an end by cutting short the affliction, so that it would not spread to more people. For people who come into this wretched life are naturally inclined to cling eagerly to these things from their youth, and wickedness is [?] their mark. God declares this too in compassionate words when he speaks to Moses about the time after the universal flood in Noah's day. That is what they asked for others. For themselves they asked for the reward that comes through the coming of the one who knows how to give the prizes fittingly to those who compete with all their strength for virtue in the present life. These are none other than those who have glorified the judge of the contest in their own bodies. What follows will show that this is so.

And another angel came and stood at the altar, holding a golden censer. Much incense was given to him, so that he might offer it with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne. And the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, went up before God from the angel's hand. Then the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar and threw it onto the earth. And there were thunders and lightnings and an earthquake. And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets made themselves ready to blow them.

This altar is Christ. In him every liturgical and holy assembly has its being, and on him the sacrifices of the martyrs are offered. The altar shown to Moses on the mountain for the tabernacle was a type of it. That is why it is also called the tabernacle of witness, since things that benefit people are brought from there through testimony. And for those who order their lives by these things, their prayers, which he likens to fragrant incense, are offered acceptably on it, as has already been said.
Before the throne.

He says that Christ is before the throne, that is, the throne of the highest holy powers, by which I mean the Cherubim and the Seraphim. Rendered into Greek, the name of the former signifies a multitude or outpouring of knowledge and wisdom, while “Seraphim” means “those who set on fire.” As we have already said, by “throne” he means the superessential nature. That is also why Christ himself is said in one place to walk from the midst of the throne, that is, from the almighty and fatherly glory, since he is in no way inferior to it. For all that befits God belongs without reserve to the three sanctifying hypostases in common, except the mode of existence. Here, “before the throne” shows this as well, and no less: I mean that the word “before” shows that nothing that belongs to knowledge is set apart from the Father. For “before” signifies what is open to view, if indeed the saying “all things are open before those who understand” is enough to make his meaning clear. That is also why the throne, as a symbol of the divine essence, is not shown with any shape, body or likeness, either here or in any of the divine prophets. So “before the throne” is not superfluous. And the highest powers, because of the outpouring in them of fiery wisdom and love, and of pure friendship and love, as the meaning of their names shows, are the order of the highest holy powers that draw near to God, as we have said. The incense is the prayers of the saints. Their wish is that if anything else is offered to God, it may be counted by him as sweet-smelling incense, once this wretched, foul-smelling life has been burned away by the fire of love for him. Their love for Christ was so fervent and fiery that they counted all the delights of the present age as refuse, if only they might be granted to be with Christ, whom they longed for. Smoke went up from the offering of the incense because smoke is a sign of wrath, as in “smoke went up in his wrath.” This is depicted as happening for no other reason than to show and make plain the fiery love of the saints for Christ, as fire, or wrath, as smoke. For they too received the same nature as the angels, yet they did not strive as the angels did to please their Maker.
From the angel's hand.
Do you see that it was through the angel that the prayers of the saints became more fragrant and worthy to be brought before God?
And the angel took the censer.

We have just set out that by the censer he means the vessel for incense, by the altar Christ, by the smoke wrath, and by the fire from the altar the fiery love of the saints for God, which we examined earlier. The pouring out on the earth through the divine fire, before the angel who carries out punishment, is like what Ezekiel saw long ago, which came from the hand of the cherubim. That fire was taken from the altar and given to the angels sent to punish the ungodly inhabitants of Jerusalem. Andrew, who worthily received oversight of Caesarea in Cappadocia, the see I now hold, compares each bishop to this angel. Whether he meant the bishops of that time, I cannot say. But as for those of our own day, what sober person would deny that they resemble an angel indeed, but that angel is Satan? They swallow the camel and strain out the gnat, even if they make themselves like him to their own shame.
From the fire of the altar.

One of the angels cast some of this fire upon Mount Sinai, since God came down there too. There were thunders and lightnings and the sound of a single trumpet, because the visitation was of a single nation. Here, however, there are seven trumpets, corresponding to this changeable world, since the examination conducted by the coming Judge will be universal.

All these things will happen before the consummation, and they mark the consummation and the coming of Christ, just as on Mount Sinai these terrors prepared the way for God's appearing. Why there was one trumpet there but seven here has already been explained in the same passage. The thunders and voices and lightnings and earthquake are terrors. Either they are meant quite plainly, or else by “thunders” he means the [?], since the calamities have seized the earthly creation from no other source. I mean unexpected deaths, which leave the living stunned as if by thunder, or other unforeseen bodily sufferings, which may also cause mournful voices to be raised. The lightnings are the changes in the midst of lamentation toward better hopes. By these, as by a flash of light, people are freed from the darkness of despondency, as the lightnings shine around them by God's providence. This happens so that those who hold to the right faith may not be swallowed up by excessive grief, for the world will not [?] the elect all at once. That is also why the days will be shortened, as the Lord foretold. The earthquakes should be understood as the earthbound allegories of the mind, which go beyond these too. They lead to falls rather than to improvement, and they cause dissension. This, then, is how these things should be considered. He presents the avenging trumpeters as ready, although the Divine is long-suffering and compassionate toward all his works, because no further time for repentance remains, since the existence of this changeable world has come to its end.

As for the trumpets that these angels keep sounding, what could they be taken to signify but the victory of the Lord, mighty in battle? At their sound he also goes up with a shout, as in a song of victory, to his rest. For this is the shout, with the trumpet sounding along with it. According to its etymology, the trumpet's name signifies nothing other than to [?] a light that gives courage to those darkened by the fear of war.
On the seven angels. When the first sounds his trumpet, hail, fire and blood are hurled on the earth.

And the first blew his trumpet. And there came hail and fire mixed with blood, and it was thrown onto the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, a third of the trees were burned up, and all the green grass was burned up.

The punishments that come from the pouring out of the altar's fire are varied, since the dwelling-places laid up as a reward for those who love God are also varied and many. That is why the Lord says, “With my Father there are many dwelling-places.”
And there came hail and fire mixed with blood.

It is clear that the present Revelation does not assign these punishments of hail and fire mixed with blood to the last day, which is reserved for the punishment of sinners. As has been said, it assigns them to the tribulations before the last day. For then not a third of the sinners but all of them would be subjected to punishment without escape.
