What does the divine Evangelist say about this? “And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”
And a third of the trees were burned up.

Those who assigned these things to the last day took the grass and trees to be sinners, following the divine Apostle Paul, who declares that the day is revealed in fire. Others did not, but referred them to the tribulation before the last day. They took them to mean the burnings and slaughters that barbarian hands inflict on many. Through these, the visible enemies have already consumed no less than a third of the whole, not only by slaughtering people but also by burning buildings to the ground. The blessed prophet Joel speaks of this too when, before the great and manifest day of the Lord, he says, “blood and fire and vapor of smoke.”
And all the green grass was burned up.

For those who have taken the tribulations described here to refer to the last day, the green grass should be understood as the half-wicked. They too will melt away in the fire of their own conscience, especially when they see those who are helped and flourish because of righteous labors freely undertaken.
On the second angel. When he sounds his trumpet, the living creatures in the sea are destroyed.

And the second angel blew his trumpet. And something like a great mountain, burning, was thrown into the sea. A third of the sea became blood, a third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.

To my mind, a great mountain [?] at the sounding of the trumpet. As we said earlier when discussing the etymology of the name, the trumpet produces a kind of light in those who are fighting, since salpinx, “trumpet,” is named from selas, which means light. It produces selas, that is, light, by giving courage to the fighters. So too in Homer, the one urging Teucer to keep shooting this way, that is, with good aim, adds, “Shoot, so that you may become a light to your comrades,” not hesitating to call encouragement “light.” So much about the trumpet.

The great mountain hints at divine wrath. For although the Divine loves humankind, it is also just. Because of this, when we slight it, it sometimes brings a just wrath worthy of itself. So David, singing the psalm, says, “Give to them according to the works of their hands.” He was a man himself and full of the same negligence, yet the gross offenses of sinners brought him to feel this way about his own people. This is how we have taken the mountain. Its being thrown into the sea points to the restless, surging state of the present life, which in its trials rages more than the sea. It is unstable at all times and every day, but especially at the arrival of the Antichrist. He will lead people so far astray by his wonders that, as the Lord said, even the elect will stumble. A third of the sea becoming blood stands for those who, perfected through martyrdom, have reddened the earthly creation. Since the number three is the beginning of plurality, as arithmetic teaches, by “the third” he indicated the greater part of those who perish, not all of them, as we explained shortly before.
And a third of the ships were destroyed.

He uses “ships” figuratively for the souls of the saints. These ships also mock the dragons in the sea, as was interpreted allegorically in the 103rd Psalm. Here especially we must take these things as symbols of a reality, since the present Revelation does not depict an actual event. It is likely that some even of those who have taken hold of salvation will be led astray. So, out of fear that this might befall them completely, he guarded against total ruin by announcing “the third.”
The third angel makes the waters of the rivers bitter.

And the third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, burning like a torch. It fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the waters, because they had been made bitter.

He says that when the third angel blew his trumpet, the great star fell, burning like a torch. This is the one whose fall Isaiah son of Amoz lamented in prophecy when he said, “How the morning star has fallen, who rose in the morning!” It is not unreasonable to suppose that he will fall. For he did fall at the Lord's appearing too, as the Lord himself says: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.” The lightning of his fall shows that in the end his former brightness was quenched, the brightness under which the error of the age of idols shone. Even if, to speak with Paul, he “is still at work in the sons of disobedience,” it is not as much as before the Lord's coming. Compared with the divine appearing, the divine visitation through Moses robbed him, the devil I mean, of hardly any of his power, so to speak. At his prompting fathers sacrificed their children. And if after [?] …, first of all they are not raised to such a height of wickedness, nor carried out with such [?]. And altogether they are permitted, to some degree at least, as a training ground in virtue for those who live until the end of this changeable and much-distracted life. But when he comes deceitfully to people in the flesh, he will use even more power than has been granted to him, out of shamelessness and madness, of course. He will try to make his deception pass not as deception but as truth. That is why he appears to the beholder as a star, though burning like a torch. The torch represents the fame of his glory, which is already failing, just as a torch fails as it is consumed by the very thing that makes it give light. So it will befall the deceiver, the Antichrist, at the Lord's second coming: his deceptive glory will fail completely, and he will be handed over to eternal fire. The rivers figuratively stand for the nations, if Isaiah son of Amoz is enough to confirm this. In his words they reprove the king of the Hebrews, who was making treaties and alliances with the king of Syria: “Why do you trust in the water of Siloam, since it could not withstand a great river?” By the great river he means the king of the Assyrians. The star's fall indicates the punishment that will come on those he leads astray, together with whom he will be handed over to the fire of Gehenna, to eternal and endless burning.
Burning like a torch.

David too declares that the burning of the mountain describes God's active wrath against those who sin without hesitation, when he sings, “Lay hold of instruction for atonement.” For in this way God's extreme [?] wrath is by nature quenched no other way than by being quickly kindled against sinners, poured down on them unexpectedly. The springs are their clans.
And the name of the star is Wormwood.

The herb wormwood is bitter, but physicians teach that it sharpens the sight of those who eat it. So he aptly called this all-daring star exceedingly “wormwood.” For he gives people bitterness to drink through pleasure, and a muddy ruin, and for this reason he is permitted to bring the punishing scourges on them here. The purpose is that those who are able to see clearly may, through patience and endurance, give thanks, in the words of the psalm, “In tribulations you have set me at large,” to the one who for their good permits them to be tested by tribulations. This is also what wins health for the sick who endure the physicians' surgery. Those who can see sharply in this way through the dishonor of tribulations gained glory and good report from dishonor and ill report, from what seemed like losses. Beyond this they gained the eternal kingdom, which is why the judge of the contest permitted them to be tested.
And a third of the waters became wormwood.

What is beset and tested shares in the character of the tempter. It shares not in his embittering, but in what strengthens the sight through bitterness, for its own salvation. That is why Paul too knows of the hope “that does not put to shame,” which comes through enduring tribulation: first it reaps proven character, and then it ends in the hope that does not put to shame. Partaking of the wormwood does not bring salvation to everyone who partakes. There are some for whom [?] entangled in human affairs [?] … profitable things, because the power of understanding is not equally awake in all. That is why Paul, boasting without reserve that he is the fragrance of Christ to those who are being saved and to those who are perishing, adds: “to some from life to life, to others from death to death.”
Many died from the waters.

Those who in a merely human way fixed their attention on the bitterness of the wormwood in their tribulations died. But those who recovered their sight through the bitterness lived. And who are the ones who died? Those who in a merely human way fixed their attention on the bitterness of the wormwood in their tribulations.
The fourth angel darkens a third of the light of the sun and the moon.

And the fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of them was darkened, and a third of the day did not shine, and likewise the night. And I looked, and I heard an eagle flying in mid-heaven, saying with a loud voice, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the remaining blasts of the trumpet of the three angels who are about to blow!”

What will happen when the fourth trumpeting angel sounds, as we have also set out before, agrees not only with Joel on the great and manifest day of the Lord, but also with what was announced by the Lord and God Jesus Christ in Matthew, when he says, “Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light.” Peter too, in his second Epistle, declares the same things when he says, “The day of the Lord will come like a thief.” He likens its unexpected onset to a thief, for it is not for human beings to know the times or seasons, which, according to the Lord's word, have been stored up for the knowledge of the Father alone. “And on that day,” to quote what follows in Peter's Epistle, “the heavens will pass away with a rushing roar,” that is, with a resounding noise, because of the collapse when such a passing away is accomplished, “and the elements will be burned up and dissolved.” For the day, as Paul holds, is revealed in fire. The present Revelation shows that all these things will take place at the consummation of the present age. He says that a third of the sun and the moon and the stars was struck, not the whole, because in God's unspeakable love for mankind not all of creation is scourged. For there may be some who turn toward conversion through these evils, and for their sake these things also prepare the way as a prelude to the Lord's second coming. So either “the third” is meant to show that these great and dreadful things, terrible even to hear of, will be accomplished within a short span of the order of day and night, or else “the third” points to the all-holy Trinity, which, in its surpassing goodness toward the world subject to it, does not inflict the punishment on the deserving in full, but in a measure equal in number to itself.

Notice that when he spoke of a third of the starry array, he did not say that the stars themselves were darkened, but what is lit by them, which is the creation around the earth. That is why he adds, “and a third of it did not shine,” that is, so that the earthly region would not be lit by the heavenly array, by which the order of day and night is brought about.
And I looked, and I heard an eagle flying.

What is the meaning of the eagle's flight here? The angels so far appointed to carry out the punishments were, I think, disregarded because of the disobedience and incorrigibility of those who were subjected to the punishments mercifully, in moderation and with a view to conversion, but who took no thought at all to better themselves. So the eagle flies and cries out to these impenitent people to make known the divine wrath, so that in fear of it they might attend to their own salvation. It is the eagle stationed about the divine throne, as Ezekiel showed, tripling the woe from mid-heaven. From mid-heaven, because they cannot go beyond this apart from the throne and the one seated on it. And it is the eagle among the four living creatures, and not any other of those shown around the throne, since none of these can fly. So it could readily reach mid-heaven, and at the same time, having the keenness of sight that is natural to eagles, it could make sure that nothing escaped the notice of those who hear what it cries out about. The woe is tripled not only to convey the abundance of lamentation, but also to suggest the indignation of the thrice-holy One, and the sympathy of the heavenly beings toward us. It is chiefly for this reason that the woe is tripled by them, giving overwhelming expression to their lament on our behalf, since we are their fellow servants. Hence their grief too was abundant. Indeed, since the intellectual nature is near to God, they take on from this the impress of his love for mankind as well; and still more because human beings, though they too received intellect through the rational soul, did not, like their kindred, transfer their citizenship [?] to heaven, but have been likened to the senseless beasts by dwelling on the earth and minding earthly things forever.
Because of the remaining blasts.

From what source did the eagle declare the woe? From the blast of the trumpet, he said. Not that the sound itself creates the evils that are about to come; but since they did not look to repentance at the trumpeting of the angels who sounded before, what else remains but that they should be roused again by the trumpet, as from sleep, to work out their salvation? And although this is impossible for those who dwell on earth, whose fall the prophet Isaiah foretold as irreversible and inescapable, nevertheless, to show their insensibility, and therefore their punishment, more fully, the evils that will overtake them are announced beforehand by the trumpet, so that those subjected to the scourges may be left without excuse.
Of the three angels who are about to blow.
The three angels are those remaining of the seven; for once the fourth has blown, the next three are still lacking to complete the seven.
Chapter 28.
On the fifth angel, the spiritual locusts coming up from the abyss of the earth, and the varied character of their form.

And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star that had fallen from heaven to the earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the abyss. And smoke rose from the shaft like the smoke of a burning furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the shaft. And out of the smoke came locusts onto the earth, and they were given power like the power that the scorpions of the earth have.
And the fifth angel blew his trumpet.

Having described in advance the portents that will be worked before Christ's second coming during the deceitful sojourn of the Antichrist, he now goes on to disclose what will happen at that true coming itself, the advent of the true Savior, for the correction of those who will hear. Scripture sets these things out to turn people back, so that those who hear of them may not suffer them; for he is kindly disposed toward his own kind, being a disciple of him who does not desire the death of the sinner but his conversion. This fifth angel is one of the seven trumpeters still remaining. He compares him to a star because of the brilliance of the ministers above the world. That he had “fallen” means that he came down to earth, unless, for the sake of precision, one takes the “fall” to refer to his role in carrying out the punishment. The key of the shaft given to him signifies that the departed are held securely and cannot escape, especially if they are sinners; unlike the souls of the saints, which come with timeless swiftness to those who call on them and grant their requests for salvation. The shaft is the one in the earth, for inescapability could not be shown in any other way than by a shaft. The abyss too is in the earth, for the punishment is on earth, in the shaft of the abyss. People call a very deep place an “abyss,” the letter alpha either indicating, by privation, that it is not stopped up and so gapes forever, or presenting its great depth by intensification. How great, then, must its breadth be when measured, since it has enclosed [?] those who from of old have stiffened their necks against the Lord! That the judgment takes place on earth, one of the holy prophets hinted through the valley of Jehoshaphat, where he prophesied that God would sit in judgment, because many wars broke out there and many were heaped up together in burial. That smoke rose from the shaft represents the wrath stirred by the memory and the exposure of the ungodly enclosed there, wrath as great as one would expect to rise from a furnace. And just as that smoke fills the surroundings with mist and darkness and dims the light of the sun, so too the memory of the ungodly, once renewed, caused whatever light of sympathy there might be to be quenched by the enormity of what they had dared.
And out of the smoke came locusts.

Locusts are mentioned to suggest the harsher memory of the sinner's utterly outrageous conduct during his temporal life. That is why he says they had their origin from the smoke, since the generation of physical locusts too takes its start from a corrupting atmosphere. The name “locusts” (akrides) was also chosen to indicate that the punishments are inflicted to the utmost (kat' akras). For the more the licentiousness of the sinners is brought to mind, the more the wrath of the one appointed to judge is kindled, ever festering in the presence of what inflames the indignation. That power was given to them, as to living beings, is a device of personification, meaning that the punishments are carried out without restraint or hindrance. But so that no one who knows that locust bites do not cause much pain should suppose the suffering bearable, he adds the example of scorpions, which cause a sharper sensation with the thrust of their sting. That is why it was said, not to the scorpions but to the locusts, keeping up the personification here too, that they should not harm, not the people, but the things that grow from the earth. And for what reason next [?] do they “have power”? That is, the power that was given; for it was given not to the scorpions but to the locusts. And over what do the locusts have power? Over the earth. The scorpions were brought in not only to emphasize that a scorpion's sting causes a more acute sensation than the bite of locusts, but also because the scorpion, striking with its tail, hints at the painful suffering stored up for evildoers hereafter. If the discourse of the Revelation does not set this out so plainly, it has often been said before that the Church of God has cared less for eloquence than for the salvation of souls. That is why the divine Paul says, “We have this treasure in earthen vessels”: a treasure in which the wealth of the wisdom of Christ's condescension is stored. This wisdom is not confined to rhetorical nonsense but lies in the exposition of instructive compositions. This is clear from the very passage cited: he ought to have said, “We have this treasure fashioned by means of earthen vessels,” but he did not say that; he said “in earthen vessels,” for in this way the one treasure might be understood as shared among many. Some of the Fathers took the locusts to mean worms, so that this interpretation would agree with Isaiah's declaration, “Their worm shall not die.”

And they were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green thing or any tree, but only the people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. And they were permitted not to kill them, but to torment them for five months; and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings a person. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, and death will flee from them.

If one wishes to follow the allegorical interpretation given above, then what is expressed symbolically, as befits divine and mystical things, the grass of the earth, the green growth and every tree, must be taken to mean chaff-like people, and those who, like trees, have become wooden through lack of reason and have advanced, as it were, to a kind of tree-like stupidity. The benevolent Godhead, judging these worthy of mercy, commands that they should not undergo the same punishment as those who do evil with forethought and deliberation and have rejected being sealed [?]. But if one occupies oneself with understanding the letter itself, and supposes that grass and trees are meant literally as stated, citing David as witness when he says, “You will renew the face of the earth,” one would have to answer for it, unless one took the renewal to mean a life corresponding to the renewal of creation. If beasts too are to be envisaged in the renewal, then it would be fitting for grass and trees also to be left for eternity, since it is for their sake that grass springs up, and green growth, and everything else needed for this corruptible life, just as timber is sought for building houses and for the warmth of a fire. But if there is none of these, then, with regard to the earth whose face is renewed, adherence to the letter must be judged a thoughtless interpretation, and one in keeping with those who revel in drinking and indulgence in the thousand-year reign of Christ after this life and this age have run their course.
But only the people.

From this it is clear that the restraint from doing harm does not concern grass and trees, as the one giving the command says, but those who are likened to grass [?], as the divine Paul also holds, as we said earlier. But if this same Paul testifies that such people will be destroyed by fire, whereas here they are judged worthy of mercy, we must understand that the grass-like are not to be reckoned as the same people in both cases. For those whom the restraint spared are charged with beast-like dullness, whereas those who give proof of themselves through fire show, by being subjected to testing, that it was not through simplicity but through faulty conduct that they met the misfortune of being consumed by fire. So the addition of “the people,” this distinction, means that it is not grass but grass-like people who are to be spared. Otherwise, since the difference between grass and people is easy to recognize, what need was there to add “but people”? Or else, clearly, since those people are understood along with them, if one attends to the letter and does not recast it into some other allegory, one will no longer take these things to refer to the Lord's second coming and his judgment at that time. For the present Revelation discloses what follows the final return of humankind to life, after which no human death remains, because there is no more sinning either, the whole of creation having been re-established in incorruption; and sinning belongs to the corruptible world, not to the incorruptible. Why, then, should those appointed to punish be instructed not to make the punishments of the unsealed so heavy as to cause death? And what is this torment of five months, when the course of the sun no longer marks out intervals of time? For what need is there of these in a world that knows no weariness and is wholly radiant?
And they were permitted not to kill them, but to torment them for five months.

“Not to kill” makes clear to those who know from experience how unbearable torments are that they usually lead to death. So the benevolent command directs the tormentors to refrain from this unbearable degree. As for the five months: since months are measures of the sensible world, from which the senses, the instruments by which it is known, also received their activity, the number fittingly hints at sin through a matching count, so as to make people remember the things for which they have had to undergo judgment. For the requital comes from these and concerns these. He compared the pain to a scorpion's sting, since this too is, generally speaking, deadly.
People will seek death.

Whoever hopes to find something also obtains it. But since death cannot dwell in the world there, what does this seeking of death mean now? Nothing other than the unbearableness of the pain, since death puts an end to everything painful. Hence the saying, “Death is rest.” But since death has been banished from incorruptible life, he added “will flee” to “not finding.” Death is personified to give greater emphasis to what the narrative shows. One may marvel at the precision with which these things are reported. For he did not say “locusts,” but “likenesses of locusts,” indicating by the name, as already said, the extremity of the pains; for a locust or anything like it might be left behind [?] in this corruptible life. And these will inflict a certain sharpness on those being punished, whereas in this corruptible life the locust's bite is very mild, not even to be compared with the prick of a needle.

And the likenesses of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle; on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold, and their faces were like human faces. They had hair like women's hair, and their teeth were like lions' teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots with many horses rushing into battle. They have tails like scorpions, and stings, and in their tails is their power to harm people for five months. They have as king over them the angel of the abyss; his name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he has the name Apollyon.

The locusts are likened to horses and not to any other animal because of the swiftness of their onset and the spirit of the horse, especially in war. The present Revelation itself has indicated this by saying that their readiness was like that of horses eager for battle.
And on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold.

He keeps to the terrifying image, and that is why he uses the comparative particle “like.” The crown like gold seems to represent the victory they won over the wretched vanquished. But it is like gold, not gold; for a punishment that brings about the destruction of God's creature does not truly win anything precious. Their faces, likened to human faces, lead the deceived astray by the resemblance, those whom these punishments have overtaken for deceit [?] in this deceitful wickedness. And the braids of women's hair serve as a covering for the deceivers. For such are the pleasures of the flesh: they delight by their outward appearance, and drag those they have lured down with them in their own slippery fall. That is why Solomon, the writer of proverbs, says that “the words of a harlot smooth the throat for a time, but afterwards produce a sensation more bitter than gall.” Hence this ready image, after the women's hair, also brings in lions' teeth as avengers, and “breastplates like breastplates of iron”: the lions' teeth are meant to show savagery, and the iron breastplates the firmness to withstand those who fight back with darts and do not readily bear what is imposed on them. And since flight is also seen in them, as they are likened to locusts, the flight hints at the swiftness of their onset and at their attacking from above, as David too says that “many are those who war against him from on high.” And that humanity's warfare comes from the upper regions, the divine Paul is a reliable guarantor, when he says, “Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities and the powers, against the world rulers of the darkness of this air.” By “the sound of the wings” he means their rush into close combat, which is not carried out quietly, since it takes place not in one spot but throughout the whole world. Hence they do not attack every human character as if it were level ground, but some that do not yield to them at all, or that yield, but only under a more violent onslaught [?]. So, as with wagon wheels jolting up and down over obstacles, a sound, that is, a clatter, arises.
And if this is especially so with war chariots, how much more with the assault and struggle of the turbulent demons against the whole [?]?
And they have tails like scorpions, and stings.

The attacks of demons on human beings are likened to scorpions' tails and stings because the demons too do not reveal their harmfulness the moment they make contact, just as the scorpion does harm not with its crab-like claws but with the tail behind it, through its sting. Meanwhile, the wicked demons do not at once have punishment imposed on them for deceiving those whom they capture by deceit; but they will be kept for the final fire together with those they deceived, and will receive their due reward. Hence Paul too urges us not to judge anything before the time. What is meant by the power to punish extending only to the fifth month we have already explained. For who can take away the everlasting fire of sinners? It is not a perceptible fire, since neither fire nor anything else perceptible is there. For just as “no perceptible eye is able to see the good things, nor ear to hear, nor have they entered the human heart,” so neither can the things that punish be known until they are experienced. The endlessness of the punishment seems to me to be this: the memory, for sinners, of the kingdom of God. For everything there is unchangeable and incorruptible, and just as the rational soul is restored to the good and saving things with which its Maker adorned it from the beginning, so it possesses them forever. Among these is also the memory of these good things. I do not think that the soul, carrying this memory away unimpaired, and then seeing others who share the same nature receiving the prizes of their good labors and rejoicing, while it is itself being repaid [?] with punishment for its wicked toils, would not be eaten away as by a worm and a moth. For what does the saying say? “[?] of the bones is a sensitive heart.” And if this is so in this corruptible life, what then will it be in the incorruptible?
Having as king over them the angel of the abyss.

Some have thought that this Angel is an evil demon, but they are wrong. The Lord declared that the punishment of fire has been prepared for the devil and his angels. How, then, could one of those set apart for punishment be granted royal authority? So the authority was not awarded to an evil Angel, but to one who carries out a ministry suited to it. For not all are "ministering spirits sent out" for saving "service," as the divine Paul put it; some are also sent for punishment. Such was the angel who destroyed the Assyrian army gathered with Sennacherib against Jerusalem, and the one who brought fiery destruction on Sodom. As we have already noted earlier, we say again that although these things are announced in the past tense, they are nevertheless to be understood as future. There are two reasons for this: either because they will certainly come to pass and nothing can hinder them, or because the one revealing these things to the Evangelist is preserving the dignity proper to prophecy.
His name in Hebrew is Abaddon.

The Hebrew name was formed from what he brings about, as is clear from the Greek. For what else does "Apollyon" mean but "the destroyer"? He received this meaning along with the name Abaddon, because he was sent for this very purpose, I mean, to destroy.
Explanation of the sixth angel, and of the angels released at the Euphrates.

The first woe has passed. Behold, two more woes are still to come after these things. Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a single voice from the four horns of the golden altar that is before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.” And the four angels were released, who had been prepared for the hour and the day and the month and the year, to kill a third of humankind. And the number of the troops of cavalry was two myriads of myriads; I heard their number.

“Woe” is an adverb of lament, and what brings pain is called grievous. So it is not the adverb that has passed. How could something that exists only as an accident and not as a substance, and that vanishes at the very moment it comes into being, move on anywhere? Rather, since the painful things that call forth such an exclamation have gone by, the “woe” too is fittingly said to have passed.
And I heard a single voice from the four horns.

The voice comes from the four horns that belong to the altar, and by these horns we must understand the divine powers that surround it. When the altar was built on which the sacrifices were burned with fire to God, a horn-shaped projection was fixed at each corner to hold the split logs together, so that the altar, once kindled, made the sacrifices acceptable. Moses at Sinai was given instructions for this lower altar as an image of the altar above. That is why the one who gave him the oracle says, “See that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.” These projections, which we have said are intellectual powers, may reasonably be taken to enclose the mystery that is beyond being and inaccessible to human nature. Because of them it cannot be readily grasped by those whose nature ranks below it, and the rational sacrifices offered to it do not drain away at random. The altar is square in shape, matching this world of four elements, because pure rational sacrifices are offered from every part of the world, as the prophet says.
Release the four angels.

Some have taken these to be divine angels bound at the great river Euphrates. In this view they keep close to the river and are occupied with it, delighting in the intellectual contemplation of it. They say that this river is God. Isaiah speaks of him as though God himself were speaking: “Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent flooding over with the glory of the nations.” David also says, “The rushing streams of the river make glad the city of God.” They identify the four angels as Michael, who appears in Daniel; Gabriel, in Matthew; Raphael, in Mordecai; and Uriel. These angels are released from this divine occupation for a ministry that suits both God’s administration of justice and their own glorious presence. Others say that these are not angels but wicked demons. They were bound at the coming of Christ by divine command, but they come out from the superhuman altar and are released by the divine angel. Their purpose is to throw the nations into turmoil, and through this turmoil to show plainly which of the faithful are wheat, fit to be stored in the granaries, and which of the sinners are chaff, useless and ready for burning. Nor is it unreasonable to say that the demons were bound at the Euphrates, since perhaps the Antichrist will come from there, from among the Hebrew captives of Jerusalem who survived and remained in those regions.

So much for these. But what of the horses [?], that is, those who were not brought to their senses by the sight of these horrors and were not changed by the experience? In his love for humankind God ordained the experience of terrible things to turn people away from evil, in accordance with the unsearchable [?] of God. Perhaps it also comes about through the punishment of the wicked, so that people may look ahead to their own salvation when the pestilent man is scourged. As Solomon, the author of the Proverbs, says, “The fool becomes more prudent.” What befell these people [?] and what punishment was brought on them, he did not say. Perhaps it is an affliction that surpasses everything. As “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered the human heart, the good things prepared for those who love God,” so it is with the evils owed to those who scorn him. Someone may object that good things are indeed promised, paradise and the kingdom of heaven, and evils likewise, the darkness and the eternal fire of the Gospels and the like. If so, why is there silence about both the better and the worse? We shall answer that the good and evil things laid up are not a recompense given without reason. Each is proportioned to the labor of those who pursue it. The divine Paul and the divine Gregory both speak to this point. Paul makes grace equal to labor. Gregory sorts the saved into three ranks, slavery, hired service and sonship, and says that to each is laid up what is due to it: to slavery, fear; to hired service, wages; and to sonship, a love without shame, which rather knows how to cast out fear. The first two ranks readily offered their rewards for comparison. But sonship, because its love is so surpassing, had no recompense to match it among the things human beings know. So he honored the comparison with silence, since eye has not seen nor ear heard anything equal to it. He honored with silence what leads us by the hand toward knowledge. Just as with the good things he left out what is surpassing, so with the evil things he left out what goes beyond any knowledge drawn from comparison.
And the number of the troops of cavalry.

He gives the number of the troops without having mentioned troops before. So it is clear that those who took the four as commanders, Michael, Gabriel, Uriel and Raphael, were not mistaken, since a host usually follows its commander. From Daniel we learn of thousands of thousands and myriads of myriads of ministering spirits. But now the seer describes the multitude following the commanders as double the number of myriads. This is because, since the Lord became man, angels live freely among human beings. That is why they are said to be ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.

And this is how I saw the horses in the vision, and those who sat on them: they had breastplates of fire, of hyacinth and of sulfur. The heads of the horses were like the heads of lions, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of humankind was killed, by the fire and the smoke and the sulfur that came out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails. Their tails are like snakes, having heads, and with them they do harm.

The riders of the horses may be taken in one of two ways. They may be divine powers whose allotted task is to curb habits and passions and train them toward what is better, much as colt-breakers mount horses and train them with muzzle and bridle. Or they may be divine commands, likened to armor of fire, hyacinth and sulfur because of their zeal against those who are perishing. David too speaks of this, I mean of the divine zeal, when he declares, “Smoke went up in his wrath, and fire blazed from his face, and coals were kindled.” Whichever of these one adopts, I would prefer the reading that applies the image to the wicked.
And the heads of the horses were like the heads of lions.

Some take the vehicle of the divine judgments to refer to people who live a spiritual and angelic life, and others to habits and passions. For anyone who does not approach the vision out of self-love, it will make no difference. The horses are likened to lions’ heads as a sign that those who serve divine things must carry out their ministry without delay. “For the word of God is living, and sharper than any sword.” Therefore, like a centurion [?], the head displays indignation with a lion’s vehemence, since in no other way would the hearer be brought to an assent that shows itself in action. Paul too was not without this kind of shrewdness when he threatened to come to the Corinthians with a rod. This, then, is what the heads hinted at. The mouths signify a deadly breath close at hand. It is not expected from afar, as something seen in the distance. It comes at the closest approach and makes escape impossible. The fire shows destruction. The smoke shows wrath, for “smoke went up in his wrath.” The sulfur, *theion*, shows that it comes from divine, *theia*, anger, or else that these things are brought on the licentious in a way that pleases God. God is accustomed to use those who live like angels as the vehicle of his own judgments and mysteries. The oracle he gave to Ananias about Paul shows this clearly enough. There he says that Paul is “a chosen vessel,” able to carry tirelessly the doctrines that befit God. He indicated these through the word “name” when he said, “to carry my name.” By “name” he meant glory and majesty and everything that is beyond reason, that is, beyond the understanding not only of mortals but also of angels.
For the power of the horses is in their mouths.

What does this mean, assigning the power to the mouth, as if that were the reason the horses were sent? Or does “from their mouths” point to threats that frighten people into abstaining from evil practices, so that they may not be handed over to the tails? By the tails he portrays the end and outcome of those who perish. Giving shape to that outcome, he likens the tails to snakes with heads. From the very attack the heads show that the outcome is deadly and inescapable, and that it brings harm without delay, since there is no longer any way to escape the harm.

The rest of humankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands. They did not give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and stone and wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk. And they did not repent of their murders or their sorceries or their fornication or their thefts.

The passage points to an extreme lack of feeling, that is, to callousness and licentiousness. Out of love for humankind God had so far spared these people and held back their punishment, giving them time for salvation. They wasted that time in vain, and so they bring on themselves the recompense their negligence deserves. This is so even though the requital of the wicked was being carried out before their very eyes. Yet the sight of the fearful things prepared for them did not make them better than they had been. On the contrary, they grew worse and persisted in even more outrageous deeds.
They did not repent of the works of their hands.

He does not mean people who failed to repent in the life to come. How could there be repentance in an unchangeable life, and what kind would it be? He means those still living who did not repent of the works they had seen [?] when they heard of and saw what would then happen. Instead they committed themselves to the chief forms of demon-madness and idolatry, and to everything hostile to true worship. They took no notice of how senseless the handmade idols are, and so they added lawlessness to lawlessness. For this reason they were also shut out from true righteousness. What righteousness is there in someone who murders a fellow human being, whether with the stroke of a sword or by a plot with poisons? And who will not hate someone who treats himself without restraint and does not shrink from devising against himself whatever even a scheming enemy might devise? Who would not feel loathing and revulsion for the filth of fornication and the devotion to it, which deprives a person of being a divine dwelling place, if we are to believe the divine Paul? As for someone devoted to thefts, only a person who had courted his own harm would take him into his household. Whoever takes in such a man is liable to have him scheme to carry off the very provisions he lives on.
On the angel clothed with a cloud and a rainbow, who foretells the common end.

And I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with the rainbow over his head. His face was like the sun, and his feet were like pillars of fire. In his hand he held a little scroll, lying open. He set his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land, and he cried out with a loud voice, as a lion roars. And when he cried out, the seven thunders sounded their voices.

The cloud represents what is hidden and invisible. The rainbow on his head sketches the chief point of the angelic order. That order is made up of the virtues in creation that are pleasing to God and of the variety in its mission, and the rainbow magnifies its nearness to God and its station. That is what the rainbow in the clouds is like: it appears in many colours from the sun's rays. And the likeness of his face to the sun, what else could it signify but its sunlike quality? It also signifies that wherever angels are present, they carry out the ordering of the works of the day, lit up by a light that is unapproachable and beyond being.
I saw a mighty angel.

Those who were still alive had not taken care to look to repentance in view of the divine torments aimed at offenders. Instead they persisted, delighting in their licentiousness. For this reason he says, "I saw an angel coming down from heaven." By his clothing, the cloud, he shows that the angel is effective and divine. For the divine David also sings that cloud and darkness surround God, likening to a cloud the invisibility of his essence, that is, its bodiless and formless nature. This is also why God's appearance to the prophets took many forms. He is unchanging by nature, and though he cannot be compared to anything, he was compared to things of sense. And since the angel is divine, how could he not be mighty? For what is impossible for divine beings, and especially for those obedient to God?
And his feet were like pillars of fire.

The feet hint at his descent, which took place for no other reason than to punish the ungodly. The cloud, the rainbow and the sunlike face are meant to show the heavenly quality of the light, and that he is truly many-coloured in virtues, as well as the luminous character of angelic essence and understanding. That is why various ministries are entrusted to angels, suited to the nature of the task being carried out. Hence also "like pillars of fire." They were likened to pillars of fire not because fire gives light but because it burns, and because of those who would not be moved from their wicked practices.

To this also belongs the hymn-writer's "The voice of the Lord divides the flame of fire." He will also reward the workers with a wage fitting their labour. And the open book in his hand, what could it mean? This open book is also mentioned in Daniel, when the court sits before him and books are opened that contain the deeds and names of all who have lived since the beginning of the age. For the time being, then, the book shows the reading of what is written in it as something [?] forbidden after this [?]. If in Daniel there are books while here the seer shows a single book, there is no contradiction. In Daniel the books belong to the judgment of the whole world and set out the verdict on both the righteous and the unrighteous. Here the book concerns only those who lived in lawless deeds. Their deeds in particular are written not in a book but in a little book. By using a diminutive, the Apostle indicates how little it contains, in view of the general pronouncement of the judgment and the fulfilment of the things that complete it.
And he set his right foot on the sea.

Planting one foot on the gathered waters and the other on dry land shows the greatness of the one who has taken possession of both. I think he set the right foot on the water and the left on the dry land simply because he followed the position of these elements. Below air, whose substance is fine, lies water, which is coarser, just as dry land lies below water. Or again, I think, it is simply because the right is always more powerful than the left. That is why David sings, "The right hand of the Lord has wrought power." There are clearly more evildoers at sea, I mean pirates and those who drown their victims, whether in sea battles or through some other plot, because the watery element gives evildoers an easier way out against those they scheme against. Since this is so, the more powerful foot is fittingly assigned against the evildoers. That this is so, the forefather of God is a trustworthy witness to confirm. He describes the assault on us of the demons who plot against us, when we make use of the help of the Most High. There he describes the fall of the plotters who walk in darkness as a thousandfold on the left side, while to the right he assigned ten times as many. So much, then, for the placing of the feet. His crying out with a loud voice, with a lion's roar, is a symbol of anger, which is why it was compared to bellowing. We have already discussed this earlier, as far as we were able by God's love for mankind. After the cry, the seven thunders spoke. We think that these seven thunders, or seven voices uttered fearsomely by one and the same angel, are the angelic powers, which is why they were likened to thunders. Or else they are the seven spirits mentioned earlier. The addition of the article suggests this to us when he says, "the seven thunders spoke." Grammarians always take the article as recalling something already known.
As a lion bellows.

"Bellowing" is not the natural word for the sound a lion makes. It belongs rather to oxen, while for lions the word assigned is brykein or brychein, "to roar" or "to gnash." Yet the narrator makes clear that he did not say this carelessly, for he does not keep to the word "bellow" but moves on to "cried out." So much, then, for those who are precise about the cry of lions. But for the painful cry of sinners being punished, what word is more fitting than brykein, from which comes brygmos, "gnashing"? For the clashing of their teeth shows that they are utterly frozen as they reckon up [?] the offences committed in this passing life. They despair of God, who knows how to warm and whose instrument is the sun [?], and are as if seized by frost. Their natural strength becomes unsteady and cannot hold itself together, so it is overcome by a trembling of the limbs. When this reaches the teeth, gnashing results. It was called brykein from its likeness to eating (brōsis), since the teeth strike against one another as in eating.

And when the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to write. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write it down." And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven. He swore by the one who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there will be time no longer. Instead, in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound his trumpet, the mystery of God will be fulfilled, as he announced to his servants the prophets.
From this it is plain that the thunders are angelic powers. For it is a being that speaks, not a thunderclap, which is only an echo and has no origin or existence of its own.
I heard a voice from heaven saying.

He was prevented from writing, that is, from making plain to people in writing the things he saw. "Keep them in your mind," he says, "as if under a seal, a secure hold, but do not publish them in writing at all." Perhaps this is because it does not help for them to be revealed before the last times arrive, since Daniel too was taught that the words about such things were sealed. That it helps to keep them stored away, we might explain by conjecture from the severity of the appointed punishments, since the merciful God, in his love for mankind, does not impose a retribution of equal weight. Hence the hymn-writer tells us, "He has not repaid us according to our iniquities, nor according to our sins." This befits the kindness and goodness of the one who punishes. On this the divine Gregory, in his discourse on Adam, says: "And the punishment becomes love for mankind; this is how I am persuaded that God punishes." And elsewhere the same writer says of them: "neither mercy without judgment, nor judgment without mercy." It is therefore a mark of the highest foresight to keep silent about such things and not to make them plain to the undisciplined [?] and the younger, as Evagrius wishes. He says: "Let these things be hidden from the younger, and also the loftier teaching about judgment; for they do not know that the pain of a condemned rational soul is ignorance." No other torment is equal to ignorance for a rational soul. After God, wakefulness toward all things is part of its very being. For this reason it has been honoured with free will, so that it may suffer no misfortune through ignorance of the things that make it what it is. If this is destroyed in it, what could be more damaging?
The seven thunders spoke.

We should take the thunders to be angelic powers, likened to thunders because of how terrifying their utterances are. Such are the voices of the holy bodiless angels. They are terrifying from the very moment they appear, as is clear from the fact that Daniel could not bear even a gentle sight of an angel, let alone a threatening one. The seven thunders are to be understood not as the voices of a single angel, but as other holy angels ranking second to the first in order. The divine Dionysius is enough to confirm this from the angelic order he set out. The command is given to seal the messages of the seven thunders, that is, to keep them secret, since the full understanding and clearer knowledge of them is, for our good, reserved for the last times.
He raised his right hand to heaven.

The hand is a symbol of action, as when David says, "I will wash my hands among the innocent." This means, "I will show my actions to be innocent, that is, blameless, so that no one who abuses me can trouble me." The raising of the right hand hints at the effectiveness and the greater power of the one swearing. That is why it is said, "The right hand of the Lord has wrought power."
By the one who lives for ever.

This seems to be poor Greek, for one is said to swear "by" someone, not "in" someone. Still, it was not out of place to swear "in the one who lives," because it presents, as intended, the one by whom the oath is taken. Those who swear customarily swear by someone greater, but God had no one greater to swear by, so he swears by himself: "By myself I have sworn, says the Lord." Angels, being creatures, swear by the Creator, and through the divinity of the one they invoke they overcome our unbelief. For he swore that time would be no more, rightly and truly: "that there will be time no longer." The flow of extended time will then have no evening and no interruption, and for that reason it will not be time. For what need will there be then of sunlight, or of its withdrawal, which brings living creatures rest from the day's labours? And apart from this, what need will there be of sunlight? The righteous will be lit by the light that is God, while the ungodly will remain in darkness through their own evil conscience. The sun will indeed still exist, since the present world will not pass into nonexistence but into renewal. But just as the stars exist now even by day and are not seen, because the sun's radiance outshines their brightness so completely that no one knows they are in the sky, so it will be then. Meanwhile, not to know that there is no reason at all for the present world to pass completely into nonexistence is no ordinary ignorance.
That there will be time no longer.

He swore that there would be no time, not of the time then present, but of the time when the seventh angel is about to sound his trumpet. So it must be understood with an addition: "that there will be time no longer from now on." The oath does not concern this, but that "in the days of the voice of the seventh angel." It is said by the figure of ellipsis. What is left out is: "then there will be the absence of time," that is, the sun will no longer measure out the intervals of time. For when the seventh angel is about to sound his trumpet, the intervals of time will also fail, and the whole punishment of the ungodly will come upon them, carried out through various acts of vengeance. So when he sounds at the proper time, the consummation will come, not now, when the sounding takes place in the vision. And at the proper time, he says, together with the things the trumpet announces, the mystery that God proclaimed to his own servants the prophets will also reach its end. For the prophets prophesied up to the judgment and the repayment of each person's life. This is also the view of the divine Paul, that at that time tongues will cease and prophecies will be done away with. He calls their fulfilment good news because of the rest prepared for the saints.

And the voice that I had heard from heaven, again speaking with me and saying: "Go, take the little scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land." So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, "Take it and eat it up. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey."

For a fuller understanding of what is said, one must either add the verb "to be" to the text before us, so that it reads, "And the voice that I heard from heaven was again speaking with me and saying," or read, "This voice I heard again saying to me." Otherwise the text must be understood in one of these two ways: either it is joined to the verb "to be," or the participle is moved from the nominative case into the accusative, "saying." The action would then be in the accusative, I mean "speaking and saying," with the added sense of attention to the action. That is: "I heard it again saying, 'Go, take the little scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.'" Some other, higher angelic power appears to command the Evangelist to receive, through the book, the knowledge of the things prophesied. And what did it say? To take the book from the angel.
Take it and eat it up.

"As I was commanded," he says, "I went to the angel and asked for the little scroll, and I took it and ate it, as he ordered." And it was, as the giver had also said, sweet at first because of the knowledge of things to come. The mouth hints at this, since eating begins with it. But it was bitter in the stomach. By "stomach" he means the faculty of thought, or the capacity that receives rational food. He learned of the punishments of the ungodly, which arose from the hateful deeds that make them abominable to God. He also knew that, for one who had been found worthy of the vision, this knowledge would cause bitterness. Out of fellow-feeling he would grieve to know that people of his own kind were abominable to God and would therefore be justly subjected to punishment. The bitter and the sweet can also be understood another way. The saint who saw these things had no experience of such wickedness. In this book were recorded the names and deeds of the ungodly and the punishments they bring. He is commanded not merely to swallow it, since swallowing suggests only a passing experience, but to eat it up. That is, he is to gain the experience of one who has done these things, so that he might be thought a doer himself, having gone through much experience of them. So at first, because of the knowledge, which people always eagerly seek, it gives an impression of sweetness. But it brings bitterness because of the certain knowledge of those who are subject to the repayment of their own wicked deeds. One can also put it this way. In this book is recorded the whole conduct of those who have lived in this life. So at first, as he read about those who did good, it naturally seemed sweetened with joy. But as he went further, which is what the swallowing suggests, and came upon the abominations of the evildoers, he was filled with pain and bitterness. He felt pain because of the wailing of sinners in torment, and bitterness because they, though of the same kind, did not come up to the level of those who had done right. How else could the sacred saying be fulfilled that counsels us "to rejoice with those who rejoice, and to weep with those who weep"?
How the Evangelist received the little scroll from the hand of the angel.

And I took the little book from the angel's hand and ate it up. In my mouth it was sweet as honey, but when I had eaten it, my stomach turned bitter. And he says to me, "You must prophesy again about peoples and nations and tongues and many kings."
And he says to me, "You must prophesy again."

These words show that what was seen in the revelation would not come to pass immediately after the vision. Rather, a long time would stretch out until the end of this mortal world, when these things would be fulfilled, and during it this blessed man had to prophesy to many. He would do this either through the knowledge contained in his Gospel, where some things still to come are set out, or through the present Revelation. So from that time until now this inspired man has been prophesying. At that time he did so in person, by himself, through the Gospel and the Revelation, as has already been said. But we should be aware that many people take this saying, "You must prophesy again," to mean that this blessed apostle will remain alive until the [?] and will come at the time of the Antichrist with Enoch and Elijah. With them he will set the people of that time right, and he will be killed by the Antichrist.

And I was given a reed like a rod, and was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship in it. But leave out the court outside the temple, and do not measure it, for it has been given to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months."

The Evangelist says he was given a reed. One might choose to call it knowledge of intelligible things. David, too, boasts that his tongue is "the reed of a swift scribe," because he was blessed with a tongue fit to express things clearly, just as a reed writes whatever is put before it to be written. In his case "reed" is meant figuratively, and in the same way the Evangelist now says that the knowledge that arose in his mind was imparted to him by the gift of a reed. The reed is also likened to a rod, and the rod in turn hints at what supports and what acts, as when the hymn-writer proclaims the good news of "dominion over the nations" through the gift of a rod "from the Lord" and "out of Zion." So it is not unreasonable to take the gift of the reed as the knowledge of intelligible things, signifying a divine communication, just as other inanimate objects do. I mean the altar, the throne and the like. These are not to be understood as inanimate, or as they appear to the eye, but in their higher and intelligible mode of being. In other words, one might take the gift allegorically as discerning knowledge of the things seen. For how could the reed, which has no life, say, "Rise and measure the temple of God"? From this it follows that the temple of God is measured with understanding. Someone might say instead that the reed was given by this angel and that the Evangelist heard him say, "Rise and measure this temple." To this we reply that it signifies knowledge in proportion to the one receiving it. That is, those worthy of knowledge are those whom God and the divine angels know by their good works, for the divine [apostle] says, "The Lord knew those who are his." So much for these matters.

However, some have taken a different view of these things, that is, of the temple and the altar, which the command says are to be measured, and of those who worship in it. They declare that the temple of God and the altar are God's old covenant and that the court is the new one. They miss the mark. If they were right, the old things would be more mystical and holier than the covenant in Christ, since the temple and the altar are more honourable than the court. The interpreter should not handle the command in this way. If they mean that the old things are more elementary than the new, and represent an earlier stage of piety, which is why those who won the prize under the old covenant can be counted, then the interpretation has some reason to it. In the same way childish things come before manhood, and an outline sketch comes before the colours are laid on. But in what befits God and in the forming of human character, and to put it more plainly, in the Creator's caring and tender love for us, the covenant under the law cannot be compared with the new covenant. That is why what belongs to it is scarce. So the finding of those dear to God, I mean, is subject to number, while those under the new covenant are beyond number. The court, then, would be the Church of God, which has no limit either in place or in the countless nations that find room in it. No one should be disturbed by the command that casts it outside the temple. It means nothing other than that the word declares the Church free from the law's narrow precision: circumcision, sabbath-keeping and the other needless purifications. The reason given is that it has been given to the nations not to live by the observances of the law, because freedom from such observance has been granted to the nations who wish to live according to Christ. As for the holy city being trampled for forty-two months, he calls the Church the holy city. We know that it is trodden by the nations, who have, as it were, been given leave to move about in it: by Christians in a God-loving way, by unbelievers with contempt and to their ruin. But some have taken the court that is cast out to be the gathering of the unbelieving nations and of the Jews. They say that these insolently persecute the faithful within it, especially at the time of the Antichrist, and so they have understood this as directed against the Christians.
And they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

We have taken the period of forty-two months to signify brevity, with reference to the coming of the Antichrist. That time will be exceedingly grievous to those who love God, and for this reason Christ, the true God, says that those very days will be cut short. Forty-two months are three and a half years, during which the faithful and tested will be trampled and persecuted. That is the interpretation of those who have taken the casting out of the court as [?] the gathering of the unbelievers and the Jews. But according to those who hold that it means the Church, the forty-two months signify not only the coming of the Antichrist but also the Lord's incarnation. These months are short compared with the time since the beginning of the world's creation. I mean the time from [?] Christ's coming until the end. For how long is this period since Christ's coming? It has not yet reached even a thousand years, measured against the more than five thousand completed before it. If being trampled is taken to mean living at ease, it would conflict with the times of the Antichrist, which are most grievous and toilsome for the pious. The interpretation would then offer those dear to God the [?] of life as a favour. But the Teacher also warned them beforehand, preparing them like athletes for the afflictions and contests of this world, when he said, "In the world you will have affliction." And for them nothing was more desirable than [?] to walk every day according to the will of the God-man, their Teacher. How then could anyone suppose that God's chosen ones would count toil a hardship? Is it not full of great pleasure to endure life's hardships, since they win eternal blessedness? For these reasons we must hold to the interpretation that the casting out of the court refers to the Church drawn from the nations.
On Enoch and Elijah, who are to refute the Antichrist.

"And I will grant my two witnesses authority, and they will prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth." These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. If anyone wishes to harm them, fire comes out of their mouths and devours their enemies. If anyone wishes to harm them, this is how he must be killed. They have authority to shut the sky, so that no rain falls during the days of their prophecy. They also have authority over the waters to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague as often as they wish.

Everything concerning the Lord's dispensation in the flesh had been portrayed to the Evangelist in the vision: the birth, the temptations, the teachings, the outrages against him, the cross, and then the resurrection and the second coming, and besides these the recompense of the saints and of sinners. Only the events surrounding the second coming had been left out, so now he goes back and is taught about them. That Elijah the prophet will come is clear, for Scripture foretold it through Malachi's oracle: "Behold, I send you Elijah the Tishbite before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes, who [will turn] the heart of the father to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbour." Christ, too, spoke this saying [?] concerning the Baptist, as Matthew reports: "And if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come," prophesying the [?]. But the Lord's first coming was very much like the last. In it the work of turning back those who had gone astray was carried out by a man whose way of life resembled the Tishbite's. That is why Christ made accepting it depend on his hearers, since this was not the proper coming but one like it. For to the well-disposed there is no difference in the purpose of the two comings except in time, because this turning back does not differ at all from that one. So much concerning Elijah.

As for Enoch, Scripture gives us no testimony about his coming, except that he was made immortal by being taken up. But an account has come down to the Church by unbroken tradition that he too will come with Elijah the Tishbite. They say that the two will come at the time of the Antichrist and warn the people then living not to be led astray by the Antichrist's deceitful signs, and that this testimony will last for three and a half years. That is the span of time made up by the one thousand two hundred and sixty days. Being clothed in sackcloth signifies that they go forth in lowliness, mourning and gloom. The prophet Zechariah likens these two to olive trees and to two lampstands. They are olive trees because oil is the source that feeds the light. They are lampstands because they have become bearers of the truth. The truth clothes itself in what is called the true light that comes through the virtues, and like a beacon it signals to those tossed at sea. This light also belongs to them as they speak boldly. And what else could standing before the Lord of the earth signify, except that they arrive very close to the coming of the judge of the living and the dead?

On the two olive trees and lampstands. The prophet Zechariah saw a lampstand standing, holding up seven lamps, and two olive branches. The branches, however, stood in the nozzles of two lamps. He says something like this: "the two branches of the olive trees that are in the hands of the two golden nozzles." By "nozzles" he means the part at the lip of the lamp that is specially hollowed out to hold the wick. When he asked about this, he heard from the angel who was speaking to him that they are the sons of fatness, who stand beside the Lord of all the earth. Here too the one who sets out the Revelation shows these figures to the apostle unmistakably, since the olive trees cannot be found anywhere else than in the prophecy of Zechariah. That they are taken from this prophet is confirmed by the use of the articles in "These are the two olive trees and the two [lampstands]," for articles always refer to something already known. The only difference is that what were two nozzles there are here called two lampstands. There the prophet shows the whole by naming a part, with prophetic brevity and obscurity. Here, since Christ's sojourn in the world has disclosed the riddles of the law and the prophets, the Revelation uses them openly and has changed the nozzles into lampstands. The lampstand carries the lamps. In the lamps is stored the oil, symbol of God's love for humankind, and the wick that supplies the light. The law shows no love for humankind beyond the dim light under the lampstand [?], as when it commands us to love our friend but hate our enemy. It has already been said that the olive trees and the two lampstands are those appointed to bear witness beforehand. They are revealed, as it were, before the Lord of the earth, because the Lord's second coming is near at hand, which is what "before" is meant to show.
Fire comes out of their mouths.

This is entirely credible. For if one of them, Elijah, had such authority even in former times, why should it be hard to believe that he will go forth with signs and wonders like these when he fulfils Christ's ministry and runs ahead of his coming? As Paul says, the coming of the Antichrist is by the working of Satan, with all signs and lying wonders, since working wonders does the most to win assent and belief. For this reason, I say, these two prophets who speak about him will also use mighty signs of their own. With their true signs they will expose what is error and deceit, and they will draw those who see them to belief and assent. Oh, the goodness of God, which has set truth against error as its counterweight! It will arm these saints with the power of true signs and wonders and so put their opponents to shame. They will turn people back with true wonders and with words of teaching, and also with scourges: drought, I mean, and fire, and changes in the elements that turn harmful for those who refuse to repent. These will receive chastisement in return for their rage and murderous attack against the saints. So it will go with the foolish and disobedient. But the better sort, who look toward turning back, will gain salvation, even if they are forced to it, according to the sayings "The chastening of the Lord opens my ears," and "The Lord chastens, and scourges every son whom he receives," and "restraining with bit and bridle those who do not come near to him." This salvation is awarded to them by the One who does not desire the death of the sinner, but in many ways brings about his repentance by turning him back.
And to strike the earth.

In keeping with God's kindness, healing is brought as a counterweight to the blow. By the working of Satan, the false Christ will outshine every sorcerer and enchanter in all signs and lying wonders. So the good God will arm these saints with the power of true signs. By comparison with these, they will expose the falsehood, bring back the deceived through every kind of turning, and make an example of the deceiver. Until the end of their prophecy they will suffer nothing painful, either from him or from anyone else.

And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up out of the abyss will make war on them, conquer them and kill them. Their corpse will lie in the street of the great city that is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord too was crucified. For three and a half days people from the peoples and tribes and tongues and nations look upon their corpse, and they will not allow their corpses to be laid in a tomb. Those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and celebrate, and will send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who dwell on the earth.
And when they have finished their testimony.

What testimony? That the one now present is not the Christ, but an impostor and a deadly deceiver. And that the Son of God will come very soon, and he must be believed in as Saviour. He came long ago for the benefit of humankind, and he is coming now.
The beast that comes up out of the abyss.

He calls the Antichrist a beast because he is savage, inhuman and bloodthirsty. By the abyss he means human life, which is made bitter and grievous by sins and is unsettled by the blasts and contrary winds of the evil spirits. This wicked man will not rise from some other nature, but from our own human substance. He will be a man acting by the working of Satan, as has already been said. So he says that this beast will make war on these holy prophets, kill them, and throw their bodies unburied into the streets of Jerusalem. For he will reign there as king of the Jews. He will deceive them and have them serve and obey him in everything. As the Lord says in John, "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him." He says that Jerusalem is called Sodom, as a kind of allegory. It is called Sodom because of the debauchery and cruelty to strangers that the Jews will practise in it at that time. It is called Egypt because it will enslave and wrong the servants of Christ, just as Egypt did to Israel.
And he will conquer them and kill them.

He says that after they have testified that people must flee the deception, the beast, the Antichrist, will come out of the dark, deep places of the earth. These are the places to which the devil was condemned when the Lord sojourned among us in the flesh. The Antichrist will make war on them and conquer them, and by God's permission he will destroy them and leave them unburied.
And their corpse.

Their corpses, that is, their bodies, are called "fallen" because by death they have fallen from the glory and height they had in life. He will leave them unburied in the street of the old, ruined Jerusalem. For there he will reign as king of the Jews, supposedly to fulfil the prophetic saying "I will raise up the tent of David that has fallen," and in imitation of the true Christ, who was also born there according to the flesh. The Jews, carried away headlong by this prophecy, apply it to the Antichrist's coming.
Where their Lord too was crucified.
Their Lord, that is, the Lord of the two witnesses.
And people from the peoples look upon.

The Jews from every tribe who have been deceived by the Antichrist will see the two witnesses killed and will rejoice, as if their own king had won the victory, and they will greet one another with gifts of thanksgiving. They will leave their bodies unburied, giving this as the repayment due to the two prophets. Yet the prophets inflicted no physical torment on them, for the plagues did not fall bodily on them [?], but rather on creation. Or else the prophets truly tormented them by mocking their sins, exposing them, and clearing away their deception.

How Enoch and Elijah, after being killed by the Antichrist, will rise again and strike the deceived with amazement. And after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw [?] them. And I heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here." And they went up to heaven in the cloud, and their enemies watched them. At that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed. Behold, the third woe is coming soon.

He says that those who have been put to death will be raised after as many days as there were years of the prophecy. Here again he has departed from the way he marks time, shifting from the future of what is yet to be accomplished to the past tense.
