For if, as some of the teachers say, such a name had needed to be clearly known, the one who saw it would have revealed it. But divine grace did not see fit to set down the destroyer's name in the divine book. As an exercise, however, one can find many names, both common and proper, that contain this number, as the blessed Hippolytus and many others have done.
On the 144,000 standing with the Lamb on Mount Zion.

And I looked, and behold, the Lamb was standing on Mount Zion, and with him a number, 144,000, who had his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the sound of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. And the voice that I heard was like that of harpists playing on their harps. And they sing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders. And no one could learn the song except the 144,000 who had been bought from the earth.
On Mount Zion.

Not the old Zion, since it too did not obey the Lamb, who is Christ. That is why it was said to the disobedient, "Behold, your house is left to you desolate." So the Lamb does not stand on the old Zion. It was destroyed by Roman hands and its temple burned when the city was taken by Titus, the son of Vespasian. He stands not on the old Zion, then, but on the new, which is the city of the living God. The Lamb is now shown standing upon it, and so the vision points to the conversion of Israel in the last times. The divine Paul also hinted at this when he says, "When the full number of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved," being united to Christ. For Isaiah too announced this good news to them, saying: "Behold, the deliverer will come for Zion's sake and will turn away ungodliness from Jacob, says the Lord."
And with him a number, 144,000.

That is, with the Lamb. This number of thousands is not the same as the one given earlier for those from each tribe who believed in Christ. Otherwise he would have used the article and said "the 144,000." But since he uses no article, we must understand him to be speaking of those from the Gentiles. In each of them the grace of the divine and apostolic seed produced a thousand twelve times over, the perfect fruit of the faith of those who are saved. He also testifies that they achieved virginity, of the flesh as well as of the soul, which is rare among the Hebrews. They have the name of his Father and of the Son written on their foreheads. This shows that they are sealed with the divine light of his divine face, and through it they become terrifying to the destructive demons who counterfeit this seal.
Like the sound of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder.

The sound of the waters, the thunder and the harp shows how piercing the saints' hymnody is, and how melodious, resonant and harmonious their song. It rings throughout the whole assembly and festal gathering of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, upon whom the title "firstborn" is bestowed. This title carried honor among the ancients, for it showed the parents to be what they in turn had made their own parents, repaying to nature the common contribution [?]. When this harmony of the saints resounds, which they were able to achieve through putting to death the body and its desires, no one but they could learn it. For knowledge extends as far as the measure of one's way of life, just as among human servants secrets are disclosed in proportion to their service. But I think that no one can even hear the mysteries of the new song except those who have been counted worthy to sing them. For each person's knowledge is in proportion to his purity. For one does not pour the Lord's new wine into old wineskins, nor put a patch of unshrunk cloth on a worn-out garment.
Who had been bought from the earth.

It is to such people that the divine Paul says, rather sharply, "You were bought with a price." Therefore, as people who have been bought, do not be careless, but carry out without delay the service for which you were bought. And he also shows what the price is, saying, "with the precious blood of the spotless lamb, who is Christ." So much for Paul. The present vision, however, speaks of "those bought from the earth." Why does it mention the land that bore them? To show the goodness of the buyer, that he did not buy out of need. For what need of earthly things does the heavenly one have? It was a work of goodness and love for humankind. He held fast to the lowly, even though they were unworthy of salvation, so firmly that he paid the price by pouring out his own blood. That much concerns the buyer. But why mention the land that bore those who were bought? To show their ingratitude as well, that they did not live in a way worthy of their calling. Otherwise all of them would have learned the song, and it would not have been limited to a number.

These are the ones who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. These are the ones who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These were bought by Jesus from among people as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouth, for they are blameless. These are the ones who follow the Lamb.

These words do not dishonor marriage, for marriage is honorable. Nor does the praiseworthiness of virginity make marriage unworthy. But since star differs from star in glory, we consider that these surpass the rest, coming next after the twenty-four elders. They do so because of their virginity and because they are blameless in tongue and in hands. After the coming of Christ they acquired the splendor of virtues, and through it they are taught the new song. To the many this song remains unknown, not only in the present life but also in the age to come.

For even if knowledge is perfect there, as the Apostle says, it is still unfolded to each in proportion to his own purification. For what does Paul say? "Then I shall know, even as I have been known." By knowledge he means not comprehension but the intimacy that comes from love. So our knowledge will abound in proportion to the intimacy with the divine that we gain through virtue, and partial knowledge will be extinguished together with this corruptible life. There too glory is not one and the same for all, but is measured out according to the different labors of virtue. One can hear this from him who says, "Each will receive his own reward according to his own labor," and from Christ: "In my Father's house are many dwelling places." The word "many" introduces difference, for things are counted only when they differ in some way from one another.
These are the ones who follow the Lamb.

This does not present the Lamb as something different from Christ. Rather, it shows the difference in virtue among those who were fortunate enough to learn the song. Some, praised for their simplicity of soul and innocence, have become fit to follow the Lamb. Others, more manly in disposition and fortified by reasoned resolve, drew near in manly fashion to Christ, who grew to manhood, and won the victory over both passions and tyrants. Still others imitated Christ their teacher, some in his innocence, others in his lamb-like nature, even to the point of shedding their own blood for him. In this way they gained the privilege of being acquired by him. But someone will say: "If the song is a reward for such labors by those who succeeded, how can they be said to have been bought?" Let him hear, then, that the purchase is not meaningless, for people cannot succeed without divine help. To choose lies in the power of the one who chooses, but to reach the goal belongs to God, who works with him. That is why it is said, "It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy." Since, then, the whole achievement comes from God, it is fitting that he also pays the price. And just as the dwelling places of glory differ, so do those of punishment. That is why it is said that "each will receive his own reward according to his own."
On the angel who foretells that the coming judgment is near.

And I saw an angel flying in midheaven, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who live on the earth, and to every nation and tribe and language and people. He said with a loud voice, "Fear the Lord and give him glory, for the hour of his judgment has come. And worship him who made heaven and earth and the sea and the springs of water."

"Midheaven" carries a twofold meaning. First, it shows that both the message he proclaims and the messenger himself, sent by God, are lofty, exalted and from heaven. Second, it shows that the judgment hoped for from the ages has already drawn near. This judgment brings salvation to those from every part of the earth and from every nation who have done what pleases God. But it is also fearful to demons and sinners. The Voice hinted at both. To the good, the word "loud" signals that the coming of the righteous judge is welcome to them, and that he will restore them to the one for whose sake they contended, holding fast to his commandments in this toilsome life. The command to "fear" does more. It encourages the righteous, whose flesh is nailed fast by the fear of God, not to fear those who kill the body, for these cannot also kill the soul. This is not seen in the command without reason. Even before the coming of the Antichrist the faithful were subjected to tortures for Christ's sake, and they will be during the Antichrist's coming as well. So for the faithful of both times fear has been taken up for their safety. But to the demons, and to the people driven to frenzy by them, it brings fear not for safety but from the expectation of what they have done. That is why the prophet says, "Behold, the Lord comes, and who will endure the day of his coming?" Since, then, the coming of the righteous judge is all but at hand, he rightly surrounds both groups with fear: the one for their safety, the other on account of eternal punishment.
And worship him.

It is right to worship him as the maker of what is in heaven, on earth and under the earth. Heaven, earth and sea indicate the visible creation, while the springs indicate what lies under the earth. For no one knows where springs rise from, just as with the things beneath the earth. And if servile submission is due to him as the cause of these things, then dishonor and contempt are rightly due to the wicked devil.
On the second angel, who proclaims the fall of Babylon.
And another angel, a second, followed, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon, the great city, because she has made all the nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication.”

“Second” is not said idly. It points back to the angel who began the threats of punishment. Following on those threats, another angel came to confirm the same calamities, and this is what “followed” suggests. And what comes next in the oracle? “Babylon the great has fallen.” With the fulfilment of what was announced beforehand, nothing more is needed for the whole confusion of the present life to be brought to a fall, that is, to be done away with. For what else would “fall” signify? In the same way, Babylon signifies nothing other than confusion. And what is Babylon? None other than this corruptible world, in which nothing is unmixed with its opposite, and good is mingled with evil. This Babylon, then, is all but shaken down, and from nowhere else than [?] from that which knows how to derange and which has led people away from all sober reasoning. He has rendered this as “wine,” because it is driven into frenzy by an impulse that cannot be turned back, for such is wrath. From it also comes being enslaved and stripped of every good. Scripture knows as “fornication” not only the licentious union of male with female but also every turning away from the good, if the saying “You have destroyed everyone who goes whoring away from you” is to be trusted. Because of these things, then, she herself is shaken down along with those she made drink. Together with the visible creation, those who dwell in it, enticed as they were by its fleeting beauty, also pass away. They do not pass into total non-existence, for what reason would there be for that? They pass toward renewal, of which David also speaks in “You will renew the face of the earth.” This renewal is joyful for those who have lived in a way pleasing to God, but ruinous for sinners and for the devil and the demons, and it stretches over an everlasting span. That this world is what is meant by “Babylon” is shown by the added word “great.” For “great” is not set in contrast with a small Babylon; it introduces what the thing actually is. But if anyone wishes to apply the passage to the Chaldean Babylon, it will make no difference. So many things have befallen the world that was made vain in imitation of her, and that archetype herself suffered them, since everything that happens in the copy is referred back to its cause.
On the third angel, who secures the Lord’s people against accepting the Antichrist.

And a third angel followed them, saying with a loud voice, “If anyone worships the beast and its image, and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand, he too will drink of the wine of God’s wrath, mixed undiluted in the cup of his anger. He will be tormented with fire and sulfur before the holy angels and before the Lamb. And the smoke of their torment goes up for ever and ever, and they have no rest day or night, those who worship the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name.”

He said “followed” because he wanted to convey something continuous, unbroken and unrelenting. The loud voice signifies how astounding the message is, and that what it declares reaches every ear. Worshipping the beast and receiving its seal mean regarding the Antichrist as God, clinging to him in submission, and carrying out and proclaiming what pleases him, whether in word or in deed. This is what the mark on the forehead and on the hand signifies: the forehead stands for word and the hand for deed. By “image” he means the impious way of life, and those who pursue it will receive a just recompense. And what does it mean to drink of the wine of wrath? He called wrath “wine” not because wine gladdens, but because it darkens the mind and drives one out of one’s senses, for such too is wrath. He says this wine is mixed undiluted. It is undiluted because in Hades repentance has ceased. “Mixed” is used in place of “poured out” or “given.” It is said this way because among the ancients cups were made from horns. Some have tried to reconcile “mixed” with “undiluted.” They say that the undiluted wrath is tempered by God’s unsurpassable love for humankind, according to the verse “If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, who shall stand?” From this they conclude that God does not use undiluted wrath against sinners. Their reasoning holds well for this changing age while it runs its course. In that pure and unchanging age, however, it has no force, for each will receive a wage equal to his own labor. It is called “wine of wrath” just as there is also “wine that gladdens.” Wine that gladdens produces forgetfulness of troubles, which is why it is said, “wine in grief.” So here punishment is called the wine of wrath, the consequence of the wine of impiety. That wine drives anyone who uses it without measure out of his right mind and pushes him, without restraint, into every beastly passion.

“Of the undiluted, mixed in the cup of his anger.” He aptly likened the undiluted wrath to undiluted wine mixed in the cup. For undiluted wine can intoxicate more than diluted wine. So too, in the age to come, the wages paid back for the lives people have lived are undiluted and unmixed with their opposite, that is, with mercy and the lasting remembrance of good works. This is because the life there is true and free of everything feigned and contrived. But if this is so, how is it “mixed” in the cup? Is it not clear that “mixed” signifies not some mingling but a giving? It may then be understood like this: “of what was mixed,” that is, of what was given out in the cup of anger. For what sparing is there in anger? Consistently with the anger, then, the torment is of fire and sulfur, both of them intensely burning: fire, whose nature is to blaze, and sulfur, which keeps stirring it up without ceasing. “Before the holy angels and the Lamb” is meant to show two things. The angels show that the torment is inexorable, since they too are not liable to sins, and [?] one who is beyond the reach of sin would not be seen to show favor toward those who readily make themselves liable to what is hated. That is the meaning of the angels. The Lamb brings to mind his slaughter for the salvation of human beings. He gave himself up for them, loving them with a burning love [?], while they took no care at all to be delivered from their own destruction. The “smoke of their torment” is either the declaration to all that the punishment is carried out by fire, since smoke is evidence of fire, or it is a kind of cloud sent up from the gasping and wailing of those being punished, rising not for a short while but forever. Isaiah also hinted at this with the undying worm and the unquenchable fire. That this goes on everlastingly he suggested by the unceasing activity throughout night and day, even though night and day will not exist there. For what need is there for the courses of the sun in the incorruptible life? In that life there is no need of sleep and no coming round of seasons, of sowing and harvest and the gathering of fruits, since human beings will no longer need the things that are known to sustain this present corruptible life.

Here is the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.” “Yes,” says the Spirit, “so that they may rest from their labors, for their works follow with them.”

At this time, he says, the time of the Antichrist, the endurance of the saints is shown. Then the passage is shaped as an answer to a question: “And who,” he asks, “are these saints you call enduring?” Then, as if answering, he says, “Those who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.” For even when trials and death are at hand, these will put everything second to the love of God and the faith of Jesus. In saying this he is not dividing or separating faith in God from faith in the Lord. He proceeds this way because he is moving forward in a more elementary manner. For the right conception of the divine was found among the Jews alone, and it turned worship away from the many vain gods to one God. Christ, however, was seen as a man and was called one, so most people did not yet regard him as a treasure of divine nature united, beyond all being, with the One who is beyond all being. For this reason he set the faith of Jesus alongside the commandments of God more distinctly. Yet one may also say that this actually strengthens the doctrine of Christ’s divinity. For if faith in Jesus accompanies the commandments of God, what need is there to separate what is seen of Jesus [?] from the divine commandments? Rather, the commandments draw their authority from this. It was for their sake, when they were being neglected, that he did not disdain to take on the lowly nature of man. He wanted to show in his own person that human nature is not incapable of carrying out the commandments, and so he united himself to that nature when he became man. Moreover, “here is endurance” is not used out of place. It strengthens the resolve of those who have chosen to endure. Once endurance has been proved in this fleeting and brief time, they will receive an eternal and indestructible reward of joy and gladness, of such a kind and so great that no mortal word could describe it.
The complete construction of this passage is as follows: “Here is the endurance of the saints: that those who keep the commandments of God should also keep the faith of Jesus.”
“Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.”

The voice from heaven does not call all the dead blessed. It blesses those who have died in the Lord, “those who have been put to death to the world and carry about in their body the dying of the Lord Jesus.” For them, departure from the body is truly a rest that releases them from their labors. The fact that their works follow them is the ground for unfading crowns and prizes of glory, since the rewards far surpass the contests. That is why the divine Paul says, “The sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.”
“Yes,” says the Spirit.

The construction is this: the Spirit says, “Write: from now on,” and, “Yes, write.” In this way the Spirit, as it were, entices those who are contending with the promise that their toils will cease and that they will gain the goods of rest. For together with the end of their labors will come the reward for their works. For God is not unjust, so as to let virtuous labors fall into oblivion.
That the one seated on the cloud brings to completion with the sickle what grows from the earth.

And I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud was one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head and a sharp sickle in his hand. And another angel came out of the temple, crying out with a loud voice to the one seated on the cloud, “Put in your sickle and reap, for the hour to reap has come, because the harvest of the earth is dried up.” And the one seated on the cloud cast his sickle on the earth, and the earth was reaped.

What we have said before we say again now. We should not understand the things now revealed by attending to intervals of time, as though they were only now beginning, or as though things that have already happened were being assigned to the future. There is no need to quibble about these matters once we have grasped one principle: what will certainly come to pass is presented as already having happened, and what is now being accomplished is presented as what must in this way be brought to completion. That is why he has proceeded in this way here too, bringing forward future things through what is now being shown. He says, then, that he saw a white cloud. It may be like the cloud that took him from the apostles’ sight when he ascended to his Father. Or it may be understood as God’s vehicle, as is said by David, “Cloud and darkness are round about him,” and by Isaiah, “Behold, the Lord sits on a light cloud and will come to Egypt.” The divine fathers have taken this cloud to be Mary the ever-virgin. She rose, as it were, like vapor from the earth, that is, she escaped earthly grossness. Lightness is ascribed to her because she was adorned with virtues that run toward heaven and because she was blessed to have the Son of God dwell among us through her. Or the cloud may be some angelic power, because of the purity and loftiness of the angelic nature, and also because the cloud is white. For the Psalmist too says, “He mounted the cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds.” This is also why Aquila rendered “cloud” as “light thickness.” It is “thickness” because it is a vehicle, for what kind of vehicle would it be if it did not provide a firm seat through its thickness? It is “light” because it is weighed down by no sin. But someone may think thickness unworthy of how we conceive the angelic nature and so consider this interpretation mistaken. [?] these in relation to the almighty and divine nature, which can scarcely be grasped even by the mind alone. [?] and to attribute thickness to it in the case of such a cloud, and that one like a son of man rides upon it [?]
“With a golden crown on his head.”

The crown hints that the Lord Jesus is king, for Christ is king of things both intelligible and sensible. He calls the crown golden, using what is precious among us to sketch its glory. That he has a sickle in his hand indicates that the consummation of this age lies in his authority. He himself called the consummation of the world a harvest, and what else would a sickle bring about but a harvest? There, in the Gospel, the gathering of the faithful was indicated. Here it is the consummation of human beings, so that anything in them that is like chaff, fruitless and fit for fire may be handed over to the fire, and anything like wheat may be stored in the divine granaries. The sharpness of the sickle shows either how inexorable and unrelenting the wrath is, or how swiftly it strikes.
“And another angel came out, crying out.”

Why did this angel come out crying out? In a roundabout way these words indicate the supplication of the heavenly powers. They long for the righteous to be honored, because the righteous imitated them in their own temporary life, and so the powers are well disposed toward them. Nor do they refuse to see vengeance taken on those who lived contrary to them. That is why it is said, “How long, Lord, shall sinners boast?” So they press for the hastening of the end, so that what moves and changes may cease and what is unchanging and immovable may be revealed. When the hour of harvest has come, then, [?] all that was sown [?] has reached its prime [?] the gathering in and [?] the cultivation of piety [?] yielding fruit to the farmer thirtyfold, sixtyfold and a hundredfold. Thirtyfold [?] of those who were approved in the times of the law of Moses. Sixtyfold, double that, [?] more elementary than the mystery of Christ, yet more perfect and double the [?]. A hundredfold, according to the most perfect strictness of the Christian life, by which [?] those who have lived in this way and [?] surpassing nature, were brought to completion.
“Because the harvest of the earth is dried up.”

The drying of the harvest signifies nothing other than the arrival of the time of the consummation. Then the human crop will have ripened like mature wheat. The part that was cultivated in piety will be counted worthy of being stored in the divine granaries. The part that ran wild and produced nothing like wheat, nothing nourishing and worthy of the divine seed, will be given over to the eternal fire. For what does sacred Scripture say? “Each will receive his own wage according to his own labor.”
On another angel, who gathers the grapes of the vine of bitterness.

And another angel came out of the temple that is in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, who had authority over the fire, and he called with a loud cry to the one who had the sharp sickle, saying, “Send in your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe.” So the angel thrust his sickle into the earth and gathered the vintage of the earth, and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood came out of the winepress up to the horses’ bridles for a distance of sixteen hundred stadia.

The angel who is sent out is identified for a reason: he is said to have been sent from the heavenly temple. Nothing of the kind was said about the angel before him, except only that he was sent from the temple. Here, however, the place where the temple stands has also been included. We say, then, that various acts of worship are performed for the almighty God by his incorporeal ministers. Some of them were allotted as overseers of the altars on earth, from the time the worship of God was proclaimed to those on earth. This extends from Abraham and Moses until the coming of Christ, and after it until the consummation of the present age. Fittingly, then, nothing of this kind was mentioned in the earlier case, unless someone counts the mention of the Lamb as an identifying mark there too. It was because of his coming on earth that angels communicated with men and God-bearing men foretold his coming on earth. So, to make it clearer that worship is offered to the almighty God not only on earth but also in heaven, it was necessary in the case of this angel to mention the place where he presides as well. He says that this angel too is armed with a sharp sickle, to indicate how swiftly the outcome comes.
Having authority over the fire.

Understand that this angel has been appointed over the punishment of the ungodly. From this we learn that angelic powers preside over all created things: water, air, and certain other parts. This one presides over fire, though it is punitive fire, and he is one of the higher angels.
He called with a loud cry to the one who had the sickle.

Not “with a loud voice” but “with a cry.” A voice simply has the effect of being perceived by the hearing, while a cry also instills a zealous impulse toward the undertaking. In this way the cry of Sodom caused the utterly impassible God to be disposed in anger toward them, and not to incline toward greater leniency even at Abraham’s intercession. In this way too the cry of the Lord-slayers against Stephen the deacon [?] admitted some gentleness [?] toward the one who prayed that their sin against him should in no way be counted. Since “cry” is taken in this sense, he lets us understand that it belongs to one who urges on the one addressed and strengthens him for the deed, and not to one who sets about it with clamour.
And gather the clusters of the vine of the earth.

The vintage of the grapes hints at the utterly lawless, by whom the cup in the Lord’s hand is made drunk, that is, filled. This is not for the joyful drunkenness that the steward of good things customarily bestows, but for punishment. That is why it also says that all the sinners of the earth will drink of it. That is also why it is said, “And your cup that inebriates me [?] is most excellent”; so the filling is not for joyful drunkenness. That this is what the vision means to portray is clear from the following. The Lord himself does not deign to do the gathering, as he did with the first harvest, nor does he send one part into the storehouses and the other into the unending fire. Instead one of the angels, because of the surpassing degree of their licentiousness, throws them straight into the winepress of the wrath of God, deeming them worthy neither of a defense nor of an inquiry. By the load [?] of their own iniquities they turned the Good One’s bestowal into punishment.
And the angel thrust his sickle into the earth.

The sickle carried by the angel is thrust into the earth. That is, it makes a punitive harvest of those who wallow about the earth, gulping down filthy deeds like swine. So too in the Gospels the just Judge, by the sentence of a just judge, sent away into the everlasting fire those condemned for refusing to share with the poor.
And he gathered the vintage of the earth.

“The vine” is more emphatic, as the addition “of the earth” shows. It also shows that this vine is the opposite of the vine out of Egypt that is extolled by the forefather of God, and of the true vine, which our Saviour Jesus did not disdain to call himself, whose branches are the apostles. How is it the opposite? The vine transplanted from Egypt spread its branches until it covered the whole earth and sea, and covered the mountains with its shadow. The mountains are those who before it had been settled on the heights of godliness above the lowly nations. I mean those who traced their lineage according to the flesh from Enosh, a line that was preserved down to Noah at the flood, and from him again lasted until Peleg. Nothing can be found surpassing the vine of Abraham’s race, drawn out of Egypt through Moses and fitted by him for the worship of God. The angel is commanded to harvest unsparingly the vine that is the opposite of this one, as we said before. That vine has advanced [?] in impiety and overshadowed all the licentious before it, since they have been driven into Bacchic frenzy by the son of perdition himself, the Antichrist. And the task was carried out with severity.

The outflow from the winepress is called blood. In the obvious sense, this is because the liquid pressed out of the grape is called so, as in “they drank wine, the blood of the grape.” In the sense hidden for the understanding, murder too is called blood, as in “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out.” Punishment is also called blood, as in “You shall not stand against the blood of your neighbour.”
And he threw it into the winepress of the wrath of God.

He speaks in rather human terms here, because he wants to show how far the people of that time exceeded all bounds in licentiousness. After all, what faith would allow that the blessed and unchangeable nature is overcome by passions? As for the grapes being trodden outside the city, by “city” he means the commercial commonwealth of the present life. In it one cannot say how great the trade in goods for sale is, as good things are exchanged for bad and bad for good. After this life comes to its end, people receive the true recompense for what they have traded, so he reasonably said “outside the city.” And since he says that blood flows from the winepress when the grapes are trodden, it remains for us to understand the grapes as the sinners. So he also takes the blood figuratively as their wicked deeds, since the just vengeance for them becomes plain to all. That vengeance is just because they did not even heed the angels appointed from above to oversee them, who restrain men from God-hated deeds by their help, as if with bridles. These men were so frenzied that they dishonoured not only the natural notions the Creator gave them for acquiring good things, but also those that come from the divine angels. He says it is customary to call the angels horses, as Habakkuk the prophet does when he says, “You mounted upon your horses.” Their unruliness was displayed even toward their divine helpers, and so the scourge for their disobedience is now made fully manifest to all. The oversight of the holy angels is not recent but has existed from the creation of the world, as Moses confirms when he says, “He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels.” For this reason the bridle of the horses is now said to reach “for sixteen hundred stadia.” The stadion is understood here not as a distance but as an epoch. That epoch was made known in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life through the flood, which purged [?] the most complete sin. The number one thousand, formed among the numbers from the hundredth of the ten [?], marks this as most complete. It has also been taken now in the sense that a second world began from that destruction, and this world will undergo its destruction [by fire]; the first was destroyed by water, according to what is contemplated under the [?].
On the seven angels who bring the plagues upon humankind before the consummation, and on the sea of glass on which he saw the saints.

And I saw another sign in heaven, great and wonderful: seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for in them the wrath of God was completed. And I saw what looked like a sea of glass mixed with fire. Standing on the sea of glass were those who had conquered the beast and its image and its mark and the number of its name. They held the harps of God, and they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying: “Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, King of the nations! Who will not fear you, Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will surely come and worship before you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”

How could it not be great, when it signifies the destruction of the whole world? And how could it not be wonderful? The world began from a week of days, and it is brought to completion by angels equal in number. It ends in the same number, both through the angels allotted the task of purging and through the plagues they hold for purging. The seven plagues are the sea of glass, fire, the image of the beast, the beast itself, its mark, and the number of its name. These are the plagues through which the wrath of God was completed. They are the last because no further contest remains for those who conquer them. Some have conquered by endurance all the instability of this life, which through its saltiness tends to dry up for the many whatever refreshes. Others have in no way been mastered by the splendours and glories of the world, which is fragile and destined to be shattered like glass. These have received not the burning power of fire but its illuminating power. They have not had the misfortune of being wrestled down by the image of the beast, or the beast itself, or the number of its name, but have conquered manfully. Standing then on the sea of glass, they bear a symbol of their own mortification in this life, in which they lived with its pleasures rendered inactive. And they sing such things as it is fitting for those who have conquered these things to sing.
With seven plagues, which are the last.

The “seven” is not to be understood as the number seven itself; it stands for a multiple. So when it says, “Repay our neighbours sevenfold,” it means “manifold.” In the same way here it means the many punishments prepared against sinners, through which the wrath of God reaches its end. These are also called the last. When you hear of the wrath of God, do not take it as though the divine were subject to passion. As has already been said, he used language in a human way. He had no other way of indicating how excessive the licentious deeds of sinners were, as though they could move even the impassible nature, so he used human language. The sea of glass would seem to signify nothing else than abundance, through the word “sea,” and through the word “glassy,” the brightness and purity of those deemed worthy of the blessed life there. That is why they will shine like the sun with their virtues. This sea is mixed with fire because, according to the divine Paul, what is built on the foundation that he himself laid [?] will be tested by fire. The structures of wood, and those likened to hay and straw, such as the works of sinners, go to utter destruction. Then there are those of gold, silver and precious stones. Those likened to gold and silver would have, besides permanence and brilliance, what is praiseworthy and acceptable. Those compared to precious stones would be none other than works accomplished in a God-loving way through toil and sweat. They do not fail to be accepted, though their brilliance has been dimmed [?]. It is likely that the fire also signifies the divine, and the gift of the divine Spirit. For he appeared to Moses in fire, and came upon the apostles in the form of fiery tongues.
Holding the harps of God, and they sing the song of Moses.

By saying “harps” he hints at the putting to death of the members that are on earth. They are “of God” because no earnest person succeeds without divine help. That is why David says, “You held me by my right hand, and guided me by your counsel.” Paul too assures the faithful that they “carry about in the body the dying of Jesus.” What else does he mean than that those who have made themselves dead to sin in emulation of their teacher are thus regarded as doing what pleases him? Whoever emulates someone in matters of virtue will surely have him as a fellow worker in the achievement. And whoever unreservedly carries out what pleases him wins his favour. The harps [?] signify the putting to death of the members. It follows, then, that a harmonious life will also exist, struck by the plectrum of the Spirit in the concord of the virtues. “And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of the Lord.” It is reasonable for all to understand this as the song he sang at the drowning of Pharaoh and the Egyptians. The drowning of the Egyptians freed Moses and those with him from slavery. In the same way, for those who have conquered the beast and its dealings, the song is understood, as has been said, from the things done through Moses at God’s command. This is the song of those who were victorious before the law and under the law. And what else could the song of the Lamb be than one composed by the very one who gives the revelation? It will be sung by those who have lived holy lives from the time of Christ and after Christ. It is the unceasing song in grace, proclaiming the majesty of the Lamb, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ. Through him the just and true guidance of the Almighty has been arranged for our salvation. He accomplished these things for his own creature through his apostles, as King (basileus), being the base (basis) of mercy. And it was said by Isaiah, “There shall be the root of Jesse, he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope.” For this reason the revelation calls him King of the nations, and says that all the nations will come and worship before him.

After this I looked, and the temple of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the temple came the seven angels who had the seven plagues. They were clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests. Then one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives for ever and ever. And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.

By “tent” here he means the one in heaven. Moses was commanded to pitch the tent below in its likeness: “See,” it says, “that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.” From this temple, once opened, the seven angels will come out. Until then the archetypal tent in heaven was inaccessible, secured on every side like an inner sanctuary, just as was the one Moses modelled on it on earth. But now it is time for what was hidden until then to be seen. All are to be given the knowledge that the Lord, making [judgments?] [?], requites each person according to the works of their hands, and a fitting seizure follows. So the avengers have rushed out from the heavenly sanctuaries as if from a starting line. Before Christ condescended to come to us, the knowledge of what lay ahead was obscure and inconceivable to men. Therefore, so that these things might be believed more clearly, at the Lord’s passion the veil of the earthly temple was torn from top to bottom. It was as though the divine mysteries, folded in secrecy since the foundation of the world, from then on became manifest and visible to all. They were no longer treasured up for one nation but displayed to all nations. It is called the “tent of witness” not by chance. From there God gave his oracles and prescribed to the priests under the law what they were and were not to do, with exact and unreserved command. This came not from the witness of the law but from the archetypal and human [?] one.
And the seven angels who had the seven plagues came out.

“Seven” has been used in place of “many.” For many terrible things will happen at the time of the consummation, as the Lord said in the Gospels: famines, plagues, earthquakes, and what follows from them.
They were clothed in pure linen.

“Clothed in new linen,” or “stone,” for some of the copies also have this reading. Linen, because they touch nothing of animal passion, which by nature dims the brightness of life. Stone, as a sign of their pure and luminous nature, which is inclined [?] toward the good. In the same way Christ, in [?] Isaiah, is said to have been “laid as a stone in the foundation of Zion,” and in David, “this very one has become the head of the corner, though rejected by the builders.” For Christ is the foundation of the pious faith. He holds together and joins the two peoples, from the Jews and from the Gentiles, to complete a dwelling of the one living God. Fittingly, then, because they are near this stone and their virtues are brilliant, those who minister were also seen clothed in bright stones. These same ones were also girded around their chests with golden sashes. The chest is the desiring part of the body, where the heart dwells, which rules over desire. Clearly they do not leave this part loose or bound by no belt of self-control. Instead it is restrained by a very dignified and precious clasp. Gold is just that: of all earthly materials, it is the most sought after and the most precious to men.
And one of the four living creatures.

The seven angels received the golden bowls from one of the four living creatures, which were discussed at length earlier. He says this is shown in Ezekiel as well: knowledge of what is to be done always passes from the first ranks to the second. This can also be found in the divine Dionysius.
Seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God.

He has rightly said that golden bowls are filled with God’s anger. For the anger is precious, since it carries within it what is good and beneficial rather than merely what is just, even if those who are punished are grieved. The wrath of God is not passionate, as we have often said, but just, because the one from whom it comes is also impassible. That is also why he is called “living,” in contrast to the dead and passionate gods of the nations. And the temple was filled with smoke.

The smoke is a sign of divine wrath, as it is said, “Smoke went up in his wrath.” Even if smoke is not mentioned here [?], the smoke is still implied by synecdoche, for smoke does not exist without fire, nor fire without smoke. Hence in Isaiah, the smoke that filled the house at the cry of the seraphim is a [?] of wrath against Jerusalem. The fiery bodyguards give it off, burning with the zeal of the one who is seated above them. The statement that the smoke came “from the glory of God and from his power” involves a kind of periphrasis. For there is no distinction between God and his power, since God is power itself and glory itself.
And no one could enter the temple.

This can be understood according to what is written: [?] no one [stands] in the counsel of the Lord. If that is so, one could hardly endure his anger. Or it can mean that the saints do not attain their lot in the Jerusalem above, and the sacred service in the temple there, until the worthy have received the rewards of their witness. Whoever applies the seven plagues to those who are alive at the consummation of the world would not miss what is fitting. For God loves mankind and moderates the affliction of complete punishment. So he will allow the punitive plagues to be brought upon those who deserve them even here, through the prophets Enoch and Elijah. That way they will not undergo the torment in full, as we said before, through the unending spans of the age to come. What reasoning [?] of the Lord would deny that this belongs to God’s unsurpassable love for mankind toward us? For “his compassions are over all his works,” as the lips have sung.
How, when the first bowl is poured out, a sore comes upon the apostates.

And I heard a loud voice saying to the seven angels, "Go and pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God on the earth." And the first went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and a foul and evil sore came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and who worshipped its image.

A loud voice: not loud in its sound (for what use is sense-perception to those who need nothing perceptible?), but loud because of the almost unbearable misery of those being punished. The voice is said to "speak" in the sense of "signify."
He poured out his bowl on the earth.

Here the "bowl", like a cup, must be taken to mean the work of punishment. When it was poured out, he says, an evil sore came about. By "sore" he means allegorically the pain that throbs in the heart. It was poured "on the earth": by "earth" he means those distracted by the vanity of earthly things. That is why, for clarity, he adds "upon the evil people." And who would the evil be, if not those who bear the mark of the beast, because they have fallen away from the living God and attached themselves to the Antichrist? This is so even though they receive no salvation from the one they have made into a god. By "mark," as we have already explained, he means the sign by which they are known. In the same way, on the coins of gold, silver and bronze, as they are called, the likenesses of the kings whose [?] they are have been stamped so that they may be recognized. By "the image of the beast" he means the Antichrist, that is, the image of the devil. By a rivalry, though a deceitful one, [?] of the Lord Jesus: in him all the fullness of the Godhead dwells in essence. This is what "bodily" is meant to show, and in this he also differed from his prophets and from Spirit-bearing men, who came to bear God through divine inspiration or illumination. In the same way the whole fullness of satanic being will be added to the Antichrist from his birth, more than to soothsayers and diviners and all that deceitful band. At the time of the consummation, those on whom the bowl is poured out will be afflicted with sores. They will also suffer bodily scourges, which Christ himself foretold to his apostles would come before the consummation, when he said, "You will hear of wars and rumors of wars," and what follows. A little later he adds this as well: "For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, and never will be." For besides the [?] turmoil that smoulders in people through what they hear, bodily pains too will [?] torment the wicked.
The second plague, against those punished in the sea.
And the second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became blood like that of a dead man, and every living soul in the sea died.

By "sea" one may wish to understand the instability of the present age. At that time nation will rise up in war against nation, and battles will be fought at sea and on land, and even the rivers will be reddened with the blood of the slain. There is nothing unlikely in that. Or one may hold that, by divine power, the waters will be changed into blood by the holy prophets Enoch and Elijah, to refute those deceived through their credulity, as the river in Egypt was changed by Moses. The wording that follows rather supports this. It says "blood," not "of a dead man" but "as of a dead man," and the particle "as" presents not a reality but a likeness in general. Either way, one would not miss the mark. "Dead man" means one who has been slaughtered.

If anyone thinks the explanation should be taken literally, it makes no difference. These things will happen as a demonstration of [?], so that even those who are firm in faith [?], and the young and unsteady, may be struck with fear by the marvellous signs when they see creation set against the coming of the Antichrist. It is likely that these things signify wars and slaughters, I mean those of Gog and Magog, stirred up against one another in the four corners of the earth, kings against kings and nations against nations. From them the battles at sea and on land will be [?] with the gore of blood.
Every living soul.

"Soul" here means the soul that is made up of merely natural life. Because it remains unable to receive the things of the Spirit of God, it is laid open to punishment, as the divine Paul also holds. But for one who obeys God [?], the present death is not death but life, sending him on to a life without toil or misery.
How through the third bowl the rivers are turned into blood.

And the third poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood. And I heard the angel of the waters say, "You are just, you who are and who were, the Holy One, because you have judged these things. For they shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. They deserve it." And I heard another from the altar say, "Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are your judgments."

This passage also shows that angels have been set over the elements. One of them, the angel over the waters, praises God, he says, for the deserved condemnation of the transgressors, who defiled their hands with the blood of the saints, both before and especially at that time, in the days of the Antichrist. In return for this he summoned those who dared such things to a different thirst, a thirst for blood. For when the rivers and the gathered waters of the springs have been corrupted, where else could they quench their thirst?
And I heard the angel of the waters.

According to the lawgiver Moses, the divine powers are overseers of the nations. But they oversee the elements of the world as well, as this Revelation from God teaches us in the present passage. We learn that these overseers too come from the same intellectual and divine spirits. God is all-powerful and provides for his creatures without lacking anything. For him merely to will is to have the work accomplished, and the whole universe received its being at the impulse of his will. How then would such a one need a fellow worker, someone to stand beside him and help in his acts of kindness? But one who benefits another while lacking nothing himself benefits himself no less than the other. So God appointed ministers of his intellectual ordering of the world. They too lack nothing, since by their nearness to the divine they are richly endowed with freedom from need, and they provide goodness for earthly beings who are pressed by need. Daniel also teaches this when he presents Michael the archangel as overseer of the Jewish people. So too the Revelation now [?] the angel appointed over the waters. Earthly creation is composed of four elements: air, fire, earth and water. (Some have assigned the heavenly bodies to a fifth kind of body because they move in a circle, whereas air, fire and water have been allotted motion in a straight line.) Three of the elements, fire, earth and air, are abundant: air for breathing, fire for warmth, and earth for food, as a mother, and for burial. Even these, though they are elements, are not simple. This is clear from the fact that fire leaps out of air when it is compressed by the collision and pressure of harder materials. Fire can even be drawn from water held in glass vessels when they are set facing the sun, especially the rising sun. Still, these are very plentiful for use. Drinking water alone is not always to be had in springs and fountains and wells and rivers. The same is true of the water in the air, which is lifted up in the clouds and by divine command gives us timely rain to nourish every living thing. Because this supply is not plentiful, one of the divine angels has been appointed as a kind of steward, to give it to those in need in full and in proportion to their need. That is why, often in keeping with our wickedness, the water either overflows or is [?] withheld, and brings affliction through droughts and famines. From this angel, he says, the one over the waters, I heard what the following scripture will set out.
You are just, you who are and who were, the Holy One.

"Just" shows that he rewards according to desert. "Who are" shows that he has no end, "who were" that he has no beginning, and "holy" that he is [free] [?] of every mortal passion. That is why he judged these things, so that those who shed the blood of saints should drink blood. The saints are those ill-treated by the henchmen of the Antichrist. The prophets are Enoch and Elijah, since they will kill them too. How will they drink blood? In war, those encamped by rivers are forced to drink water that is often defiled with the blood of the slain.
And I heard another from the altar.

The one over the altar is in harmony with the angel over the waters. [?] This one may be understood as Christ himself, since it is in him and through him that the rational whole burnt offerings and living sacrifices, which we learned from the Apostle to offer, are offered to God the Father. It may also be understood of the angelic powers, since they carry up our prayers and spiritual whole offerings. "Altar" is said by synecdoche, naming what is contained by its container. From this rational and liturgical altar, then, he says, the voice came that declares just all the judgments of God, which go beyond all reason and understanding. For it is fitting that the intellectual powers should rejoice and celebrate at the requital of what each person has done in life, and at the saving return of those who have struggled back through repentance. They rejoice also over those who, through the present punishment, may expect to find God's love for humanity milder in the future, for the Lord will not punish twice for the same thing. So let us work out our salvation with zeal from now on.
True and just are your judgments.

"True," because they do not end in mere words, alarming or charming with empty promises, but bring about their effect in impartial deeds. They are "judgments" because they do not bring things to their outcome by mere arbitrary power. They are weighed exactly by reason, and so they hold blamelessness within them.
How through the fourth bowl people are scorched.

And the fourth poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. And people were scorched with great heat, and they blasphemed the name of God, who has authority over these plagues. And they did not repent and give him glory.

Whichever way one takes these things, as allegory or as actual events, one will not stray beyond what is reasonable. One may think that "sun" means the course of the day, in which hardships that choke the licentious will overtake them from time to time to turn them back, as it is said: "With bit and bridle bind tight the jaws of those who do not draw near to you." Or one may think of the sun scorching more fiercely with its blaze through drought, siege and the distress of the hardships of war. Either way it makes no difference, since he who scourges is the same and seeks their conversion, and from either interpretation one comes to lodge at one and the same inn of meaning. In any case, they did not look to any of these scourges for conversion, as such scourges deserved. Instead they squandered both the benefits and the punishments meant to convert them, for "when the ungodly man comes into the depth of evils, he scorns." So he added that they blasphemed God, adding lawlessness to lawlessness without turning back. We can see this now too. Senseless in the evils that have come upon us from barbarian invasions, we not only fail to turn from our wicked practices but even blame the goodness of God, as though it had dealt out such afflictions to us.
Who has authority over these plagues.

By "name" he means his reputation. How astonishing [?]! How could such a name be blasphemed? Through the false reasoning of the ungodly, who despised it. For they would not have persisted in their wicked practices if any fear of punishment, as requital for their licentious deeds, had entered them. Instead they would quickly have [turned from] their wicked [?] deeds and reshaped themselves by the saving commandments. For fear [?] of keeping the commandments. By "authority" he means the coming of the Lord, who makes his second coming for this purpose: to repay each according to his works. What works? Those whose instruction he himself gave at his first coming, both in person and through his holy apostles and disciples.
How through the fifth plague the kingdom of the beast is darkened.

And the fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in agony and blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores, and they did not repent of their deeds.

By "bowl" he means wrath. At banquets we are used to toasting one another with bowls and heightening the festivity with the wine stored in them. This bowl, when poured out, brings about the opposite, for what was poured on the kingdom of the beast was full of the wrath of God. By "throne" he means the kingdom, as in "Your throne, O God," meaning "your kingdom is eternal." The beast is the Antichrist. He says that its kingdom was darkened, and the pouring out of the bowl did this through the excess of pain. For it is natural for those in great affliction to seem to be living in darkness. That is why, like people out of their minds, they injure their own limbs with their teeth: their arms, their fingers, or even, as here, their tongues. Here it is their tongues, since [?] blasphemies. But the blasphemies are not to be blamed on the pouring out. The bowl was not poured out so that they would blaspheme, but so that, punished as their licentiousness deserved, they might turn back. They, on the contrary, raved still more madly, especially because they knew beyond doubt the [?] of the Antichrist whom they had made into a god. The words that follow this passage will show that such scourges are brought on them for their conversion, not for punishment. You could also take "kingdom" to mean those appointed over the kingdom of the Antichrist.
From this it is clear that painful things are inflicted to bring about repentance, not as punishment.
How through the sixth bowl the way across the Euphrates is opened for the kings from the rising of the sun.

And the sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, so that the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun. And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the mouth of the dragon, out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet. For they are spirits of demons, performing signs.

He says that the river Euphrates is diminished so that the kings of the earth may pass through to the war fitting for them. For "nation will rise against nation," says the Lord in the Gospels, "and kingdom against kingdom." These are likely to come from the Scythian regions of Gog and Magog, as this Revelation relates a little further on. But we should not rule out that the Antichrist also sets out from the eastern regions of Persia, where the tribe of Dan of Hebrew stock lives, together with other kings or magnates. The royal title is sometimes given to such men as well, as in "The kings of the earth stood by," although Pilate was certainly not a king [?]. He says that they cross the Euphrates to bring death, either of the soul or of the body. Death of the soul comes because God brings it about that such things happen through the working of demons and by his own permission. Or rather, God himself does this to test his own servants. He does not do it as one who is ignorant, but to make plain to others who does and who does not hold fast to him. Death of the body comes upon those who live from the earth and deserve to perish, so that they may not make the earth itself useless by their foul deeds. For the earth is the work of a good Maker and a place kept unharmed for those who are ready to strive to live like the one who made it.
And I saw out of the mouth of the dragon, and what follows: three unclean spirits.

We must supply the words "coming out," so that the sentence reads: "I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the three." This shows that the devil appears in his own person as a dragon, the Antichrist as a beast, and the false prophet as someone distinct from the Antichrist. The devil is called a dragon because the divine oracles say that he is "the beginning of the Lord's creation, made to be mocked by his angels." What does Scripture mean by this? It means that he is brought to the most complete shame. He gained nothing from his first-created existence. The Creator in his goodness had given him something to make him like his Maker, namely free will, but he misused it perversely and not as he ought. From this he is also named dragon, because he set out from the movements belonging to his own nature [?] and used them crookedly. In the same way he is called the devil, the slanderer, because he slandered God to Adam by using crooked movements. The Antichrist is called a beast, for although he takes on human nature, he does not come forth in a human way but in a bestial one. The false prophet is called exactly what he is, one who, in the poet's words, "knows how to tell lies like the truth." He says that from the mouth of each of these gush out the same number of unclean spirits, which are like frogs but are not frogs. The first reason is that their harsh croaking cannot be taken up into any hymn to God. Instead it produces disturbance and uproar. This is always the way of demons and sinners, who love to linger in a miry, sodden, and muddy life. Those dear to God, on the contrary, delight in what is hard and in the endurance of the soul, and they magnify God with hymns, songs, and confessions. The destroyers, and the demons channeled out of their mouths, are three in number so that by this number they may deceive [?], as if they were pleasing to the all-praised Holy Trinity.

They go out to the kings of the whole world, to gather them for the battle of that great day of God the Almighty. "Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his garments, so that he may not go about naked and people see his shame." And he gathered them at the place that is called in Hebrew Armageddon.

They go out to stir up the war that suits them. He says that the signs worked through the demons show their aim: to drive the kings into a frenzy for war against that great day. That day is none other than the second coming of the Lord. The prophet Joel also speaks of it: "before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes." And how could it not be great, when it brings into the light what each person has done? Yet the war is not against the day itself. What war could human beings wage against the order of the sun's course? They make war rather against those who, constantly shaken by the fear of this day, have become God's portion. From that time these have put on garments of salvation and a tunic of gladness. These garments are nothing other than the virtues fitting for God, which gladden the inner man with their visible radiance. This is why "a good report fattens the bones." It lets the transcendent powers of the life lived according to God flourish again, and it gladly refreshes what has been crushed by hard labor undertaken for God's sake. That we sometimes call life "soul" is unknown only to someone who does not know the saying, "All that a man has he will give for his soul." But that it does not take life [?] . . .
"Behold, I am coming like a thief."
He allowed himself to be called a thief because the coming of the one who comes to judge is hidden and unexpected.
Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his garments.

He has kept to the figure of the thief. That is why he says that the garments must be guarded and watched over, so that they may not be lost through vainglory. He calls the virtues garments. If we cast them off, we may be found naked or even filthy and be judged unworthy of the divine wedding. Or the paltry ugliness of human nature makes it impossible for us to approach the divine [?] . . ., or the filthiness of our paltry nature will drive us away from the paths to the bright robes worn by the angels and by those who have lived like angels.
And he gathered them at the place.

He says that the evil spirits will gather into a certain place those whom they deceive at that time. Here we should understand "place" to mean "time." Scripture uses the same figure when it says, "He who dwells in Jerusalem shall never be shaken." A person who has been lifted above all earthly things throughout the whole time of this passing life dwells, as it were, in another Jerusalem during that time. Just as Jerusalem is surrounded by mountains on every side, so he is surrounded by lofty, heaven-treading thoughts and sets his mind without ceasing on the things above, "where," as the Apostle says, "Christ is." At this time, then, those deceived by the spirits will be overtaken and will meet with a cutting-off. This is what the Hebrew word means when it is carried over into Greek. And what is this cutting-off? It is the separation of the divine gift. Throughout this present life that gift stays with every human being and cannot be lost, and it gives strength to our inclinations toward better things. But at the time of death we pass from here to the things that are truly real, eternal, and free from toil. In those in whom the divine gift is then found idle, unused for the purposes for which it was given, it is separated from the one who had been counted worthy to receive it. By his sluggishness in working he brought its removal on himself in advance. According to the severity of the Gospel, his portion is set, as for one condemned, with the hypocrites, that is, with those who are nothing of what they appear to be. For he too was such in appearance and not in truth. Therefore, deprived of his helper, he suffers the misery of an idle life in Hades. This is why David says, "In death there is no one who remembers you, and in Hades who will confess you?" He does not remember the one he gave no thought to even while he was alive. How then will this same man confess him? He has been counted worthy of no good, small or great, though such goods are what the gift is known to be generously rewarded with.

Confession differs from praise. Praise expresses thankful glorification of God, who brought us, and all creation both intelligible and sensible, from non-being into being. Confession, on the other hand, consists of words of thanksgiving for the troubles from which one has been rescued. Since in Hades, after this life is over, there is no longer any time for work, all activity of this kind is naturally idle there.
How hail and earthquake come upon humankind through the seventh bowl.

And the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air. And a loud voice came out of the temple of heaven, from the throne, saying, "It is done." And there were lightnings and thunders and voices and a great earthquake, such as had not happened since human beings came to be on the earth, so mighty an earthquake and so great. And the great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell.

This angel poured out his bowl into the air, because every pestilent corruption arises from the air, and it is in the air that lightnings flash and thunders resound. The voice came from the heavenly temple, of which the tabernacle that Moses was commanded to make on Mount Sinai was a copy. On that mountain too there were lightnings and thunders, and the sound of a trumpet rang out.

"Loud": because these things are not dealt out to just anyone, but to an entire nation and by commands that cannot be refused. This is what the loud voice means to show here too. It comes from the heavenly temple, that is, from those who are initiated into the more divine mysteries. No one rules over them but God alone, the source of all that comes to be, who is above all things beyond all being. This is what the throne is meant to show. And what does the voice say? "It is done." For by his command itself the consummation is magnified [?].
And there were lightnings and thunders and voices and an earthquake.

The lightnings and thunders come from heaven. The voices are those of people on earth, raised in dread at the terrifying events. The earthquake is the shaking of the earth, since this too is counted among the signs of the end. Or by earthquake he means the transformation and change of corruptible things into incorruption, which will come about at the second coming of Christ. Then comes the phrase "such as had not happened": for never yet has the corruptible world been changed in this way into what is incorruptible and everlasting. The prophet Haggai also mentions this earthquake when he says, "Yet once more I will shake not only the heaven but also the earth and the [?] and the dry land, and I will shake all the nations together." Therefore this Revelation also says that so great and mighty an earthquake had never happened on the earth. It did not happen at the flood, nor when the Law was given through Moses, nor at the coming of Christ. On those occasions there was only a change of customs. There was no alteration of substances and persons from the corruptible and temporary to the incorruptible and everlasting.
And the great city was split.

Some have taken this to be said of Jerusalem. Its boast of greatness rests less on its crowds of people and its magnificent buildings than on the sufferings of Christ, his stay there, and the divine works he performed in it. For this reason it is set apart from the other cities, which Scripture usually calls cities "of the nations"; for apart from Israel, it usually calls other peoples "nations." Its division into three parts is meant to signify the differences among its inhabitants: Christians, Jews, and Samaritans. Or the three parts are these: Christians firm in faith; those who put on the name of Christians as a pretense, out of fear of the pious emperors; and Jews, who will not tolerate the name taken from Christ at all but openly declare their own error of their own free will. The persecution that rained down on Christians in pagan times exposed what each of these was, both the true and the pretended. The time of the Antichrist's coming will expose them still more clearly, stirring up a great storm against Christians. It is also fitting to understand the great city as the present world, divided into three periods. The first runs from the coming of Christ through the time of pagan rule, the second covers the reign of Christian emperors, and the third the time of the Antichrist's coming. The cities of the nations that fall are either the various opinions about the pious faith, which are bound to fall because they disagree with one another, or else the cities themselves. For when the earth is transformed at the renewal, how could the cities on it remain standing, defiled as they are by sinners having lived in them?

And Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and the mountains were not found. And great hail, each stone about a talent in weight, comes down from heaven upon people; and people blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, for its plague is exceedingly great.

That this Babylon is different from the city just mentioned is clear from the fact that it is inserted into the account like a digression. Otherwise it would have been introduced as part of the same sequence and as the same Babylon; but as it is [?] . . . He used "was remembered" as though speaking of another city that had been forgotten. Remembrance is needed for what lies hidden under the tongue and turns over in speech [?]. Remembrance is not always for good, as in "He remembered his covenant forever," but also for evil, as in "Remember, O Lord, the sons [?] . . ."; and here remembrance is taken in this latter sense.

By Babylon he means old Rome itself, because in it many of the holy martyrs suffered terrible things during pagan times. He does not mean the whole world, even if that interpretation has some acceptance. On that view the world is called Babylon and great because it has gained its greatness from the vain distractions of life. But if Babylon signified the world, why would the islands be distinguished from the world, when they too are part of it? It remains, then, that we may reasonably suppose another Babylon. And which is this? None other than Constantine's city. In it righteousness once lodged, but now murderers live there. In rival competition the civil authorities hasten to equal the ecclesiastical in strength [?], or rather not merely to be equal, but each to see whether one of them can carry off the prize, to the greater kindling of the divine fury. For this reason even the nature that is free from passion was thought to be moved by passion, so that the cup of the wine of the fury of wrath was given to Babylon. What the islands are can be learned from the divine words: they are the churches from the nations, newly established, rising up out of the briny sea of unbelief and "receiving firmness," as Scripture says. And what is their flight? None other than the one that happened because lawlessness multiplied and love grew cold. This love bound the faithful together for God's sake and drew them away from the company of unbelievers, and so it let them float upon the sea of love [?]. Once love has failed, the islands must also cease to be islands, since they suffer the misfortune of being sunk beneath the briny sea of unbelief. Along with them the mountains in them also vanished. These were the people among them who had been raised high above earthly human thoughts. They vanished through the rivalry of their fellow inhabitants, who were wretchedly bound to the ground and had lost the lofty and heavenly mind.
And great hail comes down from heaven.

He says that the hail was dashed down from heaven as God-sent wrath. "About a talent in weight" means complete. The sins had reached their extreme, and the punishment that calls people to turn back is equal to them. But the more hard-hearted were shown to be worse even than Pha[raoh] [?]. For he, softened somewhat by the plagues, confessed his own weakness and impiety, but they blasphemed even while they were being scourged. Here too the tenses shift from the past to the present. He turned from "were not found" to "comes down" because he wanted to show that when the one happens, the other must necessarily follow. Even under this fearful affliction, meant to bring them to turn back, they will certainly blaspheme. This is what the use of the past tense indicates: it presents what will certainly happen as having already happened.
On one of the seven angels showing the evangelist the destruction of the harlot city, and on the seven heads and the ten horns.

Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication, and with the wine of whose fornication those who dwell on the earth have been made drunk.” And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness; and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns.

Since he needed understanding of the things [?] to him, he finds none other than one of those who minister at these dread spectacles, who says to him, “Come, I will show you.” Greek grammar, which gives us a precise account of the temporal words, classes “come” among the particles used to give an exhortation. Here it has been taken to serve as a summons. For, as we said before, such precision matters very little to those who make the salvation of the soul their whole concern, and so the account of the narrative now proceeds.

By “judgment” he means her conduct, her course of action and her management of affairs. And by the harlot we should not understand old Rome so strictly [?] as the present world. This world thrives on countless bloodshed and on more kings than Rome, since from the beginning they have chosen to behave like harlots. Here fornication is understood not only as the shameful union of bodies but also as every turning away from God. So it is said, “You have destroyed everyone who goes whoring away from you,” and, “They went whoring in their practices.” Who doubts that this world has proceeded from the beginning in this way?
