For this reason she is also called the great harlot, as one engaged in great outrages. And she sits on the waters; this too can be seen from the thing itself. So the saying of the psalm declares, “He founded it upon the seas, and prepared it upon the rivers,” where “prepared” is to be understood in place of “established.” The earth cannot remain on its own by its nature unless something beneath supports it and holds it up. Wishing to show this, the word says that the earth, where our dwelling in this corruptible life is, was founded upon the seas. Since the earth is a storehouse of the moist substance and receives all its sediment, it also has its being from it. This being so, the saying fittingly says that it is settled and founded upon it, because the foundation provides its being, and the earth receives this from the waters. [?] it is a sort of creation of the store, which in a manner receives its being from the sediment of the moist substance. We can hear that this is so from Moses as well, who in the account of creation introduces God as saying, “Let the water be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear.” It is as though the thicker part of the waters was filtered out and settled into one substance, and the dry land became a storehouse of the waters themselves, and that from their sediment [it has] its being [?]… This, then, is how the harlot sits on the waters according to the natural sense. But according to the contemplative and figurative sense, which is rather to be accepted here, the waters are to be understood as the fluid life, which has nothing stable but is continually tossed about by unclean ebbings and flowings, which fill the present life.

But some others who have examined the present Apocalypse have taken the harlot to be old Rome, or the empire as a whole, which lasts until the second coming of the Lord. They take the waters to be the nations that she rules and will rule, for her power is established upon them. Since she has lost her ancient power, this is hard to suppose. Still, nothing stands in the way of it, for many other cities have returned to their ancient dignity. Divine Scripture knows how to signify nations by waters. Hear the forefather of God, who takes “from the voices of many waters” to refer to a nation. He says that the Lord reigned, clothed with majesty, because he does not use the abundance of his authority like a tyrant but like a king, to do good. For this reason he says that he girded himself; that is, he restrained the unbearable force of his power as far as a mortal mind can bear it. From this it came about that the world was made firm, “for who is able to withstand the might of his wrath?” Such is the Lord's kingship. And what of the kingship of the “many,” the overweening? Of this he says, “The rivers lifted up their voices,” calling rivers those who held rule. In the same way Isaiah calls the Assyrian a river, when he says that the great river is brought up against Jerusalem. The voices are their arrogant boasts; the [?] poundings are the [?]… the plunderings that the arrogant incursion of the many waters, that is, of the nations, would bring.
With whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication.

The kings of the earth are those whose earthly minds have sent them rolling down into the refuse of the present life. These same men have also been made drunk, because they glutted themselves with impiety from great excess rather than from small and casual use. Partly she hastened this on, and partly they themselves were thrown headlong by the luxury of life.
And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness.

The vision concerns the desolation that will come upon spiritual things. He says he saw it as a woman, effeminate, a harlot without a husband, having no mark of chastity but desolate of every good. And what else would being carried away in the Spirit mean, except that he did not see these things in actual fact but was granted them in contemplation? Hence the image of another woman was also revealed to him, sitting on a scarlet beast. The woman represents the time in which these things are carried out. In that time she rests upon the devil, who is murderous and delights in blood (this is what the scarlet color means) and works through wicked deeds; the sitting is meant to suggest this. Working through these deeds, the apostate wins power in blasphemies against God. The names of blasphemy signify ascribing to the devil the reverence due to God. These are the people whom the devil wins over to himself through the sons of disobedience.

The woman was clothed in purple and scarlet and adorned with gold and precious stone and pearls. In her hand she held a golden cup full of abominations and of the impurities of the fornication of the earth. On her forehead a name was written: “Mystery, Babylon the great, the mother of the fornications and of the abominations of the earth.” And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled with great wonder. And the angel said to me, “Why did you marvel?”

She wears purple because everything is dared with authority, as under a queen. She wears scarlet because the blood of many saints is shed. She is adorned with gold and precious stone and pearls because the word adorns her as a queen, with royal adornment. Among the harsh and those who wield power, one can see in those who suffer abuse that faith in Christ blooms like unalloyed gold. Like a precious stone, it displays its firmness through its transparency to those who do not know it. Like pearls, it rises out of the sea of trials of this many-waved life and is fitted to the royal [?] of Christ. The cup is golden because the time is ruled as if by royal power. It is in her hand because of the effectiveness of what is set before people. It is a cup, as he says of Job, “drinking scorn like a drink.” Perhaps this is to show that they pursue wickedness not to the point of satiety but thirsting for their own destruction, as David says, “They ran in thirst.” And so her abominations multiplied, that is, practices abominable to God. The sin-loving multitude is given these to drink, draining as though it were a sweet drink the abominable drunkenness of sin and the defilement of fornication away from God.
And of the impurities of the earth.

The fornication of the earth means those who are attached to earthly things, for nature did not give the earth, a creation without soul or sense, the power to commit fornication. The name written on her forehead shows that she does shameful things shamelessly. Therefore, because of the confusion of affairs, she is displayed as a mystery and must be called Babylon by those of more contemplative mind. This may be the time in which these things are accomplished, or old Rome itself, as the divine Apostle Peter also thinks, for in it much blood of Christ's martyrs was shed. Or it may be the new Rome, since in the new Rome too much blood of the Orthodox was shed in the times of the Arians. He calls her the mother of harlots because she took over the power of the other cities. Take her to be whichever you wish, old Rome, the new, or the time of the Antichrist's coming, and you will not miss the truth. For in all of them the blood of martyrs flowed, as I have shown, and indeed also in the cities born of them. So the prophetic word fits them too: “As the mother, so the daughter.” As the mother's practices are, so are those of the ones born from her.

The woman may be whichever you wish, as was considered above: old Rome, or the new, or the empire taken carnally as one body. In each of these she was not only sated with the blood of the saints; she even came to [?] it out and gush it forth. This happened earlier, from Abel to John the Baptist, but more abundantly from the coming of Christ, which began with the slaughter of the infants. For this reason he spoke distinctly of “the blood of the saints” and “the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.” These produced her drunkenness by flowing [?], especially when Diocletian and those like him were committing murder.
And I marveled when I saw.

It was natural that a good and kind man, whose gentleness was beyond words, should be overcome with extreme astonishment when he saw the savagery of beastly men. This is what the “great wonder” indicates. The history of the blessed John the Theologian teaches that he was simple in character.
He was seized by such astonishment that he could not declare what had happened to him himself; it was the one who showed him these things who did so.
How the angel interpreted the mystery he had seen.

“I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to ascend from the abyss and go to destruction. And those who dwell on the earth, whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, will marvel when they see that the beast was, and is not, and will be present. Here is the mind that has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits, and they are seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain only a little while. And the beast that was and is not is himself an eighth, and he is of the seven, and he goes to destruction.”

He calls it a “mystery” because it reveals mystically these things, which are written for you as in an image through the Apocalypse. He sketches out beforehand, as on a tablet, the things that are to be said, and so gives clarity to the account.

The beast is the devil. He began to go through in full the things set out beforehand as on a tablet. Therefore, he says, the beast “was”; it does not exist now. From this it is clear that it is the devil, for, as it is said, he is the beginning of the Lord's creatures. He “is not” now because his operations were put to death by the coming of Christ. Before that coming he worked to make men prepare their sons and daughters for his demons through sacrifices, but after Christ's coming he can no longer work these things in the same way. Therefore it was prophesied, “The swords of the enemy have failed utterly,” calling his operations swords because they wound men fatally. And he ascends from the abyss. His attendant demons [?] begged not to be sent into it, since the devil who rules them [?] together with their company, but into the herd of swine. When this happened and the herd was hurled into the sea by them, it was plainly seen that they had been drowned and removed from life, [though not] entirely [?]; for a portion of them was left on the earth as a training ground for those who contend. But their ruler himself was left for judgment in darkness, as the great Apostle Peter says, [?] for the eternal fire. [He ascends] at the coming of the Antichrist. Those who have been made Christ's own are called inseparable from Christ, as the holy Paul says to the Philippians [?], calling the saints who are in Philippi saints because they are in Christ. In the same way, since the Antichrist comes by the operation of Satan, Satan is understood to be brought up together with him. For thereafter the Antichrist, [?] Satan by his operations and deceiving men, brings to ruin and destruction himself, the one who works through him, and their followers.
And he goes to destruction.

The destruction into which he is to go does not mean passing into non-being. It means the loss of the purpose for which he came into being, and he came into being to bring about the glory of his Maker. “For the Lord made man upright,” says Ecclesiastes, “but they sought out words of wickedness.” By destruction he means not non-existence but condemnation in Gehenna, as the Lord himself says: “Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.”
And those who dwell on the earth will marvel.

They will marvel at the beast's coming. They will marvel not only that he had perished and yet lives, but also that he has come with deceitful wonders. And who will “marvel”? Those who dwell on the earth. Isaiah also speaks of them: “We shall not fall, but those who dwell on the earth will fall.” Such are those whose foundation is unsteady, because they are not founded upon the rock, Christ. So these will marvel even now, those who because of their grovelling were not written in the book of the living. From the words “from the foundation of the world” we can understand that he is giving the reason for Moses' account in Genesis, for Moses traced the genealogy of those descended from Seth but not of those descended from Cain. They will marvel, then, as has already been said: those who because of their grovelling were not securely grounded in Christ's predictions about him, as they reckon [?] how he both recovered and resumed his ancient dominion. Because of this, since he has the Antichrist dwelling in him as the fullness of his impiety, he will in turn receive a fitting end. “Here is the mind”: since the things being interpreted are spiritual, there is need of spiritual wisdom to know how he was, and is not, and is about to ascend from the abyss. For it seems contradictory that what exists should pass into what does not exist and then be about to ascend again from the abyss, unless it is understood in the way that has been explained.
Let the one who has spiritual wisdom understand spiritually what is said. The seven heads are seven mountains.

We have already said that, in the sense concerning creation, the woman is understood as the earth, on which all the business of this world takes place. In that sense, then, the earth has its being from the waters and in the waters, and it holds the waters itself. But in the contemplative and figurative sense she is this corruptible world. It is carried on by fluid and unstable deeds, and from the beginning it was allotted to be constituted by the number seven. So now we [?] that the seven mountains on which she is said to sit are seven thousand years to be completed, lasting as long as this life does. The fifth millennium has already been completed, and the sixth has arrived, and in it the present Apocalypse makes these things clear. By mountains and heads we understand seven places that stood out above the rest in eminence and worldly dominion, on which, as we know, the kingship of the world rested at different times. First there was the rule of the Assyrians in Nineveh. Second came the dominion of the Medes in Ecbatana; under Arbaces it prevailed over the Assyrians, whose king Sardanapalus Arbaces overcame and deposed. After these the power of the Chaldeans held sway in Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar was their king. Then, after the overthrow of the Chaldeans and of the Medes, the Persian kingdom was established in Susa by Cyrus. After Alexander destroyed it, the rule of the Macedonians took its place. After these came the rule and might of the Romans in elder Rome. Under Augustus Caesar it became a monarchy, after its earlier kings and consuls, and it was held by impious rulers until Constantine. After their rule was ended, the kingdom of the Christ-loving emperors was transferred to new Rome. The seven kings are to be taken in the same sense. The change of gender, masculine and feminine, in no way hinders the meaning from being the same, even though in one place he spoke of the heads in the feminine and the seven mountains in the neuter, and here of seven kings. Scripture does not usually quibble over such things. Thus it sometimes presents Ephraim as a frenzied heifer and sometimes [?] as senseless; and it speaks of things that go prosperously: a he-goat, a cock, and a king addressing the nations. Why does he now speak of heads in the feminine? It signifies cities. By the mountains, in the neuter, he means eminences that rise above the rest of the earth, not in place but in time, through the height of their glory. Likewise the kings are either the places glorified by royal preeminence or those who first reigned in the cities just mentioned, each one being taken to stand for the whole kingdom; for example, Ninus for the [?]…

“And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom, but they receive authority as kings for one hour together with the beast. These have one mind, and they give their power and authority to the beast. These will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.” And he said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the harlot sits, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues.”

They say that the ten horns are ten kings who will arise from the Roman empire in the last times, and the Antichrist will arise in their midst. They receive not a kingdom but authority as kings, and for one hour. He says “as kings” because their kingship is unsettled and shadowy. In “one hour with the beast,” he means by “hour” to indicate a brief time, or else the span by which the season of the year is completed, during which they will be subject to the Antichrist as their superior. Or “hour” may be understood as the life of pleasure.
And the Lamb will conquer them, and so on.

It is fitting that, since he is Lord of lords and King of kings, his shield-bearers are also called. They hold their calling not by chance but in a way that is timely, exact and unchangeable. For this reason they are also faithful, because the faithful man is devoted to one master, being unable to serve two lords.
The waters that you saw.

We have spoken of these before: figuratively and naturally the earth comes from the waters and continues in the waters, and on it this corruptible world, carried on in fluid pleasures, is settled. And it is understood in no other way than this with regard to the races of men. These are nations distinguished by different speech, and beyond this they are preserved by the power of kings. This is what the horn is meant to show. The image is taken from horned animals, which also protect themselves with their horns whenever they must deal with other animals. In the same way, the ordinances of kings enable nations to hold their own against other nations and not be scattered under foreign lordship.

“And the ten horns that you saw on the beast, these will hate the harlot. They will make her desolate and naked, and they will eat her flesh and burn her up with fire. For God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose, to be of one mind, and to give their kingdom to the beast until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman whom you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

What the horns mean has already been explained, and the beast is the devil. He makes no distinction in what he signifies by the beast, sometimes giving that name to the Antichrist and sometimes to Satan. The kings, then, he says, who until now were murderously disposed toward the Lamb through Satan's working, will at God's prompting hate the harlot, that is, the life of pleasure in the world. They will make idolatry desolate as well and strip it of its temples and oracles. Her flesh, the animals offered in sacrifice to idols, they will store up for themselves. They will do away with all zeal for vain things, so thoroughly that it will be thought to have been consumed by fire, and all will cry out, “Where now are those who were then devoted to the care of vain things?” And all these things, as we said when we cited them, they say would not happen without God, but by divine oversight and providence.
And to be of one mind.

Their purpose may coincide with God's, but only as something under God's care, and it agrees with what is accomplished according to the unsearchable depth of his providence. So, by this unanimity given them by God, all authority is handed over to the beast, and the beast will go on ruling until the fitting judgments lead to their end. These judgments were indicated by the words in which he says, “until the words of God are fulfilled.”
And the woman whom you saw is the great city.

To present the woman more clearly, he takes up the account of her again and says that she is the one who holds power over those devoted to earthly things. For not all who dwell on the earth are already corrupted along with earthly things.
Concerning another angel who announces the fall of Babylon, a heavenly voice that commands flight from the city, and the loss of the delights she formerly possessed.

After these things I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was lit up by his glory. And he cried out with a mighty voice, saying, "[Fallen?] is Babylon the great, and she has become a dwelling place of demons and a prison of every unclean and hated spirit; for all the nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication. And the kings of the earth committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth grew rich from the power of her luxury." And I heard another voice from heaven saying, "Come out of her, my people, so that you may not share in her sins and may not receive of her plagues; for her sins have heaped up as high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities."
And the earth was lit up.

From this one may understand the brightness and illuminating power of the divine powers, which far surpasses the light of the stars, displayed openly once the dim things of this corruptible world have passed away. He says that the authority of this luminary is great and that he lights up the region of the earth by his glory. For when heavenly and incorruptible things are set beside earthly and corruptible ones, this shows how far their glory exceeds. The mighty voice confirms what is declared, showing that it is effective and cannot be set aside. And what is this? "Fallen is Babylon the great" — by Babylon meaning the passage through this corruptible life.
And a prison of every unclean and hated spirit.

He transposes the demons into birds because their attack on human beings cannot be seen coming, since the swoop of birds too usually comes without warning. And "hated" is not said without reason. For who in his right mind does not loathe keeping company with demons? It is for this reason that they were also called abominations.
Come out of her, my people.

The voice urges those whom the Lord knows as his own to come out. To come out means that the righteous should not perish together with the ungodly. For just as in the case of Lot God commanded him, "Save, save your own life," without delay, as far as the mountain, resting nowhere on the land, so it is here too.
And God has remembered her iniquities.

These things are set out in human terms. For in the case of God, whose nature is blessed and beyond the reach of passions, it is idle even to think of such things. For where there is memory, there is also forgetting; and forgetting means that what was done is present potentially but no longer actually. But nothing is present to God potentially; everything is present actually.

"Repay her as she herself has repaid you, and pay her back double according to her works; in the cup in which she mixed, mix her a double portion. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much torment and mourning give her. For in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and I shall never see mourning.' Therefore in one day her plagues will come, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord who judges her."

It is not indicated from whom the command or the saying comes. It might be from the righteous and the martyrs of that time — that is, those who contended for Christ at the coming of the Antichrist, and were handed over to such cruelty and savagery by the ministers of the Antichrist then living in the world that even they, although they had chosen to live in imitation of God, were nevertheless overcome by the excess of their sufferings and uttered these words. We have said that the woman signifies the time of the Antichrist, not some city. And the cup signifies the disposition of those living in that period, who, exulting in the dominion of Satan, used a boundless abundance of horrors against those who opposed them. As she has done, then, so let it be repaid to her.
Repay her double.

"Double" does not mean twice as much. Rather, since God is loving and good and punishes far more lightly than is deserved, he considers that he has repaid double even when he repays only a part — and not only double, but sevenfold. Unless perhaps one should take this as not being God's threat at all. For how could he who says, "The Lord will not avenge twice for the same thing," now say that he avenges double and sevenfold? If, then, we take "double" and "sevenfold" to signify not what is deserved but something milder, perhaps there is nothing absurd in it.
As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury.
Just as, he says, having been glorified and having lived wantonly in this present life, she took no thought for the divine will, so repay her. For she says, "I shall not be deprived of my reign."
In her heart.
By "heart" he means the obstinacy of those living out their lives at that time, whom he also figured in his allegory as a lewd woman.
Therefore in one day her plagues will come.

[?] he says, just as the Lord does where he says that the day comes like a thief, stealthily and unseen. Either, then, he indicates the unexpectedness and brevity of the time in which these things will happen, as some take it of old Rome; or he indicates the course of the very day in which these things will happen. For once the enemies have become masters of her, a single day is enough to bring every punishment upon the defeated, and many kinds of death; since the Lord is able, just as he grants delightful things to those who please him, so also to punish those who sin without turning back. Those who apply the interpretation to old Rome take it this way. But it is more fitting to apply these things to this world, as forerunners that will come — the days of the Antichrist, of its final consummation, in which the Lord alone, by his incomprehensible [?] power, will mightily proceed against both the demons who with royal authority have outraged the present age [?], and against the men who wantonly abuse it with royal excess, unrestrained luxury and overweening merriment.

"And the kings of the earth, who committed fornication and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning, standing far off for fear of her torment, saying, 'Woe, woe, the great city, Babylon, the mighty city! For in one hour your judgment has come.' And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because no one buys their cargo any more: no more cargo of gold and silver, and precious stone and pearl, and fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet; and all thyine wood, and every vessel of ivory, and every vessel of most precious wood, and of bronze and iron and marble; and cinnamon and incense and ointment and frankincense, and oil and wine and fine flour and wheat, and sheep and cattle, and of horses and carriages and bodies, and the souls of men. And the fruit your soul longed for has gone from you, and all the rich and splendid things have perished from you, and you will never find them again."

He keeps to the figurative language so that the offence may be shown more clearly through the uncleanness of fornication. We have said that these are the demons, and that they stand far off. For being intellects, they are able to know the outcome even before it is experienced, and to grasp the reality as one does fire from its smoke. But someone will say: if those who goaded men into shameful deeds also become partners in the punishments for them, how are they presented as free of these and composing a lament? We will say that there is nothing impossible in some who share in the torments, since they foresee where the things they have helped bring about are leading, lamenting in advance for those who do not know. "Woe" is an exclamation of lament, customarily uttered over calamities as they happen. That is why it is now applied above all to the universal and sudden catastrophe. He calls her a mighty city because she has held her existence for an almost limitless time in an unbreakable bond that no one ever expected to be dissolved.
Your judgment has come.
By "judgment" he means condemnation, the requital, equal in weight to what has been done and worthy of what has been dared.
And the merchants of the earth will weep.

From this point the prophecies must be understood, without exception, as concerning not Babylon, not old Rome, not the new Rome, not any other single city, but this whole corruptible world, in which those who trade in temporal things will be seized by weeping and mourning, because no one will buy their cargo. By "cargo" he means the pursuits in which people are accustomed to spend themselves. For when this composite of the senses has been dissolved, the labour among the righteous and the unrighteous turned out to be [?] toward better or worse — better for the best, worse for the worst. He says that mourning arises from both sorts of merchants: for the best, because the training no longer [?] toward a greater return and reward for good work; for the worst, because the recompense deserved by their wicked deeds has suddenly come upon them.
No more cargo of gold, and so on.

He refers "cargo" to the pursuits; when this temporal life has flowed away — the life in which the trade in pursuits yields its practical result — it is not unlikely that mourning should come upon them. To gold and silver are likened those pursuits which are examined by the everlasting fire, to see whether they are kept unconsumed; to precious stones, those whose brilliance has the misfortune to be [?] because they are not free of showy uselessness; to pearls, those whose brilliance passes into non-existence together with their being. Purple and fine linen and the threads of the Seres dyed with scarlet and murex hint at those pursuits which know how to procure blessedness through the cheapness [?] of possession. To thyine wood and ivory are referred those that are hard to come by, but bring renown to those who possess them.

It should be noted that here too the syntax of the passage runs incorrectly by the standard of Greek usage. For having said "cargo of gold and silver and precious stone and pearl and fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet," where he ought to have gone on with a genitive in the same case, he did not do so but went back to the nominative. He did not care for Greek elegance, being occupied with making clear what is profitable and not troubled about a pleasing sound; for the one is necessary, the other superfluous. He likens those who live in the world to the precious materials in the world. To silver and gold he likens those who bear the trials of life with lasting endurance and are accustomed to spend themselves in the fire, yet, contending in hope of better things, remain unharmed; for such do gold and silver prove to be in material fire. To precious stone and pearls, those who make a show of their acquisition of virtue, whose brilliance has been dulled by the onset of hardships. To fine linen and purple and the threads of the Seres, those adorned in Christ with the bloom of praiseworthy deeds. To wooden vessels, and those made of the most precious thyine wood, and to ivory and cinnamon, those who have practised a life of withdrawn asceticism, unseen by the many, but who, when the sweetest fragrance of their achievements was revealed, have attained a spiritual joy beyond telling, and who cannot be caught even by the fire of envy, just as cinnamon is not caught by material fire. To bronze and iron and marble, those who look like gold but have counterfeit wealth, as iron has its sheen and marble its hardness; and fire is the test of all these. So much for the things that are tested by fire. To oil and wine and fine flour and wheat, those who swim across the sea of life in cheerfulness and a joyful state of soul, taking no part in the meddling of the malicious, whether they meet with a more costly diet or a plainer one. To sheep and cattle may be compared those who are saved by God's boundless mercy, as David says. By horses and the vehicles drawn by them — which the ancient language calls angaroi, the Greek language public post-stations, and the Roman language rhedae, from which the word rhedarius has become common, and so here too "of rhedae" has been used — he means to signify those who, having run the way of your commandments, sing of them in their deeds.
And every vessel of wood.

It was not by lapsing into solecism that he passed from the genitive case to the nominative. Rather, since vessels come to exist from something, having first spoken of the vessels, which have their being from certain materials, he then adds the very materials from which the vessels have their existence — that is, their natural [?], whether it is furnished with what is eagerly sought, or on the contrary is slighted, or is altogether loathed: such as gold, silver, bronze, iron. For gold and silver are eagerly sought by men, and likewise cinnamon and incense and frankincense and oil and wine and fine flour and wheat; bronze and iron and marble are less coveted than these; and few take care to acquire sheep and cattle.

To bronze and iron and marble are compared the pursuits that are easily obtained, which, measured by the ability of those who labour at them, have been allotted a splendid existence. Likewise also those which, by their sweet fragrances, assign what is fitting to those being saved and to those perishing, as the divine Paul also holds. Besides these, the pursuits likened to oil for cheerfulness, to wine for gladness, and to fine flour and wheat provide a life, more costly or more common, according to virtue, and serve those who pursue salvation in the manner of sheep and cattle, concerning whom it is said, "Men and beasts you will save, O Lord." Horses, and the rhedae drawn by the horses: "rhedon" signifies vehicles in a Roman word, for in their tongue they call the vehicle rhaedium [?], whose genitive plural has become rhaidōn by contraction. With horses and rhedae, then, he refers to those who by the breadth of God's commandments — as it were by their spaciousness and smoothness — [?] the things impressed on the human heart by God's influence; it is by these horses that the way of God's commandments is travelled to the end. By adding "bodies and souls of men," he makes it plain that these things too are not to be confined to one city, but concern the whole creation in its future transformation from corruption to incorruption.
"Of horses" stands for "of vehicles": horses fit for vehicles, and of bodies and souls; that is, [?] made for riders.
And the fruit your soul longed for.

Common usage also calls the season "fruit-time." Since, then, human things pass without fail from corruption to incorruption, everything that tends toward corruption will also fail and vanish entirely. This cannot happen in the case of a city still seen in the present age. For in terms of more or less, no one would deny that it could happen; but in terms of entirely, no. So the absurd proposal of anyone who would have this apply to a single city is more than refuted, while the one who looks to the whole creation carries the day.
And the souls of men.

Enslaving, he says, the free; for men are enslaved from birth by deliberate sin. For of what sins are those guilty who have not yet had a share in this toilsome life? Therefore they have not shared in its rich things either, that is, in its enjoyable and pleasurable things. [?] how will one who does not yet exist come to make use of the things that exist? Since, then, the corruptibility of the present world has been transformed into incorruption, what reason is there any longer for any remnants of corruption to be seen in incorruption?

"The merchants of these things, who grew rich from her, will stand far off for fear of her torment, weeping and mourning and saying, 'Woe, woe, the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold and precious stone and pearls! For in one hour such great wealth has been laid waste.' And every pilot, and everyone who sails on the ships, and sailors and all who work the sea, stood far off and [wept?], as they saw the smoke of her burning, saying, 'What city is like the great city?' And they threw dust on their heads and cried out, weeping and mourning and saying, 'Woe, woe, the great city, in which all who had ships at sea grew rich from her costliness! For in one hour she has been laid waste.'"

By the merchants we must understand either divine powers or demons, who are fellow workers with the heavens [?], toward whatever each of them desires. Both, he says, stand far off from these because of fear. The angels do so because of the severity of the judge, which the disobedience of sinners has brought about beforehand. We have seen in [?] that when the master of the house is angry with the wicked among his servants, even the decent and well-pleasing ones are seized with alarm. As for the angels and demons standing far off: [?] since they are not of human nature, they did not go so far as to join with men, but by an addition of their own will provided [?] a starting point for each toward what they desire. Fear will be produced in the demons by their share in the punishment of sinners, which the sentence of the judge justly [makes them] undergo, also because of [?] their oversight of sinners.
Woe, woe, the great city, clothed in fine linen.

He conveys his meaning from what is familiar about things still to come [?]. Since, then, the well-known Babylon, which grew insolent through great wealth, brings its sufferings before our eyes, he sketches the greatness of the calamity through the royal throne that was in it. And he portrays the mourning not only through the wealth and its loss but also through the swiftness of the destruction, since she lost the wealth of ages in the brief space of a day. For the second coming of the Lord will arrive with the speed of lightning, abolishing this toilsome life.
And every pilot, and everyone who sails on the ships.

The present life is figuratively compared to the sea, since it too is tossed by many affairs, especially under the winds of demonic malice. And fittingly we have taken the ships in it to be the onsets of the events that befall us, which men use like ships to sail across the sea of their own life. The pilots must be reckoned to be those who conduct their lives safely. The sailors and seafarers and workers of the sea, whom a certain wise man would call "sea-folk," are the men who have toiled over the affairs of this world of many waves. All of these, reflecting on the unfailing and certain end of this life, kept guard over themselves even before it arrived; for this is what "standing far off" gives us to understand. And it also shows that upon the wicked pursuits of those who are at sea — from the just Creator, "who made us for good works, while we have sought out wicked reasonings," as Solomon the Preacher says — upon these, then, punishment will inexorably follow, as fire follows smoke. This is why he likened the expectation to smoke, as the Saviour himself shows when he says, "As the lightning comes out of the east and shines as far as the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be." To fire is likened the exact examination of what has been done. And fittingly these will cry out in dismay and undergo all that befits those in mourning, pouring dust on their heads and performing whatever else befits mourners.
What city is like the great city?

No other such city can be found, because there is no other creator and no other world. But another Babylon can be found, in Egypt, and a city like her in Egypt itself at the Heracleotic mouth of the Nile, namely Alexandria; and in Europe, toward the west and north, Rome; and farther east, the city at Byzantium that bears the name of Constantine.
In which all grew rich.

From this it is beyond doubt that the passage is to be taken not about a single city but about this whole corruptible order. For neither Babylon nor Rome nor any other city grows rich from the voyaging of ships alone; only this world does. For allegorically it is enriched with the true wealth of [?] men, who, as though in ships, untouched by the salt flood, swim across the turmoil of the world, and who have made this city spoken of, the world, lack nothing in the trade in precious things. Therefore, since it was a place and ground of salvation, from which they found the rewards for their labours, they raised a lament when they saw it consigned to destruction.

"Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her." And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So with violence will Babylon the great city be thrown down, and will never be found again. And the sound of harpers and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will never be heard in you again; and no craftsman of any craft will ever be found in you again; and the sound of the millstone will never be found in you again; and the light of a lamp will never shine in you again; and the voice of bridegroom and bride will never be heard in you again. For your merchants were the great men of the earth, for all the nations were deceived by your sorcery. And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on the earth."

From this too we are assured that the oracle concerns the world, not a single city. The turn from lamentation to rejoicing is not the part of those in the world but of the heavenly ones, since the place of contest has now been done away with. Those who in figure have put on the victor's crown, whether among the prophets, the apostles, the saints, the hierarchs, or any other company of those who have pleased God, may from now on share in unending joy, having been counted worthy of a life free of toil and business by him who knows how to judge according to merit, that is, to award the prizes for their labors. And if something still more paradoxical must be said, not even to those who fall short of the divine prizes through their offenses is the end of the present world unwelcome, since the place is dissolved in which they, senseless, had the misfortune of adding iniquity to iniquity, and through which they also failed to attain the righteousness of God.
For God has judged your judgment.
That is, he has determined precisely the recompense due to each according to merit for their saving labors.
And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone.

He depicts the end of the corruptible world under various figures. So, in addition to those already given, he adds this one as well, likening the world to a millstone sinking violently into the water. He says that such a thing sinks all at once, so that no trace of it can be seen any longer, and that in the same way the world too will pass into complete oblivion. And to make this plainer still, he adds the things that have dwelt in it from of old, which are causes of luxury and stir up a crowd of profligacy.
For your merchants.

He calls merchants those who make up this pitiable fair on earth, and that is why he also calls them great men. For luxurious living does not belong to the poor, nor is it for the powerless to bewitch all the nations with various sorceries as with drugs, either enslaving them by dominion or destroying them by tyrannical violence. Through this the blood of those consecrated to God has been poured out like a torrent: the blood of the prophets by the Jews, and that of the holy martyrs by the Greeks, from Abel to the end of the world.
On the hymn-singing of the saints, and the threefold Alleluia that they sang at the overthrow of Babylon.

After these things I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, saying, "Alleluia! Salvation and honor and power and glory belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great harlot who corrupted the great earth, who corrupted the earth with her fornication, and he has avenged the blood of his servants at her hand." And a second time they said, "Alleluia! And her smoke goes up for ever and ever." And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who sits on the throne, saying, "Amen. Alleluia!"
I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude.

The ranks of the holy angels are beyond telling. That is why one of the Fathers said that the ninety-nine sheep that are kept safe are the angels, and the one is humankind. Daniel too presents thousands of thousands and myriads of those who minister to God. It says "what seemed to be a voice," not "a voice": it was not literally a voice, but something like a voice. For what voice could come from beings who are not shown to have organs of speech? So he rightly said "what seemed to be a voice," using a particle of comparison.

"Alleluia" means "Sing hymns, praise God." He is worthy of a hymn as the one who brought into being what did not exist, and of praise as the one who restored, for their salvation, what had been [?broken]. So they sing a song of thanksgiving for God's just judgment, because he proceeded against the great harlot without partiality. And by her he means those who are in this world. To take "the world" as only the visible creation, I mean the sun and the stars and what comes after them, is to miss the mark; for Scripture knows how to use the name "world" in a distinct sense as well, as when it says, "The earth is the Lord's, and its fullness." Since, then, its fullness is also reckoned as the world, and especially this in its transgression, and the inanimate [creation] does not [?] when scourged [?], so the praise is offered for [?justice]; which was established upon [?], not upon the insensible [creation], for neither the sun nor the stars nor the air nor the earth would [?assent], but upon its fullness. And that this is wholly reliable for confirming that through the harlot, that is, the assembly [of the wicked], [?] became for the earth [the cause] of corruption and non-existence, in avenging [?] the blood [?] at her hand; finally he introduced [?] to call the one who dwells in it a harlot, but [not?] the sensible and inanimate world.
For he has judged the great harlot.
If the passage is about a single city, how could one city have been enough to [?corrupt] the whole earth?
And a second time they said, Alleluia.

After the first comes a second Alleluia, and after this a third as well. And further on you will observe that by this threefold acclamation of the Alleluia they hymn the Trinity in three hypostases. Who the elders and the four living creatures are has already been considered. "The smoke went up": this is the stored-up expectation of punishment, hanging from eternity over those who will receive the recompense their own evil deeds deserve.

The Alleluia in the middle has broken the train of the passage, since the sequence of the sentence is this: "and he has avenged the blood of his servants at her hand, and her smoke goes up for ever and ever." What the smoke is has also been explained: that it is the inescapable [?] of the unending fire, from eternity and to eternity. In parallel with it, the doxology of the Alleluia is likewise unending, sealed with the "Amen," which, translated into the Greek language, means "truly," or "to have arrived at the end," that is, to have already laid hold of [the goal] of becoming. For what else will there be, once corruption has been changed into incorruption?
And the elders fell down.
The elders are a symbol of the intellectual and divine powers; the four living creatures, of those who received bodily existence from the four elements and have been transferred to the angelic state.

For the seraphim [are the throne], as Isaiah says that the Lord, high and lifted up, is seated [upon them]. But if someone does not wish the praise to come from the throne itself, on the grounds that the seraphim surround the throne, the praise is nonetheless from the seraphim, since the same Isaiah made this clear as well, saying that the seraphim were [around] the throne and stating that they cry out the Thrice-Holy to one another. The praise is assigned by the seraphim to the servants and to those who fear him. Not that the seraphim are not servants, since they received their being by command, as David says, "For he spoke, and they came into being," and "For all things are your servants"; but the seraphim, who make up the immaterial creation, command this material creation, whose members have attained to servitude through progress. Therefore the one who leads off has founded [the praise] on fear, and "small and great" receive their portion according to the measure of their God-fearing diligence.

And a voice came out from the throne, saying, "Praise our God, all you his servants, and you who fear him, small and great." And I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the sound of many waters and like the sound of mighty thunders, saying, "Alleluia! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns."

The seraphim are the throne of God. If, then, the voice comes from this, it also comes from the seraphim. Or if someone does not wish to understand the throne as the seraphim, even so the praise comes from the seraphim. After the threefold Alleluia there is yet another Alleluia. In the prophet Isaiah the seraphim, after saying "Holy" three times, concluded with a single lordship, signifying the threefold confession: three in properties, that is, in hypostases or persons, but one in essence. So here too the heavenly powers, having uttered the Alleluia three times and offered reverence to each of the three hypostases, now sing a single Alleluia to the Holy Trinity, showing that the holy and all-praised Trinity exists in a single essence and Godhead.
And like the sound of many waters.
He likens this voice to the crashing of a great mass of waters and to the mighty roar of thunders, indicating how piercing is the hymn of the heavenly and innumerable powers.
Our God the Almighty.

"Almighty": surely he held the might even before the ages, since he is the maker of all things. What, then, does the present hymn mean? It presents his might over all things as something new, showing how unsurpassed was the voluntary appropriation of our condition by the one who overflows with goodness: he made all that is ours his own. Hence, as the divine Paul says, he did not disdain to make his own the words "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree," when he was hung on the tree of the cross. In the same way, making his own the insubordination of the nations, for as long as this much-divided world holds together he seems to bear insubordination toward the Father. But when the discord of the present turmoil has been brought to an end and the divine will shines forth [?for salvation], at the second coming of the Lord that is in store, then, since the whole of human nature will have received the active indwelling of the divine will, even what seemed insubordinate in the Son on my account would be reckoned as submission to the Father. That is why joy and gladness would arise among the powers above the world; and if they rejoice over the salvation of one sinner, how much more over a justice dispensed to the whole world? And to represent God's union with those who are saved, he compares it to a marriage, as it is also said, "And the two shall become one flesh." He assigns the marriage to the Lamb, inasmuch as he himself was led to death for us like a lamb. That is why he commanded the sons of Israel, as they came out of Egypt toward the crossing into the promised land, to sacrifice a lamb on the day of the Passover as a reminder, sketching in advance how he too, slain at the Passover that was its type, would bring about our passage from corruption to incorruption.
On the mystical marriage, and the supper of the Lamb.

"Let us rejoice and be glad and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready; and it was granted to her to be clothed in fine linen, bright and pure"; for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints. And he said to me, "Write: Blessed are those who are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb." And he said to me, "These are the true words of God." And I fell down at his feet to worship him; and he said to me, "See that you do not! I am a fellow servant with you and with your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God." For the testimony of the Son is the spirit of prophecy.
And let us give him the glory.

All things were subject to him, both in heaven and on earth, even before the incarnation that brought salvation to all, since he is the Son and co-creator with the Father and the Spirit, and after the incarnation he likewise reigns over all; for his rule over all was in no way diminished by the incarnation. But since, according to the divine Apostle, the Lord made all things his own, so that by paying off the debt of all he might award us freedom from liability, when the penalty for disobedience will also be rendered void (and what is this if not death? That is why Paul says that the last enemy to be abolished is death), the powers fittingly sing "Our God reigns." For then, when death has been abolished and corruption has departed from the world, the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is also God, inherits the kingship over all, a kingship beyond dispute: some are sent into punishment, others before his face with honor and glory, no longer through a mirror and in a riddle, but in reality and in truth.

In the present age the spiritual marriage of the Lord consists in his betrothal to the Church, and so [?] the perfect marriage. The divine apostle hints at this when he writes to the Corinthians, "For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." So in the present it is still a matter of betrothal, and the token of the betrothal [?] of having been joined [?] of the Spirit, which Spirit [?] when with Christ [?] the Church. Just as [a husband] becomes one body with his wife, so Christ too becomes one Spirit with the Church, and this is the perfect marriage, "when he is all in all." Hence the same holy Apostle also says that the mystery of marriage is [?great] and refers to Christ and the Church. That is why the angels too, singing their hymn, say, "The marriage of the Lamb has come." For the present betrothal, the apostle's joining [of the Church to Christ], [?prefigures] this, just as the marriage in the Gospel is in one place [?a wedding] given for a king's son, and in another the lamp-bearing of virgins hastening to the bridal chamber, that is, to the restoration stored up for the worthy.
And his wife.

He calls the Church a wife by way of allegory. That is why a son's marriage is also introduced, and lamp-bearing virgins: some of them, having had enough oil, were counted worthy to enter the bridal chamber, while others, left short of it, were condemned to stay outside the door; just as, of course, the man who was not clothed in a wedding garment was declared expelled from the wedding table; and so too with those who showed themselves unworthy, being distracted by the busyness of worldly cares. In their place, those from the hedges and crossroads were seen as table-companions of the host, lacking nothing [?] by standing beside the hedges, as if walled off from the many [?] into an inaccessible mystery [?], like those who stood idle from morning because no one had hired them; for each of them, when called, did not [?refuse]; and the same is true of those by the roadside. He says it was granted to the wife, that is, to the Church, to put on fine linen, that is, what is bright. For such is byssus: the bark of an Indian tree worked into linen. Since, then, brightness is indicated by the fine linen, as the present Revelation itself shows by saying "bright and pure," what else could be meant but the virtues, by which brightness and fineness are woven into the thoughts of the divine ordinances? The feast and gladness of those who are saved are compared to a supper, to the all-harmonious heavenly kingdom, to paradise, to Abraham's bosom, to a bridal chamber, and to a marriage. For since the good things of the age to come are many, our share in them is set forth under many names: a supper, because of the surpassing abundance of the feasting; the kingdom of heaven, because of its glory and honor; paradise, because nothing good is lacking there; Abraham's bosom, because of the rest there for those who have toiled; a bridal chamber and a marriage, not only because of the unceasing gladness, but also because God's love for human beings is sincere and genuine.

The righteous deeds of the saints are likened to fine linen because of their fineness and brightness: bright, because their life and conduct are beyond reproach; fine, because in their thoughts God's doctrines are subtle and exact.
Blessed are those who are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb.

That is, those who, after being called, go as they ought. For we know of many in the Gospel who were called but declined the spiritual banquet, as we set out a little earlier, or who went but were thrown out for not having a wedding garment. And the divine Apostle too has said that many are called but few are chosen. For eagerness to answer the call is not enough unless the carrying out also runs well along with the intention. That is why he says that the words of the calling have their truth from earnest practice: "These words are true."
Do not worship me.

So says the angel, as one who foretells things to come: "For this mark of prophecy is not mine, but belongs to the confession of my fellow servants for Christ's sake; for this is what supplies the prophetic spirit." It may also be understood another way: prophecy exists for this purpose, that the testimony of Christ may be confirmed and the faith of Christ be attested by the saints. "So do not worship your fellow servant, but the one who holds power over all." From this we also learn the humble mind of the holy angels: they do not appropriate the divine glory as the [?apostate] demons do, but offer even this to the Master. And it is not only from this that one can see the moderation of the angels' mind, but also from what the apostle Jude relates in his Epistle about the archangel Michael speaking with restraint over the body of Moses. The accursed and God-hated Greeks hear that it is a doctrine among us [?] that holy angels have been appointed by God as overseers for each human being and each nation. Again, Daniel introduces [?] a prince of the kingdom of the Persians standing against him, and [the angel] returning to fight with the prince of the Persians and [?] of the Greeks; and again, "There is no one who holds with me in these things except Michael your prince"; and "At that time Michael, the great prince who stands over the sons of your people, will arise." Moreover there are [?] of churches with angels presiding over them, as we have already learned through the present Revelation. The divine Gregory understood this passage when he said in his Farewell Oration, "Farewell, angels of this church; for I am persuaded that one angel presides over one church and another over another, as the Revelation of John teaches me." And there is also an angel [?guarding] each individual person; hence the words "The angel of the Lord will encamp [around those who fear him] and deliver them," and indeed Paul's "Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?" Sharpened by all these, the Greeks lay down their doctrine to us, saying: "It is in vain that you quarrel so combatively with us, who introduce gods ruling over nations. For those whom you call angels we name gods, and we do not even differ about the name, since you too call them gods, as when you present God standing in the assembly of the gods and judging among them; and you even call judges gods, as when you say, 'You shall not revile the gods.'" To them we must reply: "You accursed people, those whom we call gods we say have attained divinity through a whole string of virtues, not those notorious for shameful deeds, like Heracles for his fornication with the daughters of Thestius and for his gluttony, which earned him the name Bouthoinas, 'Ox-Feaster'; or Dionysus for his womanish dissoluteness, suffering women's things at the hands of Corybus [?]. And as for your presiding over nations, it is not a leading toward the divine, such as Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jacob had when they were initiated by divine angels, but the sort by which the nations' murderous deeds come from Ares and their most lustful ones from Aphrodite, as with the Saracens." So the things of the Greeks are in no way like those of the Christians.
For the testimony of the Son is the spirit of prophecy.
The prophetic gift is a recompense for bearing witness on Christ's behalf. So the angel says that to him too the gift of prophesying was granted on account of his fellow servants, the martyrs.
How the evangelist saw Christ on horseback with the angelic powers, and was filled with fear.

And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse, and the one seated on it is faithful and true, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written which no one knows but himself. And he is clothed in a garment dipped in blood, and his name is called the Word of God. And the armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses, clothed in fine linen, white and pure.

That heaven has been opened shows that the coming of the awaited Judge is at hand, just as here too, in the law courts, the drawing back of the curtains shows that the judgment and sentence of the accused have been prepared. He sees him mounted on a white horse, equipped like a general, and calls him faithful and true, and says that he judges in righteousness and makes war. He rides a horse because of the swiftness of his coming, and a white one because his judgments are bright and unshadowed, enslaved to no partiality. As he also cries out through the prophet, "My judgment will go forth as light." The rider is faithful and true, and Paul also says of him, "He remains faithful; he cannot deny himself." So the same one is also called "true" with respect to the same thing, two titles being [?] applied to one subject. And the one mounted on these is he who judges justly, of whom it is also said, "Give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son". He is [?] Christ, the son of Solomon, to whom the psalm also refers. And he judges justly, because this too is set down in the psalm, which says, "He will judge your people in righteousness, and he will save the poor." The "people" are the crowd in which good and bad have been swept together indiscriminately, so that it is just to sort them out. "The poor" in judgment are, as it were, those who are few. "Good" in judgment, as opposed to in condemnation.
And in righteousness he will judge.

For the judgment will [not?] proceed unjustly, still less by tyrannical force. Rather, he judges with deliberation, and makes war against enemies both intelligible and sensible [?] on behalf of his servants. This is clear from the one who says, "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your beauty and your loveliness; and bend your bow, and prosper, and reign for the sake of truth." Then he adds, "Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one; peoples will fall beneath you." Thus, then, he judges and makes war in righteousness.
His eyes.

This is not because God, who fills heaven and is bounded by no place, is confined to such a form. Indeed, he also appears to the divine prophets in different forms. It is because he must stoop to the weakness of human understanding. From this it is also clear that God is not marked out by bodily features but makes himself like the times and the circumstances. So now, since the time of judgment has come, and each must be repaid as he deserves for the life he has lived, we see his eyes likened to a flame of fire, which both illumines and burns: it illumines angels and the righteous, and burns demons and sinners. David says this too, where he says that the voice of the Lord, that is, his command, divides the flame of fire. He means that the workings of fire are made subject to the [?].
And on his head many diadems.

The many diadems are a sign of his authority over things in heaven, on earth and under the earth. In heaven he rules the angelic orders [?], whose countless multitude Daniel presents by speaking of "thousands of thousands" and "myriads", the highest of numbers, when he too sets up the tribunal of the universal and final judgment, and the books are opened, which signify the unforgetting scrutiny of what each has lived. On earth he rules the companies of the saints and the scepters of kings. Under the earth he rules because he is Lord of the dead as of the living, and carries off the prizes of victory over all.
Which no one knows but himself.

That the name is unknown signifies that his essence is incomprehensible. He has many names from his dispensations: good, shepherd, sun, light, life, sanctification, redemption. Likewise he has many names by negation: incorruptible, invisible, unchangeable. But his essence is nameless, known to him alone. It was not made known to Abraham, nor to Isaac, nor to Jacob, nor to Moses, nor to Joshua son of Nun, nor to Manoah. That is why he also says, "My name I did not make known to them," since it is too great to be [?] by human hearing. That is also why, when he commanded his apostles to baptize the nations, he told them to baptize into names of relation, not names of nature. For "Son" and "Father" are names of relation; they do not signify nature, and signify nothing else.
A garment dipped in blood.

The garment of the Word is the undefiled flesh, which was dipped in his precious blood. For even in the vision he bore the tokens of the passion, as he also does in Isaiah's dramatic scene. That is why the one who questions him asks, "Why are your garments red?" But someone might reasonably be puzzled how he who a little earlier was declared nameless, and whose name was unknown to all, is here named the Word. This should be taken either as showing the hypostasis of the Son and his begetting from the Father [without passion?], just as our word proceeds from the mind; or because he holds within himself the principles of all things; or because he is the herald of the Father's wisdom, power and authority.
And the armies in heaven followed him.

He is Commander-in-chief of the heavenly powers, as he himself declared to Joshua son of Nun. So it is fitting that the orders of heaven follow him as the troops that make up his army, and now above all they set out to war against the ungodly. These things are framed in human terms in the Revelation, because there was no other way to make them known: they are divine, and it is impossible to show them to human beings in their own nature, for knowledge comes to us through things like ourselves. They are presented as horsemen mounted on white horses. The horses hint at the swiftness of their onset, and the whiteness of the horses at the splendor that adorns the heavenly orders, in whom a spotless purity blooms, free of the blackness of the rabble on earth [?]. And indeed the riders themselves are shown wearing white robes of fine linen. For among material and earthly things, what could be thought more fitting for the heavenly and divine company? We have already said that these things are now framed in human terms. I mean the war of the [?] and the heavenly orders, mustered for war under the Lord and God Jesus Christ as Commander-in-chief. But it is not a war waged against equals in strength and in battle, for who could appear a match for him to whom all things are slaves? Nothing created could withstand his coming in wrath. For these reasons, then, the war is understood to be presented as a drama. Perhaps it also shows that this universe is brought to its end not spontaneously or by chance, but [deliberately?] and under divine [governance?].

And from his mouth comes a sharp two-edged sword, so that with it he may strike the nations, and he will shepherd them with an iron rod. And he treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. And on his garment and on his thigh he has a name written: King of kings and Lord of lords.

The sword darting from his mouth shows that punishment is brought upon the ungodly and sinners by divine command. The sword is two-edged because the punishments that come from God upon those who despise him proceed from both sides, from wrath and from mercy. It is sharp because it does its work without delay. Now the prophet has the sword girded on the thigh, that is, on the humanity of the Lord Jesus Christ and God. For it is as man that he both asks and receives, not as the one [co-eternal?] with God the Father, since all that belongs to the Father belongs without reserve to the Son as well. He receives through the iron rod, either because at the Lord's incarnation the lordship of the whole world [came?] to the Romans too; that is why public taxes were laid on all people as subjects. Since at the Lord's coming in the flesh authority over all belonged also to the iron rod, it is [not?] idly said that he strikes the nations with the rod. And he also shepherds through it, since under Constantine, emperor of the Romans, when faith in Christ had all but failed, that faith was spread decisively to every nation, as though it had come back to life. That the thigh carries the idea of human generation, as we have already said, is shown by the words, "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is reserved." So much, then, about the two-edged sword; it was not untimely, I think, nor superfluous. About shepherding with the iron rod, this is my view. With the sword he will strike, as has already been said, those who rose up in the manner of the heathen. But with the rod he will shepherd those whom he found being shepherded in the ranks of the flock, settling them in a place of green pasture and nurturing them by the water of rest. You who have been found worthy of the blessedness there will come to know these things.
With an iron rod.

When a shepherd's and [?] rod is needed to shepherd the nations, a rod of uprightness is given, able to nourish them by the water of rest and in [a pasture?]. For the flock is naturally adorned with obedience and [?] by the shepherd's care. But when they turn aside to disobedience, goaded by the insolence of demons, it is changed into an iron rod, which brings deserved [chastisement?] upon the disorder of those under it. This happens in the last time, when even the call to conversion is dismissed as superfluous, and he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God. The iron rod is not for shepherding; it shatters those whose life is of clay and who are ready to be smashed. Why, then, is the shepherding role given to it here? Not without purpose, I think, but because shepherding also involves fighting off wild beasts. For this an iron rod is needed, which brings deserved destruction on those who resist. "He treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God." Who else but Christ? For through the judgment and requital of the wicked he fulfills the Father's will. "For the Father judges no one," in the Lord's own words, "but has given all judgment to the Son." And for what reason? Because the Son, through his incarnation, passed through the whole of human weakness and its proneness to change for the worse, he brings the punishment in [?]. For if it were equal to the transgression, who could endure it? Or this too belongs to his utmost love for humankind and compassion: that he does not deal with us according to our iniquities, nor repay us according to our wrongdoings.
And on his garment and on his thigh he has.

By the garment he means to hint at the flesh, as also through Isaiah when he says, "Why are your garments red?" By the thigh he means the nature of the flesh, as truly human and not merely in appearance, for in Scripture the thigh is taken to represent this. The aim of the passage, then, is to show that God the Word, who was united hypostatically to human nature and underwent birth in the flesh from the holy Virgin, is no less Almighty, as ruler of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth. And to him, as the one who appeared in the flesh, it is given to reign over kings and to be lord over lords. The kings are those who have reigned over the passions; the lords are those who have held sway and power over sin with the help of Christ himself. With him they will also reign together forever in the age to come, without any successor.

And I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying to all the birds that fly in midheaven, "Come, gather for the great supper of God, so that you may eat the flesh of kings, and the flesh of commanders, and the flesh of the mighty, and the flesh of horses and of those who sit on them, and the flesh of all, both free and slave, both small and great." And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to make war against the one sitting on the horse and against his army.

We have said before that divine things are immaterial and can be grasped by the mind alone, and so [?] lead to learning those who have not been prepared beforehand [?]; for what is unknown is naturally tracked down through what is similar and already known. In keeping with this, the present passage proceeds in the same way. It depicts the change of corruptible things and their transformation into incorruption, and the allotment to each according to the merit of his works, in terms of military armament and preparation. That is why he introduces an angel standing in the sun: an angel carrying out the divine command in full view, and declaring and proclaiming the things of salvation as in the light. And since the divine dispositions have been called [light?], as Amos [and?] Isaiah says, "For your commands are light upon the earth," [?] he supposes that [?] used this figure, because the one who represented the divine command as an angel had nothing among visible things more radiant to name. And he entrusts him with the role of a herald of war, using a more forceful progression of events. This is what the loud voice with its cry is meant to convey. Those in midheaven he describes as, so to speak, the souls of the saints, who, rising up from earthbound things, go up into the air to meet the Lord, according to the great Paul. And the prophet Isaiah says, "Who are these that fly like flocks, and like the young of eagles?" [?] a nestling differs in no way from a bird. And they are summoned, as to a joyful supper, to the [victory?] over the ungodly, won without a battle.
Come, gather for the supper.

He calls the confrontation between the righteous and sinners a supper, not a war. And so it is, for who is able to stand against the mighty one? And if it is also called a war, we say it is so called with regard to the sinners' onslaught, not to what actually takes place. It is called a supper above all because of the antecedent will of God, which is also called his good pleasure and the thrice-longed-for supper: that all people be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. That is the antecedent will. After this comes the consequent: that those who have brought punishment on themselves by their zeal for impure works should also receive what their zeal deserves. That he is accustomed to call the Father's will food is clear from where he himself says, "My food is to do the will of my Father in heaven." This is what is here named the supper of God: that each person receives what he desired, whether it deserves honor or blame. And those invited eat the flesh of kings. "Flesh" means that the banqueters rejoice over the annihilation and vain striving of the kings' authority in this present life. Likewise with the commanders, who enjoyed less prosperity than kings. And the flesh of the mighty, and of horses and riders and [?], and of free and slave, small and great. "Flesh" is the substance that came to them by chance in this life [?], with which they also ran the double course of their life. These pursuits [are consigned?] to annihilation when they are set beside and compared with those who were called from midheaven to the feast. That is why it is said, "The desire of the sinner will perish": the pursuits to which they were heartily attached end in nothingness. "For he who sows to the Spirit," he says, "will find life," "but he who [sows to the flesh will reap] corruption." Horses and riders, free and slave, small and great: by horses he means those mad for women, or those subordinate in wickedness, or both. By riders he means those who [excel?] in vice. He made this clear further on, saying: by the free and the great, those who sin with authority; by the slaves and the small, those who offend less, whether by [intention?], or by age, or through weakness.
So that you may eat the flesh of kings.

He calls food the requital for what has been lived, according to desert, which [?] is wont to produce in those who have not been carried off with them. By the flesh of kings and commanders and the mighty and horses and riders he speaks figuratively of the things to which they were passionately attached with all their zeal, thinking that these alone were the substance of human life. These things would be consigned to annihilation by the festive arrival of the incorruptible life.

ANOTHER INTERPRETATION, from the works of Andrew. The eating of the flesh signifies the annihilation of all fleshly things and the disappearance of earthly titles of rule. He mentions horses not because they will rise again; by them he hints either at those subordinate in wickedness, or at both; and by the riders he hints at those preeminent in vice. He made this clear further on, saying "of free and slave, great and small": by the free and the great, those who sin more with authority; by the slaves and the small, those who offend less, whether by intention, by age, or by weakness.
And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies, and so on.

In the case of the [alliance?] with the devil and the Antichrist, and of those who serve the devil in the wars against him, he speaks in the plural, going through a list of kings and the armies under them, because sin is divided in many ways and has many minds. And yet how small this is when compared with the multitude of angels and of those people who live like angels! But in the case of those with Christ, whom he describes as mounted on a horse, he refers to the multitude following him in the singular, saying "army." He is on a horse because of his royalty and the swiftness of his onset.
