And he speaks of his followers in the singular, "with his army," because of the oneness of their will and mind toward God the Word, and of the way they please him and act rightly.
On the Antichrist and those cast with him into Gehenna.

And the beast was seized, and with it the false prophet who had performed the signs in its presence, by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. And the rest were killed by the sword of the one sitting on the horse, the sword that came out of his mouth; and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.

Once the preparations for war have been announced, the end of the war is brought on while the clash is still in suspense, when he says, "And the beast was seized." He does this not without purpose, but because he is speaking concisely.

Of those before us, some have taken the beast to be the devil, others the Antichrist. We too have spoken about this. The false prophet is the one whom the devil [sets up], on the model of John the Baptist and in imitation of Christ's true coming, to prepare the way for the Antichrist. For [it is the way of] falsehood to [?] counterfeit the truth. So by portentous signs, as forerunner [?] of the Antichrist, he deceived these people. [Marked?] with the token of the sign, and bowing down before the image of the devil, which is none other than the Antichrist, they placed themselves in the devil's portion. For just as Jesus Christ, who is God, is called the image of the invisible God through his divine-human hypostasis, so too the one who stands in for the devil, who is invisible in essence, will by his activity in a visible [?] hypostasis be called [a phantom] and an image.

It belongs to the highest justice that each should receive according to his works. So the incorporeal ones are the devil, whom he also calls a beast because he shows nothing gentle but is full of savagery, and the false prophet. Some have also taken this false prophet to be the Antichrist, who presents the phantom of a body but does not truly put one on; they hold that he is some demon who ranks second after the devil. The incorporeal ones, then, receive fire [?], something of fire that is able to burn; that is why [?] it is likened to what among us is called sulfur (sic). These, then, are judged worthy of such a sentence. But the rest, the men who made up their war host, pay the penalty by death. For death has no effect on Satan, whose nature is simple, nor again on the Antichrist, since we know death to be the dissolution of what is composite. Therefore, since they are simple in essence and not subject by nature to death, they will receive for their punishment the fire that is [?]. The sword from the mouth is the command [?], which is effective and sharper than any two-edged sword; by it they were subjected to natural death and to the punishments of Hades.
And the rest were killed.

He says that the composite nature is "killed" when, after its dissolution, it becomes idle and inactive in its wicked practices. But the simple and uncompounded nature knows no such thing; even after condemnation it does not abandon its habits, since the things toward which it inclined have become one with its very essence.
And all the birds were gorged.

It has already been said that by birds he means the souls that travel through the air. He knows that these too, as it were, have their fill when the two kinds of deeds, the earnest and the worthless, are set side by side. As God also says through Isaiah, "You have become a surfeit [?] to me." So as there, here too every fleshly MOVEMENT is cloying and burdensome to the saints.
How Satan was bound from the coming of Christ until the consummation; and on the thousand years.

And I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. He seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world, and bound him for a thousand years. He threw him into the abyss, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he would deceive the nations no more until the thousand years were completed. After this he must be released for a short time.

Andrew. Here he describes the overthrow of the devil that took place at the Lord's passion. In it Christ our God, who is stronger than he, bound the one who was thought to be strong, rescued us, his spoils, out of his hands, and condemned him to the abyss. This is shown by the demons who begged him not to send them into the abyss. The proof that he has been bound is the disappearance of idolatry, the destruction of idol temples, the end of the offerings on the altars, and the knowledge of the divine will throughout the world. The great Justin says that at Christ's first coming the devil learned that he had been condemned to the abyss and to the Gehenna of fire. So, I think, these words can also be understood as Christ's sentence against the devil. He says that an angel carries out this sentence to show that the devil is weaker in power even than the ministering powers, and that his boldness against the dominion that rules all things is in vain.

Arethas, from the same. By the key he means the secure custody of the condemned, from which there is no way out; by the abyss, that which offers no end and so no escape; and by the chain, the power that holds wickedness in check. It is not reasonable to take the thousand as exactly that number, for we suppose that the number thousand signifies either a great many or completeness. So whether the thousand years are the time from Christ's coming until the arrival of the Antichrist, or ten times a hundred, or even fewer than these, it is not for us to know precisely, since it is not given to mortal nature to know the times or seasons which the Father has fixed by his own authority.
After this he must be released for a short time.

A short time — what time is that? It is the time of the Antichrist's coming, which he has cut down to a short span because the sufferings of those afflicted for Christ's sake will be so severe and almost unforeseen [?]. Of this time the Savior also says in the Gospels that there will be tribulation such as has not been since the beginning of the world. That is why he also says that those days will be cut short for the sake of the elect.
On the thrones prepared for those who kept the confession of Christ.

And I saw thrones, and they sat on them, and judgment was given to them. And I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and who had not worshipped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or on their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for the thousand years.

He says that he sees the holy apostles, through whom the nations, made wise by the word of their teaching, came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. About the thousand years enough has been said. These holy apostles, then, will sit, as the Lord's promise says, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, that is, condemning them. For when people of the same race are set side by side and a difference between worse and better is seen among them, those held fast by the worse deserve no ordinary punishment, because they did not strive to match the success of their kinsmen. 'Judgment was given to them,' then, means that they were given to condemn, since the Israelites not only refused to follow Christ their benefactor as the prophetic oracles directed, but even went directly against them. They are condemned also because of the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, that is, for their faith in God, who suffered death by the sword. Or 'being beheaded' may also be taken figuratively of those who have put to death their members that are on earth.
And they did not receive the mark.

By the mark he means a distinguishing sign, in the sense in which it is said with reference to Christ: 'The light of your face, Lord, has been marked upon us.' For as there light is stamped upon the face as the sign of those dear to God, so on the ungodly shamelessness is engraved on their foreheads, as they show openly and without restraint what sort of people they are. And to make this more emphatic, they confirmed the sign by their outrageous deeds, for the hand hints at action, just as the foot does at intention. So it is said, 'Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner shake me.' Since, then, these were not caught, being stamped by the evil one neither through shamelessness nor through deeds, they rightly lived and reigned with Christ until the end of the age. For, as we see, they are venerated by faithful emperors and rulers, and they display their God-given grace against every bodily illness and demonic activity. Because, he says, they did not worship the beast and its image, they therefore lived, that is, they performed the works of the living, namely miracles. By the beast, the image of the beast and the dragon he means the devil, the Antichrist and the false prophet.
What the first resurrection is, and what the second death is.

The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were completed. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.

He calls 'dead' those who have remained in unbelief. For just as divine Scripture teaches us of two lives, so it teaches us also of two deaths, or mortifications. The first life is the temporary and fleshly one that followed the transgression of the commandment; the other is the eternal life promised to those who keep the divine commandments. Likewise there are two deaths: the one fleshly and temporary, the other brought upon us in the age to come as the penalty for sins, endless and everlasting, which is the Gehenna of fire. Indeed, we also recognize differences among the dead. Some are to be shunned; of these the prophet says, 'The dead shall not see life.' Others are praiseworthy: those who for Christ's sake put to death the pleasure-seeking deeds of the body, carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus. The second resurrection is the general resurrection of bodies, and for the wicked that resurrection becomes the beginning of the punishment to come. But over those blessed with the first resurrection the second death, which hands sinners over from their sin to punishment, has no power; rather, they will be priests of God and of Christ. The thousand does not mean the hundred multiplied by ten. Rather, since ten is the first perfect number, made up of units, and ten in turn by a further tenfold step produced a hundred, and this again multiplied by ten made up the sum of a thousand, advancing from the perfect to the more perfect, he fittingly assigned to the more-than-perfect God the perfection of his dwelling together with human beings. It is not that it is exactly that many in number; rather, through the perfect number he shows that whatever span of time passes while Christ dwells with humankind could never be counted as imperfect.
On Gog and Magog.

When the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison and will go out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea. And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. And fire came down from heaven from God and consumed them. And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet are as well. And they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
A thousand years.

He means the time from the coming of Christ until the Antichrist. Once the devil is released, he then introduces the nations and the regions of the world in which he will display his customary deceit, and tells by whom and against whom, as leaders, this war will be waged. By nations he means those easily deceived; by places, the regions under heaven, which he calls the four corners of the earth, so naming the four quarters of the inhabited world, which take their names from the courses of the sun and from their relation to certain stars. Since these, then, are the nations with whom the war is to be joined, and this is the region, he now also introduces the leaders, Gog and Magog, as a war-chief, whom Ezekiel too prophesies will come in the last time with a heavy force. But Ezekiel speaks of an attack on Jerusalem, whereas the present Revelation speaks of the desolation of the whole world. Some have said that these are Scythian nations of the far north, which have often migrated from their own lands, destroying those they attacked and as often being destroyed themselves; that Scythopolis in Palestine was named after their incursion; that a certain contingent of Goths in parts of Asia, a military body, is called by this name, as are the Taifali and the Gothograeci, whom we commonly call Hunnic peoples; and that they are more powerful and warlike than any earthly kingdom, but are restrained by the divine hand from ruling the world until the devil is released, as is foretold here. Others interpret Gog from the Hebrew language as 'one who gathers' or 'gathering', and Magog as 'exalted'. So both the gathering and the exalting show that the invasion of this nation brings a great and arrogant evil upon those it attacks, as we have already said. As for the period of a thousand years mentioned above, some have taken it, I do not know how, to be the three and a half years from Christ's baptism to his ascension into heaven, after which they supposed the devil was released. Others have said that after six thousand years are completed, the first resurrection of the dead is granted to the saints alone, so that in this very land where they displayed their endurance they may enjoy delights and glory for a thousand years, and that after this comes the general resurrection, not of the righteous only but of sinners as well. That the Church has accepted none of these views hardly needs to be said. We, then, hearing the Lord say to the Sadducees that the righteous will be like the angels of God in heaven, and the Apostle say, 'The kingdom of God is not food and drink,' have taken the thousand years to be the time of the preaching of the gospel. For, as was written above, the thousand need not be understood as exactly that number. Neither does the saying in the Song, 'A man will give a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit,' and again, 'The thousand are for Solomon, and the two hundred for those who keep its fruit,' indicate this exact number, but abundance and perfection in bearing fruit; just as here too the fruit-bearing of faith in its perfection is signified. After this the son of perdition, the man of unrighteousness, will come, so that all who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in unrighteousness may be judged, as the Apostle says, and as the Lord's saying declares: 'I have come in my Father's name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive.' Then, as has been said, Satan, released from his prison, will deceive all the nations and will stir up Gog and Magog to war for the desolation of the world.
Their number is like the sand of the sea.

Like wild beasts from their lairs, he says, so these, led out of their own lands by the devil and his demons as their generals, will spread out over the earth and will lay waste the camp of the saints and the beloved city, that is, the Church everywhere, by encircling and surrounding it. But not for long: whether by visible fire, as with the two captains of fifty in the time of Elijah, or by the glorious coming of Christ, by the breath of his mouth, which by its nature acts upon matter like a purifying fire, he will consume both the ungodly themselves and their general, the devil.
On the one seated on the throne, and on the general resurrection and judgment.

And I saw a great white throne and the one seated on it, from whose face earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, small and great, standing before the throne, and books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to their works. And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, and death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one according to their works. And death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. And anyone who was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire.

The throne is white because every deed of the saints, in whom God is enthroned, is untouched by the blackness of sins committed in darkness. It is great because the one seated upon it is great, of whom David also sang, 'Great is our Lord.'
From whose face the earth fled.

The flight of heaven and earth does not signify a change of place — for where would they go? — but a flight from corruption to incorruption, a transformation, and the final coming of the Lord, at which this mortal body of ours puts on incorruption and the face of the earth will be renewed.
And I saw the dead.

By 'the dead' he means either all people, since they have undergone the death of the body, or those who have been made dead by their trespasses. The great and the small are either those who are so in age, or those who did the works of death to a greater or lesser degree and will be punished in proportion to their deeds; or else the great are the righteous, and the small and worthless are the sinners, because of the meanness of their soul's works.
And the sea gave up the dead who were in it.

He sets out these things to explain how the last, universal resurrection will come about. For some, who do not believe it will happen, say that it cannot take place in the same bodies, since these perished ages ago and passed into non-existence. Correcting this, the text now says that just as bodies in the beginning came from non-being into being, not by chance but from the four elements — water, fire, air and earth — so, having been dissolved back into these, they will reasonably be composed again from them. Since this is so, and the original parts come together again to constitute human beings, he therefore says that the sea, that is, the watery substance, pours out the moisture that had passed into it. By Death he means the earthy substance, since it is said of it, 'You brought me down into the dust of death' — and who with any sense does not know that dust is earth? By Hades he means the air, because it has no visible form on account of the thinness of its substance; and likewise also fire. He calls it Hades because it casts whatever it comes upon into invisibility and obscurity.
And death and Hades.
By death and Hades he means those who have done deeds deserving punishment, since they make up the company of the second death.
On the new heaven and earth, and on the Jerusalem above.

And I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from heaven saying, 'See, the dwelling of God is with human beings. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them. Every tear will vanish from their eyes. Death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain will be any more, for the former things have passed away.'

He says this not to indicate that creation ceases to exist, but that it is renewed for the better. This the divine psalmist David also foretold in his song, that all things will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak will be rolled up and changed. For what has grown old, when it is renewed, undergoes not the destruction of its substance but the removal of its age and wrinkles. Note that in saying of heaven and earth that they 'passed away', he means, as it were, not that they went into non-being but that they changed. Nothing that passes from one state into another has thereby utterly perished; rather, by passing from the one to the other it has been reshaped, casting off the features of what it left behind and taking on those of what it passed into.
Andrew. About the sea he says that the sea is no more. For what need will there be of a sea, when people no longer need to sail on it, or to obtain through it the goods grown in lands lying far away?
And the sea was no more.

If this perceptible world is nothing other than the system and compound of heaven, earth and what lies between them, then, since heaven and earth are certainly renewed, as we have already set out, the things that make up this system will certainly not be left without a share in the renewal. Why, then, has the sea alone, being one of the natures in between, missed not only renewal but existence altogether? If someone says that, since there will be no one sailing on it, it will necessarily no longer be what it now is, fair enough; but to let it pass into complete non-existence would be the work of one who carries out the renewal only by half. What, then, can be said to this? Surely this: since the ancestor of God likened the present world to a sea, he necessarily — so that no one would attribute to the renewed heaven and earth the turmoil that belongs to them — signified and removed that turmoil by the complete disappearance of the sea, following David's figurative language, since at the renewal the sea too will be gone.
And the holy city, the new Jerusalem.

Of old, he says, Jerusalem was considered the most holy dwelling, in which the temple and all the mysteries of the knowledge of God were stored up. That it is now new is not unreasonable, since at the Lord's coming those things became obsolete through age. It was necessary, then, that at the renewal of all things a new Jerusalem should appear, coming down from heaven, from where the Renewer, the Lord Jesus Christ, came. So it is called a new Jerusalem for this reason; a city, because it will be the dwelling place of all angels and human beings; and prepared by God, for what saving good can anyone achieve for himself without sharing in God's help? He has adorned it figuratively and magnificently as a bride, so that from things described in terms of the senses we may lead our mind on to the spiritual blessedness and life of the saints.
And God himself will be with them.

The Apostle made this clearer when he said, 'Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.' In this tabernacle not made with hands, then, there will be no weeping or tears, which belong to this perishable life, nor pain — I mean the hardship the saints endured in this wretched life. In that life to come, since grief, pain and sighing have fled away, as from what is incorruptible, all these things are idle and superfluous.
For the former things have passed away.

The former things — those subjected to corruption since Adam's transgression, whether the troubles and pains that come upon those dear to God because of their virtue, or those that follow the God-forsaken because of their arrogance and folly — have all passed away.
On what was said by the one who was seen seated on the throne.

And he who sat on the throne said, "Behold, I make all things new." And he says to me, "Write, for these words of God are faithful and true." And he said to me, "I have become the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the one who thirsts I will give from the spring of the water of life freely. The one who conquers, I will give him these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly and the faithless and sinners and the abominable, and murderers, and fornicators, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all who are false, their portion is in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death."
The throne of God is those who by their virtues have made themselves his chariot. Of them the one who rides upon them said, "I will dwell in them and walk among them."
For these words of God are faithful and true.

"Do not think, John," he says, "that because the things being made new are changed so greatly, what is told you is some extravagant fantasy and will turn out false. They are so true that I charge you to set them down in writing, so that it may never be forgotten that they will come to pass." For the words are true and faithful, since they are spoken by the very Truth itself. Christ is the beginning and the end, who also ascribed to himself the Alpha and the Omega: the beginning, as first by reason of his divinity; the end, as extending his providence from the first creation of the incorporeal beings to the last of humankind. To the one who thirsts is given the promise of the spring of the water of life, but it is to one who thirsts for righteousness, as Christ also says: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled." The relief of thirst is promised from the spring of the water of life, and that spring is none other than Christ. The supply of such water is promised freely, even though elsewhere he says that the way leading to life is found with toil and much violence. What then does "freely" hint at here? Perhaps that temporal things cannot be measured against everlasting ones, about which Paul also says, "For the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us." "But as for the cowardly and the faithless," and so on.

He calls cowardly those who through willing weakness have sunk to the pleasures of the present age, since they will choose to undertake nothing manly; in this way he holds in dishonor the limp queasiness of the effeminate. "All who are false" he says, and not "liars," because this word also includes activity concerned with the things done. For on what will the liar spend his zeal, if not on false things and on what corrupts natural beauty with deceptive enticements?
Concerning the angel who showed him the city of the saints and its wall, and measured it together with its gates.

And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues came and spoke with me, saying, "Come, I will show you the woman, the bride of the Lamb." And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain. And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God; and its radiance was like a most precious stone, like a jasper stone, clear as crystal; and it had a great and high wall.

Those whom he earlier presented as avengers he now presents, on the contrary, as physicians, who at one time set about cutting and at another sprinkle on soothing remedies. For the one who then brought the plague on those who deserved it now displays the blessedness of the Church of the saints. By "the last plagues" he does not mean plagues last in time, but those able to inflict harm at its most severe. He rightly calls the woman "the bride of the Lamb." For when Christ was slain as a lamb, he then took her as his bride with his own blood. Just as the woman was fashioned by the removal of the rib while Adam slept, so too when Christ willingly fell asleep in death on the cross, the Church, brought into being by the outpouring of blood from his side, was joined to him who suffered for us.
And he carried me away in the spirit.

"In the spirit" is well said. For no human mind is raised up without spiritual grace so as to come to comprehend the glory of the saints. And fittingly the Church, the supramundane life and citizenship of the saints, was shown on a great and high mountain. For among them there is nothing low, humble or groveling; all things are lofty and exalted.
And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven.

The evangelist has seen the worship of the law coming down out of the obscurity of riddles. This is not a descent from place to place, since even the parable in the Gospels, which introduces someone going down from Jerusalem, does not imply a descent in place but a change in the knowledge of divine doctrines. Here, since the God of glory is also involved, the descent is to nothing lowly; it is nothing other than the disclosure of what was obscure and hidden, brought about not by human impulse, as in the [parable?] [?], but by the inclination of God.
And its radiance.

He calls Christ the radiance. The radiance is likened to a most precious stone, because the wall of the Jerusalem from heaven is also compared to a jasper stone. Jasper is green, displaying the life-bearing and life-giving character of Christ's providence, whose enclosure is the wall made of jasper, which is visible to humans as something perceptible to the senses. So the wall was seen to be made of jasper stone because of the greenness of its color; for green growth comes first in all earthly food. Moreover the jasper, being clear as crystal, hints at the purity and blamelessness of what the wall encloses. He also says it is high and great. For the Most High is not pleased to dwell among the lowly and groveling, but among those whose thoughts are lofty and cleave to heavenly dignity. The appearance of the radiance is compared to a most precious stone, yet he does not show what its form is like, since the most divine things, which are not subject to the senses, cannot by nature be represented by things mortal and incorruptible [?].

It had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names inscribed, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel: on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

None of these is a difficult idea that needs to be drawn out into clarity. The number plainly indicates the apostles of the Lord, and the function of the gates, as leading into the treasury of life, represents his apostles, through whom the nations were brought into the treasury of Christ. They place twelve angels at the gates, taking them to be the apostles, through whom our entrance and our access to the Father has been brought about, with the cooperation of an equal number of the foremost angels, and especially of those assigned to the oversight of the twelve tribes of Israel, by the kinship established in holiness. And very fittingly so: for if we believe that an angel accompanies each of the faithful, it follows much more that angels should be understood to work together in the preaching of the gospel with the foundations of the Church and the sowers of the gospel word.
And names inscribed.

In the worship of Moses it was commanded that the names of the heads of the tribes be written on the ephod. But in the covenant of the Lord Jesus, the names of the new Israel are on the gates, that is, on those who lead in, of whom it is also said, "I will declare your name to my brothers." By "name" he means the mystery of faith in Christ, which he promises to set forth not in secret silence but in plain view of all. The gates correspond to the tribes descended from Jacob, because not everything of the old covenant has been abolished by faith in Christ, but only so far as childish things are weaker than the state of manhood.
Which are the names of the twelve tribes of Israel.

Having called the faithful Israel, he dwells also on the number of their fullness. For he speaks of twelve tribes, which are evidently divided by threes according to the fourfold shape of the world, and are equal in number to the arms of the sign of the cross multiplied three times; and having marked out the separate portions, he describes each of them as having been allotted its entrance through three gates in turn. For no one can grow great [?] in initiation into the crucified Lord without having been granted entrance by the supremely divine Trinity. For the divine apostles divided among themselves all the ends of the world, preached the consubstantial Trinity to the nations, and baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
And on them the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

He has already, and rightly, made it clear that his purpose is to indicate the twelve apostles, whom he calls both gates and foundations: foundations, because they laid the groundwork of faith in Christ; gates, because through them, that is, through their preaching, one now finds entrance into faith in Christ.

And the one who spoke with me had a measure, a golden reed, to measure the city and its gates and its wall. And the city lies foursquare, its length the same as its breadth. And he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand stadia; its length and breadth and height are equal. And he measured its wall, a hundred and forty-four cubits, by a human measure, which is an angel's. And the material of its wall was jasper.

The reed with which he measured the holy city was a surveyor's rod. It was golden because of the dignity of the angel measuring and of the city being measured. These things were seen in human form, because otherwise it was not possible for them to be seen, being divine as they are by nature. By the city he means the mystery of Christ, into which the gates have been appointed to lead, because faith in Christ is made known through preaching.
And the city lies foursquare.

The shape of the wall and of the city is square, and the gates number twelve. For the city, being square, was divided along its diameters by the sign of the cross, and from this the four sides were each granted entrance through three gates [?], as we have already set out.
Twelve thousand stadia.

The stadia are equal in number to the blessed apostles, since the inheritance laid up there is the fruit of their preaching. It is equal in measure in every dimension, and the virtues of the godly life exist in due proportion, according to the divine Paul, who knew how to be brought low and to abound, to be full and to be hungry. This number too gives an indication of the blessed apostles: for twelve multiplied by itself makes a hundred and forty-four. Having called the measure of a hundred and forty-four cubits a human measure, he adds that this measure is an angel's, even if it is expressed in cubits as humans reckon. But let no one suppose that the one who measured was a man; he was an angel who measured in a human way, and not angelically, by simple apprehension and understanding.
And the material of its wall was jasper.

By "material" he means the building, that is to say, the zeal and exactness of the apostles concerning their preaching. The greenish jasper hints at the course of the gospel, which is ever green and keeps the preaching unfading.

And the city was pure gold, like pure glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every precious stone. The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald, the fifth sardonyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls.

The ever-living preaching leads to a dwelling in blessed and unending life. This city, that is, this dwelling, is compared to pure gold, and by its wondrous transparency is likened to pure glass. "The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every stone": by precious stones he portrays the virtues of the divine apostles, whom he also calls the foundations of the city. Though there are twelve stones on the high priest's breastplate, he places only eight of them in the foundations and changes the other four, so that from these may appear both the harmony of the old covenant with the new, and how far the new, and those who shone in it, surpass the old. The apostles, then, are adorned with every virtue that the stones display.
1. The first, jasper.

By the jasper, which is green in color like the emerald, it is likely that Peter, the chief of the apostles, is indicated. Before the Lord's passion he was ever fresh and youthful in all the Lord's questions to him, yet at his teacher's passion he was caught and overcome by the green pallor of fear, so far as to go on to denial. But being restored again for the better to the same evergreen vigor, he himself was freed by streams of tears from the thirst that brings death, and he made us dwell in a green pasture through the water of saving baptism.
2. The second, sapphire.

This stone, of the color called kalainos, which some call venetos, is likened to the color of heaven, that is, to the depth of the air that lies in front of the heavenly body, if indeed that body is perceptible to the senses and is not, as the Stagirite holds, made of the nature of some fifth body. But even if that is so, and our sense of sight cannot make out precisely what is very far off because of what lies in front of it like a curtain, he nonetheless attempts the color by likening the second foundation to sapphire. This sapphire is likened to the heavenly body, and how this is so has been said. They say that the lapis lazuli color is also made from this sapphire. To this stone the blessed Paul is justly likened, who was caught up to the third heaven and from there draws those who obey him.
3. The third, chalcedony.

This stone does not appear on the priestly breastplate; the carbuncle does, and it is not listed here. One must therefore consider whether they perhaps called the carbuncle by this name. The carbuncle is the blessed Andrew, who in the gloom of life under the law found by his own light the Messiah who was being sought, and told of him and made him known to those close to him. At the same time, it must also be considered whether the chalcedony is another stone of a color similar to the carbuncle, so called because it is found together with precious stones at the strait of Chalcedon, above Chrysopolis, near the Clashing Rocks, in the desolate places beyond them, where the shores are made useless by reefs and crags, as has been reported by those who compiled the ancestral history of the Bithynians.
4. The fourth, emerald.

By the emerald, which displays a leek-green color and takes from it its translucence and beauty, we think the preaching of John the Evangelist is indicated, who with divine oil brightens the dejection that comes upon us from sin.
5. The fifth, sardonyx.

We have taken James the son of Zebedee to be represented by this. For as this stone holds within it a blood-red hue, so this blessed man, at the very beginning of the bright, white and divine preaching, was sent on by the path of blood after Christ his teacher to the heavenly, ever-living inheritance, full of light.
6. The sixth, carnelian.

This stone, fiery red in color, points to Philip by the fervor of his devotion to Christ. For as this stone has the power to heal fleshly swellings and wounds from iron, so too it takes on the beauty of Philip's virtue.
7. The seventh, chrysolite.

Bartholomew is likened to the precious chrysolite. He too gleams with the golden splendors of the virtues, yet he does not suffer gold's misfortune of melting, but is rich in a stony firmness that remains steadfast in preaching.
8. The eighth, beryl.

Thomas is likened to this stone, whose color is like the sea and tinged with hyacinth, suggesting his wavering in faith, and above all the great distance of his apostolic mission, which was carried out as far as the Indians, and by sea.
9. The ninth, topaz.

The topaz, which is red and like a carbuncle in appearance and gives off a white juice that relieves those with diseased eyes, will have the divine Matthew likened to it. He was fired with divine zeal, so as to record God's becoming human, even to flesh and blood and being nursed with milk. By these things he brought those blind in heart and infantile in faith, I mean those being schooled by life under the law, up to the state of manhood in Christ.
10. The tenth, chrysoprase.

To this stone is assigned Thaddaeus, who preached the faith of Christ to Abgar, king of Edessa. That faith is gold in appearance and therefore precious in itself, yet it does not lack the leek-green either, whether the Revelation is hinting at the deadening of the passions through faith in Christ, or at its ever-living quality through the evergreen leek-green color.
11. The eleventh, jacinth.

To this stone, which is dark blue in color, that is, the color of the air, Simon the Zealot is likened. He belonged to the ever-roaming [?] band of the Zealots, and was therefore airy and windblown in mind; but nevertheless, through the knowledge of the truth, though late, he redirected his zeal to what is best.
12. The twelfth, amethyst.

This stone, which appears fiery in color, will fittingly be assigned to Matthias, who shared with the eleven the fiery dew of the vision that flowed down from heaven, on account of which the foolish suspected them of being overcome by drunkenness, though they were above all sobriety. For this reason he was also given the amethyst, because it is widely said that whoever wears the amethyst is not overcome by drunkenness. Each of the gates was made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass. And I saw no temple in it, for God the Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. And the city has no need of the sun or the moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gave it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. And the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory and honor into it. And its gates will never be shut by day, for there will be no night there. And they will bring the glory and the honor of the nations into it, that they may enter. And nothing common, and nothing that practices abomination and falsehood, will ever enter it, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life.

He likens the holy apostles to pearls, each of whom displays something wondrous, not only in the whiteness of his life but also in bringing amazement through the greatness and loftiness of his undertakings. The street of the city, that is, the open and habitable space of the blessed dwelling, he likened to gold.
And the city has no need of the sun or the moon.
Since all things perceptible to the senses have become unnecessary, the sun and moon too have fittingly become unnecessary, since everything in that state will then be illumined spiritually.
For there will be no night there.

Moreover, there is no night there, the time when safety is secured by bars and bolts, because there too the divine gates, which we have said are the apostles, will be at work in initiating the more perfect. For since it is always day, when the works of light will be done, how could the idleness of night slip in there, when there is no night at all? The expression has two meanings. Either it means that there will be peace and security, so that there is no need to guard the city by shutting the gates; or it means that there too the divine gates of the apostolic teaching stand open to all, for the instruction of the more perfect. There will be both day and night there, for night will be the portion of sinners.
And they will bring the glory and the honor.

Those who have overcome earthly passions will bring glory to God, who helps them. For none of the good things humans achieve could come about without divine aid. Those whom he earlier called kings of the earth he here calls the ones who bring in the glory and honor of the nations. What does he set forth by this? Either that those who have wrestled down the passions that wallow in the mire of the earth have, by their own example, opened the way into the Jerusalem above to the other nations as well, and that example is glory and honor; or that this contributed to the glory and honor of the nations.

Concerning the pure river that was seen flowing from the throne. And he showed me a pure river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of its street. And on either side of the river was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit each month; and the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. And there will be no curse there any more. And the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him, and they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And there will be no night there, and they have no need of a lamp or the light of the sun, for the Lord God gives them light; and they will reign forever and ever.

We know that a river does two kinds of good: it relieves thirst and it washes away dirt. The life lived according to Christ's gospel proclamation is full of both. It relieved the thirst of the prophets who came before Christ's coming, who said, "Our [?] has thirsted for you." It also purifies those who are washed in divine baptism. That the Evangelist means the river to point to baptism, he gives a sure pledge here: he states that it proceeds from the throne of the Lamb and flows through the middle of the street, that is, of the gospel proclamation. For, as the Lord said, no one can enter the heavenly Jerusalem without being born again from above through water and the Spirit.
And on either side of the river.

On either side of the gospel proclamation: on this side in the present life, and on that side in the age to come. By the tree of life he means divinely inspired wisdom. The teaching of this tree, which is held according to Christ, will lead from right conduct here to blessedness. What is right conduct here? It is to practise the virtues that make us godlike fittingly and at the right time, and not to toil in vain at the wrong time, or beyond due measure, in fruitless effort. The timely practice is equal in number to those who labour, since the workers should never go beyond the right time but always fall short of it, and should carry out everything in order, doing all things in wisdom. He also says that the leaves of the tree are proclaimed, that is, made known, for the healing of the nations. What does he want to establish by this? We know that the leaf is a covering around the fruit. From this we understand that the more perfect of the works done according to God, those that shine with a crystal clearness, are set out for examination by those who are most perfect in virtue. "For the mighty will be mightily tested." But whatever has no share in the nourishing part of the fruits, and is taken only as a sign that the plant has died [?], is assigned to the healing of the nations. Once these have been brought into the service of Christ, it is pointless to examine them with precision.
And the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it.

Whoever has made himself ready, through virtues pleasing to God, to be a divine chariot, and has run without tiring toward the rest of God and of the Lamb by means of the divine teachings of the Old and New Testaments, and has been granted a divine dwelling, will himself be a citizen of the city, the heavenly Jerusalem. He will see God face to face, not in riddles, but as he was seen by the holy apostles on the holy mountain, as the great Dionysius says.
And they will reign for ever and ever.
That is, the saints will reign with Christ for the endless ages.
That Christ is the God of the prophets and the Master of all.
And he said to me, "These words are faithful and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place."

Here this blessed evangelist does what he usually does, as he also does in his Gospel, as a mark of genuineness: "And we know that his testimony is true." In the same way he sets his seal here, saying that the words have been set out as faithful and true, since they draw their trustworthiness from that source, namely from the Lord God, who is also Lord of the gift of the prophets. This is what he means by "Lord of the spirits": it is as if he said, "Lord of the prophetic gift."
On the trustworthiness of what the apostle saw.

"See, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book." I, John, am the one who saw and heard these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me. But he said to me, "Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and with your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God!"
By "those who keep" he means those who strive not to fall into the punishments described in this book, but to have no part in them through a godly [?] life.
I, John, am the one who saw and heard these things.

This too is typical of the apostle's soul. What he did in the Gospel, when he said, "He who has seen has borne witness, and his testimony is true," he does here as well, declaring that he was an eyewitness of what was prophesied. By this he confirmed what he had seen. And, as was said before, he showed both the dignity of the angel who showed him the visions and his own reverence.
How he was commanded not to seal up the Revelation but to proclaim it.

And he said to me, "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy. See, I am coming soon, and my reward is with me, to repay each one according to his work. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last."
Do not seal up, and so on.

That is, do not shut it up and keep it to yourself, but make it known to everyone. By "the time is near" he means something like this: the time when what has been said will be fulfilled is not very far off from the telling of it, as it was then [?], yet not so near that you have no need to hear these things now. So insofar as it is not yet present, there is need to hear; but insofar as it is all but present and almost already taking effect, hearing is superfluous.
Let the evildoer still do evil.
This is not an exhortation, but an exposure of each person's inclination toward whatever he wishes.
See, I am coming soon.
"Soon" is said either in comparison with the endless ages, or to encourage those who are waiting for their reward, or because it will certainly come to pass without fail and without delay.
I am the Alpha and the Omega.

It is not hard to see that by the example of the letters he indicated the beginning and the end, since he himself added these words. But the more inquisitive are left to ask why he showed this through letters and not through something else. Our answer is this. Since only those who have been honoured with reason can await such promises, he made this known in this way and not in some other. The invention of letters is evidence of this kind of workmanship. And letters, according to the Stagirite, are symbols of what is in the meaningful speech of human beings. That is why he thought fit to use speech that signifies by names [?]. So he fittingly used such workmanship and such examples for the beginning and the end.

Blessed are those who do his commandments, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and the sorcerers and the sexually immoral and the murderers and the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practises falsehood.

It has already been said that by the tree of life he means the divinely wise oracles. These are concerned in the wisest way with practical matters, and they carry [?] the authority of the saints freely, through the apostolic sayings, speeding them on their way to the heavenly Jerusalem. That the gates are the apostles has already been discussed.
Outside are the dogs and the sorcerers and the sexually immoral.

He drives out not only the shameless unbelievers, but also those who have prostituted themselves, because of their shamelessness and impurity. Of these the inspired Moses also says, "You shall not bring the wages of a prostitute or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God in payment of any vow."
CHAPTER 72.
How the Church and the Spirit in her call for the glorious appearing of Christ; and on the curse that falls on those who falsify the book as though it had no authority.

"I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you for the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, the bright morning star." The Spirit and the bride say, "Come." And let everyone who hears say, "Come." And let everyone who is thirsty come, and let anyone who wishes take the water of life as a gift.

Here too the sovereign dignity of the one who sent the angel is shown. "To testify" means to bear solemn witness, not in secret or in a corner, but in the hearing of all the churches everywhere, so that no one can wilfully plead ignorance and remain uncorrected in his wicked disposition. "I am the root and the offspring of David" is more consistently understood like this: "I am the branch that sprang from the root of David." He is called "offspring" because he sprang from David according to the flesh, so that Emmanuel is of both divinity and humanity. "Morning star" is the Lord himself: "morning" because he is the cause of all sound-mindedness, and "bright" because he enlightens everyone who comes into the world. By "Spirit" he means those who have been found worthy of the spiritual marriage, and by "bride" the Church. "And everyone who hears" points to those who have not yet been received into the flock, but are prepared to hear the divine teachings and are eager to know the Lord.

I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the seven plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are written in this book. He who testifies to these things says, "And I am coming soon." Amen. Come, Lord Jesus Christ. The grace of Christ be with all the saints. Amen.
I testify.

This stands for "I solemnly testify," that is, "I affirm." I declare trustworthy and inviolable everything set forth in the words of this prophecy. And I testify that all these plagues, which have been announced throughout this whole book, will be brought upon them without fail.
If anyone adds to them.
He solemnly charges his hearers neither to take away nor to add, and not to regard Attic constructions and dialectical syllogisms as more trustworthy or more venerable than the idioms of Scripture.
He who testifies to these things says.

He says that the one who solemnly testifies to these things speaks through him. What does he say? "Yes, I am coming soon." He broke the thread of the discourse, as he also did earlier, when he brought in Christ, the one giving the revelation, speaking in his own person in the middle of his own words. So now too, perhaps to console the one receiving these revelations, who was truly an old man, he says, "Yes, I am coming." So it should be understood as said either by the one giving the revelation or by the one receiving it, and taken to mean this: "I who testify to these things, even if I am driven by the necessary limit of life before these things come to pass, yet I too, without delay [?], say: 'Come, Jesus Christ,' at your second coming." And the words "The grace of Christ be with all the saints" are those of one confirming what has been said.
